For a tenant's assistance animal, including a trained service dog, the broader housing assistance-animal rules also apply (for example, a person moving from another state may use a provider licensed there); see Assistance Animals.

title: Unconscionable Terms
bodyText: Where the Uniform Residential Landlord and Tenant Act applies, a court that finds a lease term unconscionable when made may refuse to enforce it, enforce the rest without it, or limit it, after letting the parties present evidence. Kentucky's consumer protection act also treats unfair practices in trade as unconscionable ones; whether it reaches a residential lease is not stated.

title: Liability Waivers
bodyText: Where the Uniform Residential Landlord and Tenant Act applies, a lease may not excuse or limit the landlord's liability arising under law, or make the tenant indemnify the landlord for it; such terms are unenforceable. That is why this library's Kentucky parking, storage, insurance and utility clauses omit 'Landlord is not liable' sentences. Elsewhere, enforceability is case law.

title: Tenant Unions
bodyText: Where the Uniform Residential Landlord and Tenant Act applies, a landlord may not raise rent, cut services, or bring or threaten an eviction to retaliate because a tenant organized or joined a tenants' union or similar organization, though the landlord may still evict for unpaid rent.

title: Out-of-State Owners
bodyText: Where the Uniform Residential Landlord and Tenant Act applies, a landlord who is not a Kentucky resident may designate an in-state agent for service of process with the Secretary of State (as may a corporation not authorized to do business in Kentucky); if none is designated, or the agent cannot be served, process can be served on the Secretary of State, with a copy mailed to the landlord by registered or certified mail. The manager and owner disclosure must name an address for notices. Three general rules apply statewide, whether or not your locality has adopted the Act. First, an out-of-state limited liability company, corporation or other foreign entity must obtain a certificate of authority from the Secretary of State before transacting business in Kentucky; while it transacts business without one it may not maintain a proceeding, an eviction included, in any Kentucky court, and it owes a civil penalty of $2 for each day, though its leases stay valid and it may still defend a suit (KRS 14A.9-010(1), 14A.9-020). Owning real property "without more" is not transacting business, but the list of exceptions is not exhaustive and renting the property out may be more than owning it; that is a case-law question, so if your entity collects rent here, get advice or register before you need to file (KRS 14A.9-010(2)(i), (3)). Second, anyone, resident or not, who rents under a name other than their real name must first file a certificate of assumed name, an individual with the county clerk where the principal place of business is and an entity with the Secretary of State (and the county clerk where it has a registered agent or principal office); a violation is punished by a fine of $25 to $100, 10 to 30 days in jail, or both, and each day is a separate offense (KRS 365.015(2)-(3), 365.990(1)). These sections do not say that a missing certificate bars a suit. Third, a nonresident person or entity that has an interest in, uses or possesses real property in Kentucky can be sued in a Kentucky court on a claim arising from it, and the Secretary of State is deemed its statutory agent to receive the summons and mail it to you by certified mail (KRS 454.210(2)(f), (3)). A foreign entity that has no registered agent may also be served by registered or certified mail at its principal office (KRS 14A.4-040(2)).

title: Counterclaims and Rent Paid Into Court
bodyText: Where the Uniform Residential Landlord and Tenant Act applies, in a nonpayment eviction or rent suit the tenant may counterclaim for amounts recoverable under the lease, and the court may order the tenant to pay accrued and future rent into court; a bad-faith counterclaim lets the landlord recover attorney fees. A tenant sued for rent who is no longer in possession need not pay rent into court. In every locality, a party who appeals a forcible detainer judgment must deposit the rent owed since the case began and rent as it comes due during the appeal.

title: Unfit or Condemned Units
bodyText: No general Kentucky statute bars collecting rent after a unit is condemned. Where the state health cabinet finds lead hazards that are not fixed within 60 days, it posts the unit unfit for children under six, and a finding that a child under six is in immediate danger is cause for releasing the occupant from the lease without prejudice. Where the Uniform Residential Landlord and Tenant Act applies, the landlord's code and habitability duties and the casualty rule also apply.

title: Lead Hazards and Children
bodyText:
Beyond the federal lead paint disclosure, Kentucky's health cabinet inspects a home, or another place a child routinely spends time, where a child 72 months old or younger has an elevated blood lead level, orders the owner to remove or cover accessible lead hazards within 60 days, posts the unit unfit for young children if the owner does not, and a finding that a child under six is in immediate danger is cause for releasing the tenant from the lease without prejudice.

Under the state lead regulation, once a corrective order is issued, if the occupant then living there moves out the unit may not be let to anyone else until the order is complied with; and an owner who lets children under six occupy a posted unit after the 30-day period is fined $25 a day ("Kentucky Lead Notices and Orders").

title: Substitute Housing
bodyText: Kentucky does not require a landlord to provide alternate housing. Where the Uniform Residential Landlord and Tenant Act applies, if the landlord willfully fails to supply an essential service, the tenant may, after written notice, move to reasonable substitute housing, owe no rent for that period, and recover attorney fees, unless the tenant, family or guests caused the condition.

title: Heat and Hot Water
bodyText: Where the Uniform Residential Landlord and Tenant Act applies, the landlord must supply running water and reasonable hot water at all times and reasonable heat from October 1 to May 1, unless the building is not required to be equipped for it or the tenant controls the heat or hot water through a direct utility connection; in a single family residence the parties may agree in writing that the tenant supplies them, if the agreement is made in good faith and not to evade the landlord's duties.

title: Repair Requests in Writing
bodyText: Where the Uniform Residential Landlord and Tenant Act applies, the tenant's termination, repair-and-deduct and essential-services remedies all start with written notice to the landlord, so ask tenants to put repair requests in writing and say where to send them.

title: Quiet Possession
bodyText: Kentucky's statutes do not state a covenant of quiet enjoyment. Where the Uniform Residential Landlord and Tenant Act applies, unlawfully removing or excluding a tenant, or willfully cutting services, lets the tenant recover possession or end the lease and recover up to three months' rent and attorney fees; abusive entry has its own remedies.

title: Tenancy at Will
bodyText: Where the Uniform Residential Landlord and Tenant Act does not apply, a landlord ends a tenancy at will or by sufferance with one month's written notice requiring the tenant to leave. Where it applies, a tenancy with no fixed term is week-to-week (a roomer paying weekly) or month-to-month and ends on 7 days' written notice (weekly) or 30 days' written notice ending on a rent due date (monthly); a tenancy continuing after a written lease ends needs 10 days' notice.

title: Statutory Forms
bodyText: Kentucky's statutes supply the forms of the forcible detainer warrant and the warrant of restitution, and the Petition to Remove Persons Unlawfully Occupying Real Property for squatters; the courts publish the eviction forms (AOC-215 notice and summons, AOC-216 complaint, AOC-217 judgment, AOC-218 settlement, AOC-220 warrant for possession). No statute prescribes a form for a lease or a landlord's notice.

title: Statutory Ways a Tenant Can End a Lease Early
bodyText: In every Kentucky locality a tenant may end a lease early as a protected tenant with a domestic violence or interpersonal protective order (leases made or renewed on or after June 29, 2017; at least 30 days' written notice with a copy of the order, and a new safety concern if the order predates the lease), or be released from it when the health cabinet finds that a child under six is in immediate danger from lead hazards. Where the Uniform Residential Landlord and Tenant Act applies, a tenant may also end it for the landlord's uncured material breach, failure to deliver possession, a casualty that substantially impairs use, unlawful ouster or service cuts, or abusive entry. Federal law adds servicemember rights.

title: Displaying the U.S. Flag
bodyText: Whatever a lease or other agreement says, a tenant may display a United States flag no larger than two feet by three feet from the tenant's residence, if displayed in a manner proper under state or federal law. Any agreement against this right is void, and a landlord may not discriminate or retaliate against a tenant who properly displays the flag.

title: Nuisance Laws
bodyText: Anyone who owns, leases or subleases a house of prostitution is guilty of a nuisance that shall be enjoined and abated, and the premises may be closed for a year, unless the owner and agent tried in good faith to prevent the use; an alcohol nuisance can bar occupancy for six months; and local governments may adopt nuisance abatement ordinances with liens on the property, for which the owner is personally liable. In every locality an owner may not let junked vehicles, rubbish or excessive weeds create a public nuisance, or let a structure become unfit and unsafe for human habitation; local governments enforce these with fines and liens. No Kentucky statute found lets a court order a lease terminated or rents escrowed because of a tenant's crime.

title: Consumer Protection Act and Leases
bodyText: Kentucky's Consumer Protection Act makes unfair, false, misleading or deceptive acts in trade or commerce unlawful, and 'unfair' means unconscionable. Its private damages action belongs to a person who purchases or leases 'goods or services' primarily for personal, family or household purposes, and the statutes do not say whether a residential lease is 'goods or services'. The ban itself reaches trade in real property, so the Attorney General's enforcement can reach rental advertising and dealings even if the private damages action does not. The act lists no specific unfair practices for leases, such as blank spaces or failing to give a copy.

title: Mid-Term Rent Increases
bodyText: No Kentucky statute specifically addresses a lease term that raises rent during a fixed term; where the Uniform Residential Landlord and Tenant Act applies, the parties may include terms on rent not prohibited by the Act or other rule of law. A fixed-term lease's rent stays as written unless the lease provides for an increase. The optional Mid-Term Rent Increase clause adds one. Where the Uniform Residential Landlord and Tenant Act applies, a landlord may not raise rent to retaliate, and the statute has no safe harbor for market increases. In every locality a landlord may not retaliate against a tenant for being protected by a protective order.

title: Methamphetamine Contamination
bodyText:
When law enforcement has posted a methamphetamine contamination notice on a property, an owner who leases or rents it must disclose in writing to any potential tenant that it is contaminated and has not been decontaminated, until the property has been decontaminated and released by the Energy and Environment Cabinet. Leasing a property that has been determined to be contaminated without that written notice is a Class D felony; the felony turns on the determination, not on the posting, so give the notice whenever the property has been determined contaminated and not yet released. Removing a posted notice against the regulations is a misdemeanor.

The disclosure must reach the prospective tenant before the lease is signed; the optional lease clause records it. The Department for Public Health's regulation sets what the disclosure must say: the property address, the location used to make methamphetamine and a copy of the posted notice; you sign, date and keep it while you own the property, and on request give the tenant copies of the contamination documents you received. Only certified contractors may decontaminate, and the owner must certify the cleanup.

title: Lease Guaranties
bodyText: A guaranty of a tenant's obligations that is written on the lease, or that expressly refers to it, needs no special terms. A separate guaranty that does neither is valid only if it is in writing, signed by the guarantor, and states the guarantor's maximum total liability and the date the guaranty ends; ending on that date does not release the guarantor from obligations incurred before it, or from extensions or renewals of those obligations and related interest, fees and costs. No Kentucky statute limits a guarantor to the original lease term, so otherwise whether a guaranty covers a renewal depends on its own words. Have the guarantor sign the lease or a guaranty that names the lease. A guaranty is lawful; this library has no guaranty clause because a guaranty is the guarantor's own contract. A landlord who wants one can add their own clause after taking advice.

title: Mediation and Dispute Resolution
bodyText: No Kentucky statute requires mediation, arbitration or a pre-suit meeting in landlord-tenant disputes, but the courts are authorized and encouraged to refer parties to mediation before trial, and the Uniform Arbitration Act makes an arbitration clause in a written contract valid, enforceable and irrevocable, so either side could use one to stay a court case, including a forcible detainer case. Where the Uniform Residential Landlord and Tenant Act applies, whether such a clause is an unenforceable waiver of the tenant's rights under the Act is a question for case law. Such a clause is lawful outside the Act's localities, but this library does not offer one: it would add delay to the seven-day nonpayment route and the forcible detainer case. A landlord who wants one can add their own clause after taking advice.

title: Renting an Accessory Dwelling Unit
bodyText:
No Kentucky statute lets you build or rent an accessory dwelling unit by right, sets rental terms for one, or stops cities and counties from regulating them. Whether a lot may have one, and whether it may be rented, is for local zoning under chapter 100 KRS. The Kentucky Revised Statutes, the Kentucky Constitution, the 2025 and 2026 Acts and the state regulations on building and fire safety, public health, utilities, environment and human rights and those of the Attorney General and the Real Estate Commission contain no other state rule on them.

One state rule reaches renting one, in a county containing a consolidated local government (Jefferson County, Louisville Metro). There, for new leases initiated after June 27, 2025, an owner may not lease or let anyone occupy a single-family home, multifamily unit or accessory dwelling unit on a lot that has a single-family home in a traditional single-family zone (KRS 383.199(2)). The exception is that an owner primarily resides in one of the homes or units on that lot. The rule does not apply to a lot with only one single-family home and no accessory dwelling unit (KRS 383.199(2); "Jefferson County: Leasing in Single-Family Zones"). In the same county, a density development project with multifamily housing proposed in a traditional single-family zone goes through the zoning map amendment procedure, and accessory dwelling units do not count as multifamily housing for that rule (KRS 100.2101(1)(d), (2)).

A lease of an accessory dwelling unit otherwise follows the same landlord-tenant law as any other home. Where your city or county has adopted Kentucky's Uniform Residential Landlord and Tenant Act ("Where Kentucky's Landlord-Tenant Act Applies"), that includes keeping common areas clean and safe (KRS 383.595(1)(c)); where it has not, the older statutes (KRS 383.010 to 383.302) and the lease govern.

No state statute limits how other cities and counties zone accessory dwelling units. A local landlord-tenant ordinance still may not conflict with state law (KRS 383.198; "Local Landlord-Tenant Ordinances"). To record the lot layout, the shared areas and who lives in the main house, use "The Premises Is an Accessory Dwelling Unit" clause.

title: When a Notice Counts as Received
bodyText: Where your city or county has adopted Kentucky's Uniform Residential Landlord and Tenant Act ("Where Kentucky's Landlord-Tenant Act Applies"), the Act defines notice. A person has notice of a fact if he actually knows it, has received a notice of it, or has reason to know it from the facts he knows (KRS 383.560(1)). A person gives notice by taking steps reasonably calculated to inform the other in ordinary course, whether or not the other actually learns of it (KRS 383.560(3)). A tenant receives a notice when it comes to the tenant's attention, or is delivered in hand, or is mailed by registered or certified mail. The mail must go to the place the tenant held out for notices or, if none, the tenant's last known residence (KRS 383.560(3)(a), (c)). You receive a notice when it comes to your attention, or when it is delivered in writing, or sent by certified mail, to your place of business or the place you held out for notices (KRS 383.560(3)(a), (b)). The Act does not list text messages or email. Such a notice is received once it actually comes to the other person's attention, and the sender must be able to prove that. Electronic notices also need both sides' agreement to deal electronically ("Delivering Notices"). A notice to an organization takes effect when it reaches the person handling the matter, or when it would have with reasonable diligence (KRS 383.560(4)). Notices to you may also go to the person you disclose for receiving notices and demands (KRS 383.585(1)(b); "Manager and Owner Disclosure" clause). Kentucky's general definitions let certified mail be any delivery method with proof of sending, of the delivery date and of the recipient's signature (KRS 446.010(8)). Registered mail is any method that records the chain of custody, offers insurance and gets the recipient's signature (KRS 446.010(36)). Where the Act has not been adopted, no statute defines notice or says when a landlord-tenant notice is received; the lease and the older statutes (KRS 383.010 to 383.302) govern. The Uniform Commercial Code's definition of notice applies only to transactions governed by that Code (KRS 355.1-102, 355.1-202). The Kentucky Revised Statutes, the Kentucky Constitution, the 2025 and 2026 Acts and the state regulations on building and fire safety, public health, utilities, environment and human rights and those of the Attorney General and the Real Estate Commission contain no other definition of notice or receipt for landlord-tenant notices. In both tiers, name in the lease the address and method for notices (the library's `notices` clause, which defers to any method a statute requires). Use hand delivery or certified mail for termination and default notices ("Notices That Must Be in Writing").

title: Notices of Claims and Proceedings Against the Property
bodyText:
No Kentucky statute requires a tenant to tell you about a lawsuit, foreclosure, tax notice or other claim against the property, in either tier. If you want the tenant to pass such notices on, the lease must say so. The Kentucky Revised Statutes, the Kentucky Constitution, the 2025 and 2026 Acts and the state regulations on building and fire safety, public health, utilities, environment and human rights and those of the Attorney General and the Real Estate Commission contain no such duty.

Kentucky does protect your position in other ways, in every locality. A tenant's attornment to a stranger is void unless you consent or a court judgment requires it (KRS 383.100(1)). A sale of your interest is valid without the tenant's attornment, but a tenant who pays rent to you before notice of the sale suffers no loss for it (KRS 383.100(2)). A pending lawsuit over the title, possession or use of the property binds a later tenant who leased for value without notice only from the time a memorandum of the action is filed with the county clerk (KRS 382.440(1)). Eviction cases are excluded. Tenants can receive tax notices about your property.

A delinquent-tax notice returned as undeliverable is re-sent by certified mail addressed to the "Occupant" at the property (KRS 134.490(3)(a)6.). Going the other way, no Kentucky statute requires you, your lender or a court commissioner to notify tenants of a foreclosure or judicial sale ("Foreclosure and Tenants", "Disclosing a Pending Foreclosure").

Federal law protects bona fide tenants after a foreclosure ("Federal Tenant Protections After Foreclosure"). Where your city or county has adopted Kentucky's Uniform Residential Landlord and Tenant Act ("Where Kentucky's Landlord-Tenant Act Applies"), unless otherwise agreed, a landlord who sells in good faith to a bona fide purchaser is relieved of liability under the rental agreement and the Act for later events only after written notice of the sale to the tenant (KRS 383.600(1)). Where it has not, no statute sets that notice; the lease and the older statutes (KRS 383.010 to 383.302) govern.

The library does not offer a Kentucky clause requiring the tenant to forward notices of proceedings. If you want one, add your own, and don't make it bar the tenant from dealing with a buyer or a court-appointed successor.

title: Alarm Tampering Fees
bodyText: No Kentucky statute deals with a tenant tampering with or disabling a smoke or carbon monoxide alarm, or with a fee for it, in any locality. Kentucky's alarm duties are in "Smoke and Carbon Monoxide Alarms". Kentucky's fire safety regulation applies to all buildings except one- and two-family dwellings and adopts the NFPA 1 fire code by reference (815 KAR 10:060, Sections 2(1) and 3(4)(c)). A tampering rule in it is not ruled out. Where your city or county has adopted Kentucky's Uniform Residential Landlord and Tenant Act ("Where Kentucky's Landlord-Tenant Act Applies"), the tenant must meet the building and housing code duties placed on tenants (KRS 383.605(1)). The tenant also must not deliberately or negligently damage, impair or remove any part of the premises (KRS 383.605(6)). You may recover damages for the tenant's breach of those duties or of the lease, and actual damages and reasonable attorney's fees if the breach is willful (KRS 383.660(3)). A fixed tampering fee is not the same as damages, and a court could refuse it as a penalty; that is case law. Where the Act has not been adopted, the lease governs. The cautious course in every locality is to charge the actual, documented cost of repairing or replacing a disabled alarm, not a fixed fee. The library offers no alarm-tampering fee clause for Kentucky. The Kentucky Revised Statutes, the Kentucky Constitution, the 2025 and 2026 Acts and the state regulations on building and fire safety, public health, utilities, environment and human rights and those of the Attorney General and the Real Estate Commission contain no alarm-tampering rule.

title: Caring for a Tenant's Animal
bodyText:
No Kentucky statute gives you a special right to enter a rental home to feed, care for or remove a tenant's animal, in either tier. The Kentucky Revised Statutes, the Kentucky Constitution, the 2025 and 2026 Acts and the state regulations on building and fire safety, public health, utilities, environment and human rights and those of the Attorney General and the Real Estate Commission contain no such right.

Where your city or county has adopted Kentucky's Uniform Residential Landlord and Tenant Act ("Where Kentucky's Landlord-Tenant Act Applies"), you may enter without the tenant's consent in an emergency (KRS 383.615(2)). The Act does not define an emergency; whether an animal shut in without food or water is one is not settled by the statute. During any absence of the tenant of more than seven days, you may enter at times reasonably necessary (KRS 383.670(2)). The lease may require the tenant to tell you of an absence of more than seven days (KRS 383.620; "Notice of Extended Absence" clause). Once the tenant has abandoned or surrendered the unit, the Act's limits on your access end (KRS 383.615(4)(c)). Otherwise you need the tenant's consent and must give at least two days' notice (KRS 383.615(1), (3); "Landlord's Right of Entry" clause). Where the Act has not been adopted, no statute governs entry; the lease is your source of an entry right.

In every locality, the optional animal care clause ("Animal Care in Tenant's Absence" clause) lets the tenant name a caretaker in advance and lets you admit that person. If you take in a tenant's animal yourself, the law may treat you as its owner. For the dog laws, an owner includes every person who keeps or harbors the dog or has it in his or her care (KRS 258.095(5)). An owner is responsible for damage the dog causes to a person, livestock or other property (KRS 258.235(4)).

For rabies control, an owner is any person owning, keeping or harboring a dog, cat or ferret, and every owner must keep the animal vaccinated (KRS 258.005(2), 258.015(1), both as amended effective July 15, 2026). The animal health chapter counts anyone having in charge a domestic animal as its owner (KRS 257.010(14)). No Kentucky statute sets a number of days after which a keeper becomes an owner; the definitions apply as soon as you keep the animal. Subjecting an animal in your custody to cruel neglect is cruelty to animals in the second degree (KRS 525.130(1)(b)).

So the safer course is to call the tenant's named caretaker, the local animal control officer, a peace officer or an animal shelter rather than keep the animal yourself. A tenant who leaves an animal behind may commit a crime. Cruelty includes cruel or injurious mistreatment through abandonment (KRS 525.130(1)(a)). Torture of a dog or cat, a felony, can include extreme pain or death that results from the animal being abandoned in a building for three days or more with no provision for its care (KRS 525.135(1)(a), (3)). A peace officer or animal control officer may destroy an animal found abandoned and suffering, after a veterinarian's judgment, two citizens' judgment or the owner's consent (KRS 257.100(1), (2)).

Impounded dogs are held at least five days unless reclaimed, and the owner pays the impoundment fees (KRS 258.215(2), (4)). See "Pets" clause for pet terms and "Belongings Left Behind" for belongings left behind.

title: Appliances You Do Not Want to Supply
bodyText: No Kentucky statute presumes that appliances left in a rental home are ones you supply, and none says how a lease may exclude one, in either tier. The Kentucky Revised Statutes, the Kentucky Constitution, the 2025 and 2026 Acts and the state regulations on building and fire safety, public health, utilities, environment and human rights and those of the Attorney General and the Real Estate Commission contain no such rule. Where your city or county has adopted Kentucky's Uniform Residential Landlord and Tenant Act ("Where Kentucky's Landlord-Tenant Act Applies"), you must keep in good and safe working order the appliances supplied or required to be supplied by you (KRS 383.595(1)(d)). The Act's premises include the facilities and appurtenances in the dwelling unit (KRS 383.545(9)). The Act does not say when an item you leave in the unit for the tenant's use counts as supplied. A lease term that leaves an appliance in place but says you will not repair it could be read as letting you receive rent free of your repair duty, which a lease may not do (KRS 383.575). It could also be read as a waiver of the tenant's rights or a limit on your liability, which the Act makes unenforceable (KRS 383.570). The Act's way to have the tenant do work you would otherwise owe is a written agreement that meets KRS 383.595(3) or (4) ("Shifting Maintenance Tasks to the Tenant"). Equipment for running water, hot water and heat cannot be left out unless the Act's own exception applies (KRS 383.595(1)(e); "Landlord's Repair Duties"), or, in a single family residence, the tenant agrees in a good-faith writing to perform those supply duties (KRS 383.595(3)). Where the Act has not been adopted, no statute governs; the lease decides what you supply, so an exclusion is a contract term there. This library does not offer an appliance-exclusion clause, because its effect in URLTA localities is unsettled. The cautious course is to remove any appliance you will not maintain before the tenant moves in. List the appliances you do supply in the lease ("Appliances & Equipment Included" clause) and keep them working. If the tenant brings an appliance, say in writing that it is the tenant's property and the tenant's to maintain. If you want an exclusion clause, for example outside URLTA localities, you can add your own after taking advice. No statute requires you to supply a stove or refrigerator ("Stoves and Refrigerators").

title: Asbestos in Rental Buildings
bodyText: No Kentucky statute or regulation requires you to inspect a rental for asbestos, to disclose asbestos to a tenant, or to give tenants an asbestos notice. The Kentucky Revised Statutes, the Kentucky Constitution, the 2025 and 2026 Acts and the state regulations on building and fire safety, public health, utilities, environment and human rights and those of the Attorney General and the Real Estate Commission contain no such rule. The posted-warning rule for friable asbestos covers only buildings owned, leased or operated by the state (KRS 56.062). What does reach landlords is renovation and demolition. Kentucky adopts the federal asbestos emission standard, and owners and contractors of the work it covers must file a notification form with the Division for Air Quality before renovation or demolition (401 KAR 58:025, Section 2). Under the state abatement rule, renovation or demolition that could disturb friable asbestos in a covered facility must be done by a certified asbestos abatement entity (401 KAR 58:040, Sections 1(3), 2(1) and 3). A covered facility does not include an apartment building with no more than four dwelling units (401 KAR 58:040, Section 1(12)). Ask the Division for Air Quality whether your project is covered before work starts. A local air pollution control district may also regulate the work (KRS 77.155, 77.195). Its exemptions for a single owner-occupied private residence do not reach asbestos work in a building that is one of a group under common control, or whose use is commercial or not known (KRS 77.160(1); KRS 77.195(8)(b)). There, notice to the air pollution control officer is required and a permit may be needed. A rented home is not owner-occupied, so the safer reading is that the exemption does not apply to your rental at all. The rules for larger residential buildings apply in full (KRS 77.160(1)). Where your city or county has adopted Kentucky's Uniform Residential Landlord and Tenant Act ("Where Kentucky's Landlord-Tenant Act Applies"), the fit and habitable and building code duties apply (KRS 383.595(1)(a), (b)); see "Landlord's Repair Duties". In every locality, an owner must not let conditions exist that are dangerous to the occupants (KRS 65.8840(5)). If you know a unit has damaged or crumbling asbestos material, telling the tenant and keeping it undisturbed is the cautious course.

title: Condominium and Homeowners Association Rules for Rentals
bodyText:
No Kentucky statute requires you to disclose association obligations in the lease of a condominium or planned-community home, or to give your tenant the declaration, bylaws or rules, in either tier. The Kentucky Revised Statutes, the Kentucky Constitution, the 2025 and 2026 Acts and the state regulations on building and fire safety, public health, utilities, environment and human rights and those of the Attorney General and the Real Estate Commission contain no such duty. The documents can still bind your tenant. In a planned community (a homeowners' association of lots, not a condominium), owners, residents and tenants must comply with the recorded covenants, conditions and restrictions and the association's bylaws, rules and regulations (KRS 381.785(13), 381.798).

The association can assess your lot for fines, enforcement costs and repairs caused by the willful or negligent act of your tenants (KRS 381.797(1)). It must first give you written notice and a chance to be heard (KRS 381.797(2)). Its governing documents may not bar an owner or resident from displaying political yard signs from 30 days before to seven days after an election (KRS 381.800(1)).

For a condominium created after January 1, 2011, the Kentucky Condominium Act applies (KRS 381.9103(1)). Older condominiums stay under the Horizontal Property Law (KRS 381.805 to 381.910), which says nothing about tenants. Some sections of the newer Act also reach older condominiums for events after that date, including the association's powers and the resale certificate (KRS 381.9103(2)). The declaration must state any restrictions on use, occupancy and alienation of the units (KRS 381.9133(1)(l)), so read it for leasing limits.

After notice and a chance to be heard, the association may levy reasonable fines for violations of the declaration, bylaws and rules (KRS 381.9167(1)(k)). If the declaration gives lessees the vote on specified matters, your tenant votes on them instead of you and gets notice and records access (KRS 381.9181(3)). A lease interest with renewal options totaling 20 years or more appears to make the tenant a purchaser, entitled before conveyance to the documents and association certificate a seller must furnish (KRS 381.9105(19)(a), 381.9203(1)). The text does not say how that applies to a landlord, so talk to a lawyer before signing a lease that long.

Where your city or county has adopted Kentucky's Uniform Residential Landlord and Tenant Act ("Where Kentucky's Landlord-Tenant Act Applies"), your own rules bind the tenant only if the tenant had notice of them at signing or when adopted (KRS 383.610(1)(f)). A later rule that substantially modifies the bargain needs the tenant's written consent (KRS 383.610(2)). Where it has not, the lease governs.

The library's "Homeowner / Condominium Association Compliance" clause has the tenant follow association rules and pay fines the tenant causes. The optional "Association Documents Given to Tenant" clause records that you gave the tenant the documents. See also "Association Rules and Rentals".

title: No Balcony Inspection Requirement
bodyText: No Kentucky statute or regulation requires you to have balconies, decks, porches or other elevated exterior elements inspected on a schedule, or to report or disclose such an inspection. The Kentucky Revised Statutes, the Kentucky Constitution, the 2025 and 2026 Acts and the state regulations on building and fire safety, public health, utilities, environment and human rights and those of the Attorney General and the Real Estate Commission contain no such rule. Balcony and deck construction falls under the building codes, which adopt the 2015 International Building Code and the 2015 International Residential Code by reference (815 KAR 7:120, 815 KAR 7:125). A guard or inspection rule in them is not ruled out; check with your local building official (editions: "Which Code Editions Apply"). Where your city or county has adopted Kentucky's Uniform Residential Landlord and Tenant Act ("Where Kentucky's Landlord-Tenant Act Applies"), you must keep the premises fit and habitable and keep all common areas clean and safe (KRS 383.595(1)(b), (c)). A shared balcony, deck or exterior stairway is part of those duties; see "Landlord's Repair Duties". Where it has not, the lease and local housing codes govern. In every locality, an owner must not let a structure become unfit and unsafe, or let conditions exist that are dangerous to the occupants or neighbors (KRS 65.8840(5)). Local governments enforce that duty with fines, abatement and liens. A periodic check of balconies, decks and railings by a qualified person is a sensible precaution, not a Kentucky requirement.

title: Bed Bug and Pest Treatment Cooperation
bodyText:
No Kentucky statute or regulation sets rules for bed bug or other pest treatment in rental housing. None makes a tenant report an infestation, prepare the unit for treatment or pay for it, and none says how you must treat. The Kentucky Revised Statutes, the Kentucky Constitution, the 2025 and 2026 Acts and the state regulations on building and fire safety, public health, utilities, environment and human rights and those of the Attorney General and the Real Estate Commission contain no such rule. The hotel and motel code bars renting an infested guest room, and similar rules cover care homes, youth camps and manufactured home communities; none of them is a residential lease rule.

For disclosure, see "Bed Bugs". Where your city or county has adopted Kentucky's Uniform Residential Landlord and Tenant Act ("Where Kentucky's Landlord-Tenant Act Applies"), the tenant must not unreasonably withhold consent for you to enter to make necessary repairs or supply necessary services (KRS 383.615(1)). Except in an emergency or where it is impracticable, you must give at least two days' notice and enter only at reasonable times (KRS 383.615(3)). You must keep the premises fit and habitable (KRS 383.595(1)(b)). The tenant must keep the part of the premises the tenant uses as clean and safe as its condition permits and dispose of garbage in a clean and safe manner (KRS 383.605(2), (3)).

You may recover damages for the tenant's breach of those duties or of the lease (KRS 383.660(3)). Where the Act has not been adopted, no statute sets entry or pest rules; the lease governs. The optional Pest Reporting and Treatment clause covers reporting, entry for treatment through "Landlord's Right of Entry" clause, preparation instructions, and cost when the tenant is at fault. In every locality, an owner must not let conditions exist that are dangerous to the occupants (KRS 65.8840(5)).

title: Binding Arbitration Clauses
bodyText: This library does not offer its binding-arbitration clause ("Binding Arbitration of Money Claims" clause) in Kentucky. Kentucky's arbitration act makes a written agreement to arbitrate future disputes valid, enforceable and irrevocable, except on grounds that would let any contract be revoked (KRS 417.050). Its exclusions are collective bargaining agreements, insurance contracts and certain captive insurers, not leases (KRS 417.050). On request, a court must order arbitration under such an agreement and stay a court case on an issue subject to it, which could include your own eviction case (KRS 417.060(1), (4)). The library offers its clause only where state law allows it and no statute voids prohibited lease terms or penalizes enforcing one. Kentucky has both. Where your city or county has adopted Kentucky's Uniform Residential Landlord and Tenant Act ("Where Kentucky's Landlord-Tenant Act Applies"), a lease term by which the tenant waives or forgoes rights or remedies under the Act is unenforceable (KRS 383.570(1)(a), (2)). Whether an arbitration clause is such a waiver is a question for case law. In every locality, a landlord who knowingly enforces a lease containing a prohibited police-call term can owe the tenant damages, attorney fees and up to two months' rent (KRS 383.302(2); leases created or renewed on or after June 29, 2017). No Kentucky statute bars or regulates arbitration clauses in residential leases as such. The Kentucky Revised Statutes, the Kentucky Constitution, the 2025 and 2026 Acts and the state regulations on building and fire safety, public health, utilities, environment and human rights and those of the Attorney General and the Real Estate Commission contain none. For mediation and court referral, see "Mediation and Dispute Resolution". If you want an arbitration clause anyway, you can add your own, but take legal advice first, especially where the Act applies.

title: Carpet Cleaning at Move-Out
bodyText: No Kentucky statute deals with carpet cleaning or sets a cleaning charge. Where your city or county has adopted Kentucky's Uniform Residential Landlord and Tenant Act ("Where Kentucky's Landlord-Tenant Act Applies"), a security deposit secures you only against damage the tenant's occupancy causes beyond ordinary wear and tear (KRS 383.545(13)). At move-out you inspect and list any damage charged to the deposit, with its estimated repair cost, and you and the tenant sign the list (KRS 383.580(3)). So you may charge carpet cleaning to the deposit only for soiling or stains beyond ordinary wear and tear, listed with the estimated cost. A fixed or automatic cleaning charge taken from every deposit is not a listed item of damage, so do not use one there ("Preset Cleaning or Damage Charges"). There, the tenant must keep the part of the home the tenant uses as clean as its condition permits (KRS 383.605(2)). A lease may add terms the Act does not prohibit (KRS 383.565(1)), but a term asking the tenant to clean the carpets does not widen what the deposit covers. A separate nonrefundable cleaning fee counts as rent there, so do not call it a deposit (KRS 383.545(10); "Nonrefundable Fees"). Where the Act has not been adopted, no statute governs deposits or cleaning charges, and your lease governs ("Where to Keep the Security Deposit"). A fixed charge well above the real cost could be refused by a court as a penalty; that is case law. The cautious course in every locality is to charge only the actual, documented cost of cleaning beyond ordinary wear and tear. The library offers no Kentucky carpet-cleaning clause, because no statute settles whether ordinary carpet soiling is damage under the Act. A landlord who wants one can add their own clause after taking legal advice. The Kentucky Revised Statutes, the Kentucky Constitution, the 2025 and 2026 Acts and the state regulations on building and fire safety, public health, utilities, environment and human rights and those of the Attorney General and the Real Estate Commission contain no carpet-cleaning rule.

title: Waiving the Casualty and Mitigation Rules
bodyText:
Where your city or county has adopted Kentucky's Uniform Residential Landlord and Tenant Act ("Where Kentucky's Landlord-Tenant Act Applies"), a lease cannot take away the tenant's rights under the casualty or mitigation rules. After a fire or other casualty that substantially impairs enjoyment of the home, either side may end the lease with 14 days of notice, and the tenant may leave at once (KRS 383.650(1)). The party harmed by a breach has a duty to mitigate damages (KRS 383.520(1)).

If a tenant abandons the unit, you must make reasonable efforts to re-rent it at a fair rental (KRS 383.670(3)). A lease term by which the tenant waives or forgoes these rights or remedies is unenforceable (KRS 383.570(1)(a), (2)). Where the Act has not been adopted, the casualty rule is a default the written lease can change (KRS 383.170). Unless the written lease expressly says otherwise, a promise by the tenant to repair does not oblige the tenant to rebuild after a fire or other casualty that was not the tenant's own fault. And unless the tenant contracts otherwise, a tenant whose leased building is destroyed during the term without the tenant's fault or neglect owes no rent for the rest of the term. This library does not offer a clause keeping the tenant liable for rent on a destroyed home; "Fire or Casualty Damage" clause lets either side end the lease instead.

If you want such a term outside the Act's localities, you can add your own clause, but take legal advice first. No statute outside the Act sets a duty to mitigate, and whether one applies there, or can be waived, is a question for case law. The Kentucky Revised Statutes, the Kentucky Constitution, the 2025 and 2026 Acts and the state regulations on building and fire safety, public health, utilities, environment and human rights and those of the Attorney General and the Real Estate Commission contain no such statute. The cautious course is to try to re-rent and not to rely on a no-mitigation clause ("Re-Renting After a Tenant Leaves Early"). Damage the tenant causes is covered separately ("Damage Caused by Tenant" clause).

title: No Certificate of Occupancy Disclosure
bodyText: No Kentucky statute or regulation requires you to tell a tenant whether the rental has a certificate of occupancy, to attach or post one, or to mention it in the lease, in either tier. The Kentucky Revised Statutes, the Kentucky Constitution, the 2025 and 2026 Acts and the state regulations on building and fire safety, public health, utilities, environment and human rights and those of the Attorney General and the Real Estate Commission contain no such rule. What Kentucky law does require is the certificate itself, for many buildings. A building whose construction began after the Uniform State Building Code took effect may not be occupied until the local building official or the state issues a certificate of occupancy (KRS 198B.060(13)). A single-family dwelling needs no permit, inspection or certificate of occupancy unless your local government requires one by ordinance (KRS 198B.060(1), (13); 815 KAR 7:125, Section 2(2)(a)). Anyone damaged by a violation of the building code may sue the person who committed it (KRS 198B.130(1)). If no certificate of occupancy was issued, the award may also include reasonable attorney's fees (KRS 198B.130(1)). That claim must be brought within one year after the damage is or should have been discovered, and never more than 10 years after first occupation or settlement, whichever is sooner (KRS 198B.130(2)). Where your city or county has adopted Kentucky's Uniform Residential Landlord and Tenant Act ("Where Kentucky's Landlord-Tenant Act Applies"), you must also comply with building and housing codes materially affecting health and safety (KRS 383.595(1)(a)). Where it has not, no landlord-tenant statute adds a code duty; the lease and local codes govern. Before renting a newly built unit, confirm with your local building official that any required certificate has been issued. The code editions in force are in "Which Code Editions Apply"; no lease registration or rental licence is required by the state ("Recording a Lease Is Optional").

title: Cold Weather and Vacant Units
bodyText:
Kentucky has no rule requiring a tenant to warn you before leaving a unit empty in cold weather, no winter limit on evictions, and no minimum temperature a tenant must keep. The Kentucky Revised Statutes, the Kentucky Constitution, the 2025 and 2026 Acts and the state regulations on building and fire safety, public health, utilities, environment and human rights and those of the Attorney General and the Real Estate Commission contain no such rule. What Kentucky has instead: where your city or county has adopted Kentucky's Uniform Residential Landlord and Tenant Act ("Where Kentucky's Landlord-Tenant Act Applies"), you must supply reasonable heat between October 1 and May 1. That duty does not apply where the building is not required by law to be equipped for heat, or the heat comes from an installation in the tenant's exclusive control with its own utility connection (KRS 383.595(1)(e)). There the lease may also require the tenant to tell you, by the first day, of any absence over seven days.

If the tenant willfully fails to, you may recover actual damages (KRS 383.620, 383.670(1); "Notice of Extended Absence" clause). During an absence over seven days you may enter at times reasonably necessary (KRS 383.670(2); "Landlord's Right of Entry" clause). A tenant must use the heating and plumbing facilities in a reasonable manner and must not negligently damage the premises (KRS 383.605(5)-(6)). Where the Act has not been adopted, no statute speaks to any of this; the lease governs.

In every locality the library offers an optional cold-weather clause ("Cold Weather Notice Before Vacating" clause): heat kept at 55 degrees and written notice of absences over three days from October 1 to May 1, with tenant liability for freeze damage. Its figures are drafting choices, not Kentucky law. No Kentucky statute stays an eviction for weather ("Eviction Stays").

title: Lighting Shared Areas
bodyText:
No Kentucky statute or regulation sets a lighting level or lighting rule for the hallways, stairways, entrances or parking areas of an ordinary rental building, in either tier. Where your city or county has adopted Kentucky's Uniform Residential Landlord and Tenant Act ("Where Kentucky's Landlord-Tenant Act Applies"), you must keep all common areas clean and safe (KRS 383.595(1)(c)). You must also keep the electrical facilities you supply in good and safe working order (KRS 383.595(1)(d)), and comply with building and housing codes materially affecting health and safety (KRS 383.595(1)(a)). The Act does not say whether a safe common area must be lit; the cautious course is to keep shared halls, stairs, entrances and exits lit. Where it has not, no statute governs; the lease, the building code your building was built under, and any local housing code do.

Exit lighting in buildings other than one- and two-family dwellings is a matter for the fire code: exits or fire protection not working can be a distinct fire hazard (815 KAR 10:060, Section 3(4)(a); "Kentucky's Fire Code"). For the lighting details, check the model codes or ask your local building official. The specific lighting rules Kentucky does have reach licensed facilities, not ordinary rentals. Boarding homes must light each hall, stairway and entryway to at least 50 foot-candles (902 KAR 20:350). The hotel code expressly excludes apartments (902 KAR 7:010, Section 2). Mobile home communities have their own lighting rule (902 KAR 15:010, Section 5).

If shared-area lights are wired to a tenant's meter, no statute forbids having the tenant pay for that electricity. The library's optional "Common-Area Lighting on Tenant's Meter" clause does that while keeping maintenance and the clean-and-safe duty with you. The Kentucky Revised Statutes, the Kentucky Constitution, the 2025 and 2026 Acts and the state regulations on building and fire safety, public health, utilities, environment and human rights and those of the Attorney General and the Real Estate Commission contain no general common-area lighting rule for rentals.

title: No Communal Land Lease Approval
bodyText: Kentucky has no communal, tribal or native land system, and no statute or regulation requires a government officer to approve a residential lease of such land before it is valid, in either tier. The Kentucky Revised Statutes, the Kentucky Constitution, the 2025 and 2026 Acts and the state regulations on building and fire safety, public health, utilities, environment and human rights and those of the Attorney General and the Real Estate Commission contain no such rule. If land is held in trust by the United States for a tribe or tribal member, federal law, would govern its leasing.

title: Confession of Judgment
bodyText: A lease may not give you, or anyone, the power to confess judgment against the tenant. In every Kentucky locality, a power of attorney to confess judgment, or to let judgment pass by default, given before a lawsuit is filed is void (KRS 372.140(1)). No one may appear for a defendant under such a power in any Kentucky court (KRS 372.140(2)). Where your city or county has adopted Kentucky's Uniform Residential Landlord and Tenant Act ("Where Kentucky's Landlord-Tenant Act Applies"), a lease also may not have the tenant authorize anyone to confess judgment on a claim arising out of the lease (KRS 383.570(1)(b)). Such a term is unenforceable there (KRS 383.570(2)). No Kentucky statute lets a lease authorize a confessed judgment for rent or possession. The Kentucky Revised Statutes, the Kentucky Constitution, the 2025 and 2026 Acts and the state regulations on building and fire safety, public health, utilities, environment and human rights and those of the Attorney General and the Real Estate Commission contain none. A tenant can still confess judgment in person in court, with your agreement, once you have a claim (KRS 454.090). See "Lease Terms Kentucky Voids".

title: Habitability Protections Kentucky Does Not Have
bodyText: Kentucky lacks several habitability protections other states have. Knowing they are absent tells you what a tenant cannot claim under statute. (1) Outside localities that adopted Kentucky's Uniform Residential Landlord and Tenant Act ("Where Kentucky's Landlord-Tenant Act Applies"), no statute sets a habitability or repair duty, a warranty of habitability, or a tenant repair remedy ("Landlord's Repair Duties", "Habitability Duties Cannot Be Waived"). (2) No statute lets a tenant withhold rent or pay it into escrow on the tenant's own decision because of a repair problem, apart from the Act's limited repair-and-deduct and essential-services remedies (KRS 383.635, 383.640); rent goes into court only when a court orders it in your nonpayment or rent action where the Act applies ("What a Tenant Can Do When You Breach"). (3) No statute sets a minimum indoor temperature for a rental; where the Act applies you must supply reasonable heat from October 1 to May 1, unless the building is not required by law to be equipped for heat or the heat comes from an installation in the tenant's exclusive control on a direct utility connection. No statute requires you to supply air conditioning, but where the Act applies you must keep any you supply in good and safe working order (KRS 383.595(1)(d)-(e)). (4) No statute defines material or lists conditions that always materially affect health and safety ("How Serious a Repair Problem Must Be"). (5) No statute presumes a habitability breach or an unreasonable repair delay ("No Presumption of a Habitability Breach"). (6) No statute requires a habitability statement in the lease ("No Required Habitability Statement in the Lease"). (7) No statute lets you end a lease because repairs cost too much ("No Right to End the Lease Because Repairs Cost Too Much"). (8) No statute requires repair promises to be in writing with a completion date ("Promises to Repair or Improve"). (9) No statute addresses smoke drifting between units ("No Smoke-Drift Rule, and No Smoke-Drift Waiver"). The Kentucky Revised Statutes, the Kentucky Constitution, the 2025 and 2026 Acts and the state regulations on building and fire safety, public health, utilities, environment and human rights and those of the Attorney General and the Real Estate Commission contain none of these. What Kentucky does have is the duties and remedies of the Act where it applies ("Tenant Remedies for Repairs and Services"). Statewide, every owner must not let a structure become unfit and unsafe for human habitation, a duty local governments enforce (KRS 65.8840(5)), and a health cabinet determination that a child under six (72 months) is in immediate danger from lead hazards is cause for releasing the occupant from the lease (KRS 211.905(5)).

title: Other Rules Kentucky Does Not Have
bodyText: Kentucky lacks a number of rules other states have. Knowing they are absent tells you what your lease, not a statute, decides. (1) No rent cap, just-cause eviction rule or tenant right to buy the property, so no notice of one and no exemption notice to give ("No Tenant Protection Act Notice", "No Good-Cause Eviction Notice", "No Rent-Cap or Just-Cause Exemption Notice"). Only the General Assembly may control rents (KRS 65.875). (2) No owner move-in ground for ending a tenancy, and no limits on one ("No Owner Move-In Rule"). (3) No Kentucky rule on a tenant's bankruptcy; federal bankruptcy law governs ("When a Tenant Files for Bankruptcy"). (4) No statutory right for a tenant to pay what is owed and stop an eviction ("No Right to Pay and Stop an Eviction"). (5) No requirement that a tenant initial or separately sign a lease term, except that where the Act applies an agreement for the tenant of a unit other than a single family residence to do repairs or maintenance must be in a separate writing signed by both of you (KRS 383.595(4)(a); "No Initials Requirement"). (6) No statute on when fixed damages in a lease are valid liquidated damages or a penalty ("No Statute on Liquidated Damages in Leases"). (7) No tenant right to political access or signs, or to religious or cultural displays, that overrides the lease ("No Candidate Access or Political Sign Right Against the Lease", "No Religious or Cultural Display Right"). (8) No state incentive program for renting to veterans ("No Veteran Landlord Incentive"). (9) No special district statement in the lease ("No Special District Statement Required"). (10) No expiry date on Kentucky landlord-tenant law. (11) No statute saying a part payment restarts the time to sue, or letting a lease shorten it ("Time Limits to Sue for Rent or Damage"). Each absence holds in every locality, whether or not your city or county has adopted the Uniform Residential Landlord and Tenant Act ("Where Kentucky's Landlord-Tenant Act Applies"). The Kentucky Revised Statutes, the Kentucky Constitution, the 2025 and 2026 Acts and the state regulations on building and fire safety, public health, utilities, environment and human rights and those of the Attorney General and the Real Estate Commission contain none of these. Where the Act applies, a lease still may not take away the tenant's rights under it (KRS 383.570(1)(a)); where it has not, the lease and the older statutes (KRS 383.010 to 383.302) govern.

title: Kentucky Rules Outside the Landlord-Tenant Statutes
bodyText: These points sit outside, or at the edge of, Kentucky's landlord-tenant statutes. Each point holds across the whole Kentucky Revised Statutes, not only chapter 383. (1) Squatters: since June 27, 2025, you or your agent may ask a law enforcement officer to remove a person who never was a tenant and never had an agreement to occupy, using the statutory petition. The property must not have been open to the public when the person entered, you must have told the person to leave, the person must not be your immediate family member, and no case between you may be pending. It never applies to a current or former tenant (KRS 383.290(2), (9); "Squatters and Unauthorized Occupants"). (2) Cash rent receipts: no statute requires you to give a receipt for rent, cash or otherwise, and no general law gives a payer that right. If a licensed real estate broker manages the property for you, the Real Estate Commission's rules require a receipt for money received (201 KAR 11:121, Section 10(6)). Give one anyway; it is your proof too. (3) Registration before eviction: Kentucky has no statewide landlord registration or rental license, and no statute makes one a condition of an eviction case. Check for local programs. (4) Out-of-state entities: a foreign LLC or corporation transacting business here without a certificate of authority cannot bring any case, an eviction included, until it gets one (KRS 14A.9-020(1)). Its leases stay valid and it may still defend a suit (KRS 14A.9-020(5)). Owning real property without more is not transacting business, but that list is not exhaustive, so renting may be more (KRS 14A.9-010(2)(i), (3); "Out-of-State Owners"). (5) Business names: anyone renting under a name other than their real name must first file a certificate of assumed name (KRS 365.015(2)(a)). A violation is a fine of $25 to $100, 10 to 30 days in jail, or both, for each day (KRS 365.990(1)). These sections do not say a missing certificate bars a suit. (6) Service on an out-of-state owner: where your city or county has adopted the Uniform Residential Landlord and Tenant Act ("Where Kentucky's Landlord-Tenant Act Applies"), a nonresident landlord may designate a Kentucky agent with the Secretary of State. Otherwise process may be served on the Secretary of State, with a copy mailed to you (KRS 383.540(2)). Your disclosure must name a person to receive notices and service (KRS 383.585(1)(b); "Manager and Owner Disclosure" clause). In every locality, a nonresident owner can be sued in Kentucky on a claim arising from the property, with the Secretary of State as statutory agent for the summons (KRS 454.210(2)(f), (3)(a)). (7) Reports that bind any person, including you and your manager: suspected child dependency, neglect or abuse must be reported at once to police or the state (KRS 620.030(1)). Suspected abuse, neglect or exploitation of an adult must be reported at once to the cabinet (KRS 209.030(2)-(3)). Finding a body after a death of the kinds listed in KRS 72.025(1) to (12), such as one that appears to be from homicide or violence, suicide, drugs, fire or drowning, or otherwise not natural, requires notifying the coroner and police at once, and leaving the body alone (KRS 72.020(1)). (8) Foreclosure: no Kentucky statute requires notice to tenants of a foreclosure or judicial sale ("Foreclosure and Tenants", "Notices of Claims and Proceedings Against the Property"); federal law protects bona fide tenants ("Federal Tenant Protections After Foreclosure"). The Kentucky Revised Statutes, the Kentucky Constitution, the 2025 and 2026 Acts and the state regulations on building and fire safety, public health, utilities, environment and human rights and those of the Attorney General and the Real Estate Commission contain no rule for items (3) and (8), and none for item (2) beyond the broker rule above.

title: No Defective Drywall Disclosure
bodyText: No Kentucky statute or regulation requires you to disclose defective, corrosive or imported drywall to a tenant, or sets any drywall rule for rental housing. The Kentucky Revised Statutes, the Kentucky Constitution, the 2025 and 2026 Acts and the state regulations on building and fire safety, public health, utilities, environment and human rights and those of the Attorney General and the Real Estate Commission contain no such rule. Drywall appears in the statutes only in building permit definitions, condominium unit boundaries and a waste rule. Where your city or county has adopted Kentucky's Uniform Residential Landlord and Tenant Act ("Where Kentucky's Landlord-Tenant Act Applies"), a drywall problem that affects health or safety, or damages wiring or other facilities you supply, falls under your code, habitability and repair duties (KRS 383.595(1)(a), (b), (d)); see "Landlord's Repair Duties". Where it has not, the lease and local codes govern. In every locality, an owner must not let conditions exist that are dangerous to the occupants (KRS 65.8840(5)). If you know of defective drywall in a unit, fixing it, or telling the tenant in writing before the lease is signed, is the cautious course.

title: Move-Out Notice and the Deposit Refund
bodyText: No Kentucky statute makes the deposit refund depend on the tenant giving advance notice of moving out or a forwarding address, in any locality. Where your city or county has adopted Kentucky's Uniform Residential Landlord and Tenant Act ("Where Kentucky's Landlord-Tenant Act Applies"), the refund rule runs from your own notice instead. If the tenant leaves owing no rent and is due a refund, you send a notice of the refund amount to the tenant's last known or reasonably determinable address (KRS 383.580(7)). If the tenant does not respond within 60 days after you send it, you may keep the deposit (KRS 383.580(7); "Refunding the Security Deposit"). So asking the tenant for a forwarding address in writing helps you, and "Return of Security Deposit" clause does that. A lease term forfeiting the deposit just because the tenant gave no move-out notice goes beyond what a deposit secures there (KRS 383.545(13)). Such a term could also be an unenforceable waiver of the tenant's rights under the Act (KRS 383.570(1)(a), (2)). A tenant who leaves without proper notice may still owe rent, which you can claim. If the tenant leaves without paying the last month's rent and does not ask for the deposit back, you may apply it to that debt after 30 days (KRS 383.580(6)). Where the Act has not been adopted, no statute governs deposits, so your lease governs, except that a licensed broker managing the property must follow KRS 383.580 for deposit adjustments and put its deposit-return procedure in the lease (201 KAR 11:121, Section 10(2)(i), (8); "Where to Keep the Security Deposit"). Forfeiting a whole deposit for a missed notice could still be refused by a court as a penalty; that is case law. The Kentucky Revised Statutes, the Kentucky Constitution, the 2025 and 2026 Acts and the state regulations on building and fire safety, public health, utilities, environment and human rights and those of the Attorney General and the Real Estate Commission contain no surrender-notice condition on a deposit.

title: Who Does Repairs
bodyText: No Kentucky statute lets a lease name the repairer a tenant must use, or requires you to name a repairer or repair contact, in either tier. The Kentucky Revised Statutes, the Kentucky Constitution, the 2025 and 2026 Acts and the state regulations on building and fire safety, public health, utilities, environment and human rights and those of the Attorney General and the Real Estate Commission contain no such rule. Where your city or county has adopted Kentucky's Uniform Residential Landlord and Tenant Act ("Where Kentucky's Landlord-Tenant Act Applies"), a tenant has a limited right to repair at your expense. It applies to a condition that materially affects health and safety and costs less than $100 or half a month's rent, whichever is greater. After written notice, if you willfully fail to comply within 14 days, or as promptly as conditions require in an emergency, the tenant may cause the work to be done in a workmanlike manner and deduct the cost (KRS 383.635(1); "Tenant Remedies for Repairs and Services"). The statute does not let you choose who does that work. A lease term requiring the tenant to use your repairer, or to get your approval first, could waive a right under the Act, which a lease may not do (KRS 383.570(1)(a), (2)). The tenant may not repair at your expense if the tenant, a family member or a guest caused the condition (KRS 383.635(2)). You choose who does your own repairs, and the tenant may not unreasonably withhold consent to your entry to make necessary or agreed repairs (KRS 383.615(1); "Landlord's Right of Entry" clause). If a health-and-safety condition the tenant must fix can be remedied by repair, replacement of a damaged item or cleaning, and the tenant fails to remedy it within 14 days after your written notice specifying it (or as promptly as an emergency requires), you may enter, cause the work to be done and bill the reasonable cost as rent (KRS 383.665). Where the Act has not been adopted, no statute gives the tenant a right to repair and deduct, so you decide who makes repairs and the lease may say so. In every locality, give the tenant in writing the name and address of the person who manages the property, so repair requests reach you. Where the Act applies this is required (KRS 383.585(1); "Manager and Owner Disclosure" clause). This library offers no designated-repairer clause. In URLTA localities it would cut into the tenant's repair right, and elsewhere there is no tenant repair right for it to govern.

title: Tenants Sheltering Disaster Evacuees
bodyText: No Kentucky statute deals with tenants who take in people displaced by a fire, flood, tornado or other disaster, in either tier. None lets a tenant house evacuees despite the lease's guest or occupancy terms, and none bars you from enforcing those terms. No statute gives hotel or motel guests displaced by a disaster special status either. The Kentucky Revised Statutes, the Kentucky Constitution, the 2025 and 2026 Acts and the state regulations on building and fire safety, public health, utilities, environment and human rights and those of the Attorney General and the Real Estate Commission contain no such rule. Your lease's guest and occupancy terms apply as written ("Guest Policy" clause, "Guest Policy (14-Day Limit)" clause, "Permitted Occupants" clause; "Guests"). Where your city or county has adopted Kentucky's Uniform Residential Landlord and Tenant Act ("Where Kentucky's Landlord-Tenant Act Applies"), a rule adopted after the tenant signs that works a substantial modification of the bargain is not valid unless the tenant consents in writing (KRS 383.610(2)). So do not tighten guest limits mid-lease because of a disaster. Where the Act has not been adopted, the lease governs. The Act does not govern transient occupancy in a hotel, motel or lodgings subject to the state transient room tax (KRS 383.535(4)). During a declared emergency, once the Governor implements Kentucky's price-gouging law by order, its price limit covers rental housing, including hotel and motel housing (KRS 367.372(7), 367.374(1)(b)). A rent increase in the declared area during that period is limited the same way, unless an exception applies, such as an increase of 10% or less (KRS 367.374(1)(c)). Read any emergency order for your area; the Governor may suspend a statute the order names, with the Attorney General's written approval (KRS 39A.180(2)(b)). Local occupancy and zoning codes still apply. For what a disaster does to the lease itself, see "Leases After a Declared Disaster".

title: Leases After a Declared Disaster
bodyText: No Kentucky statute sets special landlord or tenant rules for a declared disaster, in either tier. A declaration of emergency does not by itself end a lease, stop rent, pause evictions or change your repair duties. The Kentucky Revised Statutes, the Kentucky Constitution, the 2025 and 2026 Acts and the state regulations on building and fire safety, public health, utilities, environment and human rights and those of the Attorney General and the Real Estate Commission contain no such rule. The ordinary rules apply. Where your city or county has adopted Kentucky's Uniform Residential Landlord and Tenant Act ("Where Kentucky's Landlord-Tenant Act Applies"), damage by fire, casualty, the elements, an act of God or other cause may substantially impair the tenant's enjoyment of the unit. Then you or the tenant may end the lease on 14 days' notice, and the tenant may leave at once (KRS 383.650(1)). You must return unused prepaid rent, accounted for as of the date of the casualty (KRS 383.650(2)). Your repair, heat and water duties continue meanwhile (KRS 383.595(1); "Landlord's Repair Duties"). In every locality, a tenant owes no rent for the rest of the term if the leased building is destroyed by fire or other casualty without the tenant's fault or neglect, unless the lease says otherwise (KRS 383.170); where the Act is adopted, its casualty rule also applies, and a lease cannot take away the tenant's rights under it (KRS 383.650; KRS 383.570(1)(a)). The library's casualty clause gives you a termination right by contract in every locality ("Fire or Casualty Damage" clause). No statute says whether rent is owed for a unit that is undamaged but cannot be reached or occupied under an evacuation order. The Governor, or a county judge/executive or mayor, may declare a state of emergency, and a person who refuses to leave an area under a written evacuation order may be removed to a place of safety or shelter (KRS 39A.100(1)(f), (3)(b)). The Governor may suspend a statute only by an executive order that names it and that the Attorney General approves in writing, and only while the emergency order is in effect (KRS 39A.180(2)(b), (c)). Read any order that covers your area. Once the Governor implements Kentucky's price-gouging law by order, you may not rent housing in the declared area for a price grossly in excess of the price before the declaration, unless an exception applies, such as an increase of 10% or less (KRS 367.374(1)(b), (c); "Ending a Lease After an Environmental Event"). A tenant who intentionally or wantonly damages residential rental property, causing a loss of $500 or more, commits a felony, and a higher class of felony during a declared disaster emergency in the disaster area (KRS 512.020(1)(a), (2)(a)).

title: Deposits When a Protected Tenant Leaves Early
bodyText: No Kentucky statute sets a special deposit rule or deadline when a protected tenant ends a lease early under the domestic violence statute. The Kentucky Revised Statutes, the Kentucky Constitution, the 2025 and 2026 Acts and the state regulations on building and fire safety, public health, utilities, environment and human rights and those of the Attorney General and the Real Estate Commission contain none. KRS 383.300 does not mention the deposit, and the deposit statute has no domestic violence rule. In every locality, for leases created or renewed on or after June 29, 2017, the protected tenant owes rent prorated to the termination date and no other rent or fees due solely to the early termination (KRS 383.300(5)(c); "Early Termination by Protected Tenants"). So an early-termination charge is not owed and cannot come out of the deposit. Where your city or county has adopted Kentucky's Uniform Residential Landlord and Tenant Act ("Where Kentucky's Landlord-Tenant Act Applies"), the ordinary deposit rules apply when occupancy ends: the signed move-out damage list and the refund rules (KRS 383.580(3), (6)-(7); "Refunding the Security Deposit"). Kentucky sets no refund deadline. Where the Act has not been adopted, the lease governs the deposit ("Where to Keep the Security Deposit"). If other tenants stay, the tenancy continues for them (KRS 383.300(7)). No statute says whether the protected tenant's share of a shared deposit is settled when that tenant leaves or only when the whole tenancy ends, or how one deposit is divided. Because the law is unsettled, get legal advice before splitting a shared deposit. The restrained person is liable to you for economic losses from the early termination, including unpaid rent, reletting costs and repair costs (KRS 383.300(5)(d)).

title: Where the Protective Order Laws Are
bodyText: Kentucky's statute protecting tenants who hold protective orders, KRS 383.300, relies on orders issued under chapter 403 (domestic violence), chapter 456 (interpersonal protective orders for dating violence, sexual assault and stalking) and KRS 431.064 (pretrial release). Every section it cites is current, and none has moved. Domestic violence orders are issued under KRS 403.740 and emergency protective orders under KRS 403.730. Interpersonal protective orders are issued under KRS 456.060 and temporary interpersonal protective orders under KRS 456.040. A court releasing a person charged with assault, a sexual offense or a protective-order violation may bar contact with the alleged victim as a condition of release (KRS 431.064(2)(b)). Chapter 456 and the present KRS 403.730 and 403.740 took effect on January 1, 2016, before KRS 383.300 took effect on June 29, 2017. None of the cited sections has been renumbered or repealed since, and no 2025 or 2026 Act amends them or KRS 383.300. Later amendments kept the restraint on unauthorized contact that KRS 383.300 requires of a qualifying order (KRS 403.740(1)(a), 456.060(1)(a)). One naming difference: KRS 431.064 speaks of conditions of release, while KRS 383.300 calls the same thing a pretrial release no-contact order. Which orders count for which protection is in "Which Protective Orders Qualify"; see also "Early Termination by Protected Tenants".

title: Which Protective Orders Qualify
bodyText: Kentucky's protections for tenants who are victims of violence rest on court orders. KRS 383.300 accepts only the orders it lists (KRS 383.300(2)(b)). The protections apply in every locality to leases created or renewed on or after June 29, 2017 (KRS 383.300(1)(a)). For every protection, including ending the lease early, a protected tenant is a tenant, applicant, or tenant with a minor household member who is protected by a valid domestic violence order (KRS 403.740) or interpersonal protective order (KRS 456.060). That order must restrain the other party from any unauthorized contact (KRS 383.300(2)(b)1.). For the bar on retaliation, the eviction defense and the lock change only, three short-term orders also count: an emergency protective order (KRS 403.730), a temporary interpersonal protective order (KRS 456.040) and a pretrial release no-contact order (KRS 431.064) (KRS 383.300(2)(b)2., (3), (4)). To end the lease early, the tenant gives you written notice and a copy of the valid order. If the order was obtained before the lease was signed, the tenant must also show you a safety concern that arose after the lease was signed (KRS 383.300(5)(a)-(b); "Early Termination by Protected Tenants"). For the lock change, the tenant must tell you of the plan to install a new lock; the statute does not require a copy of the order (KRS 383.300(4)(a); "Lock Changes by Protected Tenants"). The statute sets no time limit on how recent an order must be; it must be valid when the tenant relies on it. A domestic violence order or interpersonal protective order lasts up to three years and can be reissued (KRS 403.740(4), 456.060(3)). The emergency and temporary orders end at the conclusion of the court hearing unless extended (KRS 403.730(2)(a), 456.040(2)(a)). The list names Kentucky orders only. Kentucky courts and peace officers must give full faith and credit to a valid foreign protective order (KRS 403.7521(1)), but KRS 383.300 does not say whether one qualifies. The cautious course is to treat a valid order from another state as qualifying for the tenant's own protections: no retaliation, early termination and the lock change. A landlord who acts in good faith in accordance with the statute is immune from civil liability (KRS 383.300(8)), but whether a foreign order qualifies is unsettled. Take legal advice before refusing a key or access to a co-tenant named only in a foreign order (KRS 383.300(4)(b), (6)). A person who is both the restrained person and a protected tenant gets none of these protections (KRS 383.300(1)(b)). See "No Adverse Action Against Protected Tenants" and "Victim Information".

title: Electric and Gas Submetering and Resale
bodyText: No Kentucky statute or regulation requires a lease disclosure when you submeter or resell electricity or gas to tenants, in either tier. Electric submetering should be uncommon. Each dwelling unit in a nontransient multi-unit residential building whose building permit application was made after May 31, 1981 must have its own electric meter (807 KAR 5:046, Section 2). The rule does not reach electricity for central heating, ventilating and air conditioning, high rise buildings over four stories, or transient buildings such as hotels and dormitories (807 KAR 5:046, Sections 1(3) and 3). An applicant who wants a master meter where one is barred must prove to the Public Service Commission that separate meters cost more than their long-run benefit (807 KAR 5:046, Section 4).
