Kentucky's utility law covers anyone who distributes electricity, gas or water to or for the public for compensation (KRS 278.010(3)). The Kentucky Revised Statutes do not say whether a landlord reselling by meter to its own tenants is serving the public; that is a question for the Public Service Commission and the courts, and the utility's tariff may also limit resale. Take advice before you resell. Gas is clearer on safety. A master meter system includes an apartment complex where the operator buys metered gas and resells it through its own pipes, whether tenants pay by meter or through rent (KRS 278.495(1)(b)). The Commission regulates the safety of such a system under the federal pipeline safety standards (KRS 278.495(2)(b)). Where your city or county has adopted Kentucky's Uniform Residential Landlord and Tenant Act ("Where Kentucky's Landlord-Tenant Act Applies"), utility charges the lease makes payable to you count as rent (KRS 383.545(10)). Where it has not, the lease decides. In every locality, state in the lease how you measure and bill each utility, and never cut off service to collect ("No Right to Cut Off Submetered or Landlord-Billed Utilities"). See also "Submetering and Utility Charge-Backs" and, for water, "Utility Allowances and Overage Charges". The Kentucky Revised Statutes, the Kentucky Constitution, the 2025 and 2026 Acts and the state regulations on building and fire safety, public health, utilities, environment and human rights and those of the Attorney General and the Real Estate Commission contain no submetering disclosure rule for electricity or gas.

title: Emergency Contacts
bodyText:
No Kentucky statute requires you to give tenants an emergency or 24-hour contact number, to post one, or to collect an emergency contact from the tenant, in either tier. The Kentucky Revised Statutes, the Kentucky Constitution, the 2025 and 2026 Acts and the state regulations on building and fire safety, public health, utilities, environment and human rights and those of the Attorney General and the Real Estate Commission contain no such rule.

Where your city or county has adopted Kentucky's Uniform Residential Landlord and Tenant Act ("Where Kentucky's Landlord-Tenant Act Applies"), you must give the tenant in writing, at or before the start of the tenancy, the name and address of the person authorized to manage the premises and of an owner or agent for notices and service of process (KRS 383.585(1); "Manager and Owner Disclosure" clause). You must keep that information current (KRS 383.585(2)). The Act requires a name and address, not a telephone number. Where the Act has not been adopted, no statute requires any contact information, but the "Manager and Owner Disclosure" clause is still good practice. Giving the tenant a telephone number for urgent repairs is sensible in every locality.

Collecting the tenant's own emergency contact is a lease term. The optional clause ("Tenant's Emergency Contact" clause) limits its use to emergencies and says the contact takes on no lease duties. Treat the information as confidential, especially for a tenant protected by a protective order ("Victim Information"). The statutes that do require an emergency contact reach licensed care settings, not ordinary rentals: an assisted living community's lease must include the resident's emergency contact person (KRS 194A.713(1)(a)).

title: When the Government Takes the Property
bodyText:
A government or other condemnor may take private property for public use only with just compensation paid first (Ky. Const. §§ 13, 242). Kentucky's Eminent Domain Act (KRS 416.540 to 416.680) sets the procedure in Circuit Court. The Act calls the owner of the property interest being taken the condemnee (KRS 416.540(3)). It measures the award for the whole tract: the fair market value of the entire tract just before the taking, less the value of what remains just after (KRS 416.580(1), 416.660(1)).

No section divides that award between you and your tenant. Where claimants conflict, the condemnor pays the award to the Circuit Court clerk, and the claimants may settle their rights in a separate action (KRS 416.640). Since April 13, 2026, a condemnor must deliver any purchase offer to the property owner in writing, by certified mail or verified hand delivery (KRS 416.550(2)(b)). The owner then has 60 days to get an independent appraisal (KRS 416.550(2)(c)). The owner must also get 10 days' notice before the condemnor enters to survey or appraise (KRS 416.560(4); 2026 Ky. Acts ch. 112). These notices go to the owner, so your tenant may learn of a planned taking only from you.

No Kentucky statute ends a lease, cuts the rent, or lets a court cancel a lease when the property is taken, in either tier. Neither the Uniform Residential Landlord and Tenant Act, where your city or county has adopted it ("Where Kentucky's Landlord-Tenant Act Applies"), nor the older statutes (KRS 383.010 to 383.302) where it has not, address a taking. The Kentucky Revised Statutes, the Kentucky Constitution, the 2025 and 2026 Acts and the state regulations on building and fire safety, public health, utilities, environment and human rights and those of the Attorney General and the Real Estate Commission contain no such rule.

Without a lease term, what happens to the lease and the rent is a case-law question. The library's optional "Condemnation" clause ends the lease on a total taking, reduces rent on a partial one, and gives the award to you. It leaves the tenant any relocation or moving payment. Where a public project displaces people, relocation assistance may be paid under the federal Uniform Relocation Act, and those payments are not compensation for the real property (KRS 56.620(1)-(2)).

title: Background Checks on Your Staff
bodyText: No Kentucky statute requires you or a property manager to run background checks on leasing staff, maintenance workers or others who enter tenants' homes, and none bars you from doing so, in either tier. The Kentucky Revised Statutes, the Kentucky Constitution, the 2025 and 2026 Acts and the state regulations on building and fire safety, public health, utilities, environment and human rights and those of the Attorney General and the Real Estate Commission contain no such rule. Screening is still prudent, because you answer for how your staff use entry. Where your city or county has adopted Kentucky's Uniform Residential Landlord and Tenant Act ("Where Kentucky's Landlord-Tenant Act Applies"), entry needs the tenant's consent, which may not be unreasonably withheld, and at least two days' notice except in an emergency or where impracticable. You may enter only at reasonable times, and you may not abuse the right of access or use it to harass the tenant (KRS 383.615; "Landlord's Right of Entry" clause). Where the Act has not been adopted, the lease governs entry. Any employer may require an applicant or employee, as a condition of employment, to agree to a background check, following any state or federal law that requires the consent of the person checked (KRS 336.700(3)(d)). How you screen is governed by employment and consumer-report law. A person who manages or rents property for others for pay practices real estate brokerage and needs a Kentucky real estate license (KRS 324.010, 324.020(2)). License applicants must pass a national criminal history check (KRS 324.045(5)). The license law does not apply to an owner or the owner's regular employees managing the owner's property, or to a property manager who is a regular employee of the owner or principal broker or whose main pay is the use of a rental unit (KRS 324.030(1), (5)). Licensed care settings, such as assisted living communities and child-care facilities, have their own staff background-check rules; they do not reach ordinary rentals.

title: Energy Usage Data Releases
bodyText:
No Kentucky statute or regulation lets, requires or forbids a utility to release a tenant's energy or water usage data to the building owner, in either tier. None sets up building energy benchmarking for private rental property. Kentucky's consumer data privacy law does not reach this. It exempts data processed by a utility (KRS 367.3613(3)(q)), and it applies only to businesses that control or process the personal data of at least 100,000 Kentucky consumers a year, or 25,000 with most revenue from selling data (KRS 367.3613(1)). That is true of the version in force since January 1, 2026 and of the version that takes effect July 1, 2027 after 2026 Ky. Acts ch. 118; the 2027 changes add terms for smart television and monitor data, not energy data (KRS 367.3611).

A statute bars a utility's employees from sharing confidential customer information with the utility's affiliates without the customer's written consent (KRS 278.2213(5)); it does not deal with landlords. So a release to you rests on your tenant's consent and the utility's own release form. The library's optional "Energy Usage Data Authorization" clause has the tenant sign that form on request, limits your use of the data, and lets the tenant withdraw.

Where your city or county has adopted Kentucky's Uniform Residential Landlord and Tenant Act ("Where Kentucky's Landlord-Tenant Act Applies"), nothing in the Act's list of barred lease terms reaches such a consent (KRS 383.570(1)). Where it has not, the lease governs. If you submeter water yourself, you already hold each tenant's usage, because the charge must follow actual usage (401 KAR 8:020, Section 2).

The Kentucky Revised Statutes, the Kentucky Constitution, the 2025 and 2026 Acts and the state regulations on building and fire safety, public health, utilities, environment and human rights and those of the Attorney General and the Real Estate Commission contain no energy-data release or benchmarking rule.

title: Who May Represent an Entity Landlord in Court
bodyText: In Kentucky, representing someone else in court is the practice of law, which needs a license from the Supreme Court (SCR 3.020, a court rule; KRS 524.130(1)). If you own the rental in your own name, you may represent yourself. If you own through a corporation, limited liability company or partnership, the entity is the party. A member, officer, manager or property manager who is not a lawyer generally may not appear for it. The court rule makes one exception, for the small claims division of District Court. There, an officer of a corporation or partnership that is a party, or a person it regularly employs in a managerial capacity, may appear for it (SCR 3.020). The rule names corporations and partnerships only and says nothing about limited liability companies. Whether an LLC's member or manager may appear is unsettled, so the cautious course is to use a lawyer or ask the court before relying on it. An outside property manager is not employed by your entity, so the exception does not cover it. The small claims division hears claims for money, damages or personal property up to $2,500, such as unpaid rent or damage after a tenant leaves (KRS 24A.230(1)). A lawyer may appear there but is not required (KRS 24A.240(1)). Assigned claims, lenders and collection agencies are barred (KRS 24A.240(2)-(3)). A party may file no more than 25 claims a calendar year, though a business may file that many for each established location in business at least six months (KRS 24A.250(1)). Recovering possession is a forcible detainer case in District Court, not a small claims money claim (KRS 383.210(1); "The Eviction (Forcible Detainer) Process"). No Kentucky statute, and nothing in SCR 3.020, lets a non-lawyer appear there for an entity landlord. The only forcible detainer statute naming an agent lets a party demand a jury in person or by agent or attorney (KRS 383.210(2)). The cautious course is to have a lawyer file and try an entity's eviction. An out-of-state LLC or corporation transacting business here without a certificate of authority cannot bring any case until it gets one (KRS 14A.9-020(1); "Landlord Registration", "Out-of-State Owners"). These rules apply in every locality; the Uniform Residential Landlord and Tenant Act ("Where Kentucky's Landlord-Tenant Act Applies") does not change who may appear. The Kentucky Revised Statutes, the Kentucky Constitution, the 2025 and 2026 Acts and the state regulations on building and fire safety, public health, utilities, environment and human rights and those of the Attorney General and the Real Estate Commission contain no statute letting a non-lawyer appear for an entity landlord.

title: Ending a Lease After an Environmental Event
bodyText: No Kentucky statute lets you end a lease because of contamination, an environmental or public-health event, a disaster or evacuation order, or a finding that the home is unfit, apart from the casualty rule where the Uniform Residential Landlord and Tenant Act applies. The Kentucky Revised Statutes, the Kentucky Constitution, the 2025 and 2026 Acts and the state regulations on building and fire safety, public health, utilities, environment and human rights and those of the Attorney General and the Real Estate Commission contain no such rule. Where your city or county has adopted the Act ("Where Kentucky's Landlord-Tenant Act Applies"), either you or the tenant may end the lease on 14 days' notice if the unit or premises are damaged or destroyed by fire or casualty, or so injured by the elements, an act of God or other cause that the tenant's enjoyment is substantially impaired. The tenant may leave at once (KRS 383.650(1)). You must return unused prepaid rent, and rent is accounted for as of the date of the casualty (KRS 383.650(2)). Whether other cause reaches contamination or a government order with no physical damage is not settled by the statute. In every locality, a tenant owes no rent for the rest of the term if the leased building is destroyed by fire or other casualty without the tenant's fault or neglect, unless the lease says otherwise (KRS 383.170); where the Act is adopted, its casualty rule also applies, and a lease cannot take away the tenant's rights under it (KRS 383.570(1)(a)). Where the Act has not been adopted, no statute gives you a termination right. The library's casualty clause supplies that right by contract in every locality, for damage by fire, other casualty, the elements, an act of God or any other cause ("Fire or Casualty Damage" clause). Tenant rights to leave: in every locality, a health cabinet finding that a child under six is in immediate danger from lead hazards is cause for releasing the tenant without prejudice (KRS 211.905(5); "Lead Hazards and Children"). See "Statutory Ways a Tenant Can End a Lease Early". Methamphetamine contamination triggers a disclosure duty, not a termination right. During a declared emergency, once the Governor implements the price-gouging law by order, you may not rent housing for a price grossly in excess of the price before the declaration (KRS 367.374(1)(b)). If you want a broader right, for example to end the lease after a contamination order, it would be a contract term of your own; take advice first.

title: Chargers When the Tenancy Ends
bodyText: No Kentucky statute says who owns a tenant-installed charger when the tenancy ends, or whether the tenant may remove or sell it. The Kentucky Revised Statutes, the Kentucky Constitution, the 2025 and 2026 Acts and the state regulations on building and fire safety, public health, utilities, environment and human rights and those of the Attorney General and the Real Estate Commission contain none. The lease decides. Under "No Alterations" clause, an alteration you approve stays with the property at the end of the term unless you require its removal. If you want a different result for a charger, such as removal by the tenant or a sale to you, put it in writing when you consent ("EV Charging"). Without an agreement, whether a charger attached to the building has become part of it is a question of fixtures law, which is case law.

title: EV Charging: Tax, Licensing and No Tenant Right
bodyText: No Kentucky statute gives a tenant a right to install an electric vehicle charger or requires a landlord to provide one. A charger needs your consent under the lease's alterations terms ("EV Charging"; "No Alterations" clause). No Kentucky statute or held regulation requires EV-ready or EV-capable parking in rental housing. The Kentucky Revised Statutes, the Kentucky Constitution, the 2025 and 2026 Acts and the state regulations on building and fire safety, public health, utilities, environment and human rights and those of the Attorney General and the Real Estate Commission contain none. Two state rules may reach you if you provide charging. Kentucky taxes electric vehicle power distributed by an electric vehicle power dealer, starting at three cents per kilowatt hour and adjusted each year (KRS 138.477(2)-(3)). A dealer is anyone who owns or leases a charging station of 20 kilowatts or more, or who is paid for power through a charging station, meaning a place accessible to general public vehicular traffic (KRS 138.477(1)(d), (f)). A dealer who charges no price still owes the tax on the power distributed, except for a station installed before July 1, 2022 (KRS 138.477(6)(b)). The statute does not say whether a parking lot used only by tenants is accessible to general public vehicular traffic. Beginning January 1, 2027, a dealer needs a retail electric vehicle charging license, with a fee per port and inspections (KRS 363.785(1)-(2), (4)). That licensing law covers only stations of 20 kilowatts or more that are open to general public vehicular traffic and sell electricity at retail (KRS 363.510(16)-(17)). Before billing tenants for charging, check with the Department of Revenue or a lawyer whether you are a power dealer.

title: No Rules for Chargers in Shared Parking
bodyText: No Kentucky statute addresses a tenant's charger in a shared parking area, a fee to reserve the space, or who pays for damage to the charger or other property. The Kentucky Revised Statutes, the Kentucky Constitution, the 2025 and 2026 Acts and the state regulations on building and fire safety, public health, utilities, environment and human rights and those of the Attorney General and the Real Estate Commission contain none. No statute gives a tenant a right to install a charger at all, so a charger in a shared area needs your written consent under the lease's alterations terms ("EV Charging"; "No Alterations" clause). If you consent, set the location, any space fee, insurance, power costs and damage responsibility in the written consent. If tenants pay you for charging at a place open to the public, see "EV Charging: Tax, Licensing and No Tenant Right" for the state's charging tax and license.

title: No Specific Ban on Eviction Penalty Clauses
bodyText: No Kentucky statute bans, by name, a lease clause that charges a tenant a fee or penalty for being evicted. The Kentucky Revised Statutes, the Kentucky Constitution, the 2025 and 2026 Acts and the state regulations on building and fire safety, public health, utilities, environment and human rights and those of the Attorney General and the Real Estate Commission contain no such rule. Other rules still limit what such a clause can do. In every locality, a lease may not let you end the tenancy or penalize a tenant for asking the police or anyone else for emergency help (KRS 383.302(1); leases created or renewed on or after June 29, 2017). If you knowingly enforce such a term, the tenant can recover actual damages, attorney fees and costs, and up to two months' rent (KRS 383.302(2); "Calls for Police or Emergency Help"). Where your city or county has adopted Kentucky's Uniform Residential Landlord and Tenant Act ("Where Kentucky's Landlord-Tenant Act Applies"), a lease may not make the tenant pay your attorney fees (KRS 383.570(1)(c)). An "eviction fee" that covers your lawyer is unenforceable there (KRS 383.570(2)); attorney fees come only where the Act awards them ("Attorney Fees in Landlord-Tenant Cases"). Where it has not, no statute lists prohibited lease terms; the lease and the older statutes (KRS 383.010 to 383.302) govern, and a written attorney-fee term for a default may be enforceable (KRS 411.195; "Attorney Fees (Only Where the URLTA Is Not in Effect)" clause). In both tiers, the judgment in an eviction (forcible detainer) case awards court costs to the side that wins (KRS 383.240). Whether a fixed eviction charge set in advance is an unenforceable penalty is a question for the courts. The cautious course is to leave any fixed eviction charge out of the lease and recover your actual, documented losses instead. See "Lease Terms Kentucky Voids" and "No Statute on Liquidated Damages in Leases".

title: Who Serves Eviction Papers
bodyText: Every Kentucky eviction summons (court form AOC-215) goes to the sheriff or any constable, who must give the tenant at least three days' notice of the trial (KRS 383.210(1), 383.215). Constables have this power by statute (KRS 70.325(1)(h)), and for good cause the court may appoint another person to serve a particular process (KRS 454.145). You are not on that list, so don't serve the summons yourself. If the officer cannot find the tenant at the premises, the officer may explain and leave it with a family member over 16 living there. If no such person is found, the officer may post it on the premises and mail it by regular mail (KRS 454.030). No Kentucky statute lets a lease name a person to accept the eviction summons for the tenant. The Kentucky Revised Statutes, the Kentucky Constitution, the 2025 and 2026 Acts and the state regulations on building and fire safety, public health, utilities, environment and human rights and those of the Attorney General and the Real Estate Commission contain no such rule. The library offers no such clause: the service statute already says who may receive the papers. The notice you give before filing is different. No statute says who must deliver it, so you or your agent may deliver it yourselves. Where your city or county has adopted Kentucky's Uniform Residential Landlord and Tenant Act ("Where Kentucky's Landlord-Tenant Act Applies"), a tenant receives a notice delivered in hand, or mailed by registered or certified mail to the place the tenant named or, if none, the last known residence (KRS 383.560(3)(c); "Delivering Notices"). Where it has not, the notice ending a tenancy at will must be in writing (KRS 383.195), and no statute sets a delivery method. Keep proof of delivery: the sworn complaint (AOC-216) states the date you gave written notice to vacate. A tenant in the Secretary of State's Safe at Home address-confidentiality program designates the Secretary of State as agent for service of process (KRS 14.304(2)(e)). Once a participant tells you in writing that they are in the program, you must not knowingly disclose their name or home, work or school address, unless an exception applies (KRS 14.304(9)-(10)). No statute says how an eviction complaint, which names the tenant and the premises, fits these rules; talk to a lawyer or the court clerk before filing against a participant. See "The Eviction (Forcible Detainer) Process".

title: No Expedited Deposit Procedure
bodyText: Kentucky has no expedited deposit procedure and no rule letting you charge a fee for settling a deposit early, in any locality. There is no general deadline to shorten: Kentucky sets no deadline for returning a deposit ("Refunding the Security Deposit"). Where your city or county has adopted Kentucky's Uniform Residential Landlord and Tenant Act ("Where Kentucky's Landlord-Tenant Act Applies"), the only timing rules are the 30-day wait before applying a deposit to an unpaid last month's rent (KRS 383.580(6)) and the 60-day refund-notice rule (KRS 383.580(7)). Nothing stops you from inspecting, listing damage and refunding sooner if the tenant asks (KRS 383.580(3)). A fee for doing so could not come out of the deposit there, because a deposit secures only against damage beyond ordinary wear and tear (KRS 383.545(13)). Where the Act has not been adopted, no statute governs deposits, and your lease governs, except that a licensed broker managing the property must follow KRS 383.580 for deposit adjustments (201 KAR 11:121, Section 10(8); "Where to Keep the Security Deposit"). The library offers no early-disposition fee clause for Kentucky. The Kentucky Revised Statutes, the Kentucky Constitution, the 2025 and 2026 Acts and the state regulations on building and fire safety, public health, utilities, environment and human rights and those of the Attorney General and the Real Estate Commission contain no expedited deposit procedure.

title: Family Child Care in a Rental Home
bodyText: No Kentucky statute requires you to let a tenant run a family child-care home, stops a lease from forbidding one, or sets conditions such as insurance or a liability waiver, in either tier. The Kentucky Revised Statutes, the Kentucky Constitution, the 2025 and 2026 Acts and the state regulations on building and fire safety, public health, utilities, environment and human rights and those of the Attorney General and the Real Estate Commission contain no such rule. The state's child-care regulations (Title 922 KAR) may still contain a rule. Under the statutes, a family child-care home is a private home that is a person's primary residence where that person cares for six or fewer children who are not relatives (KRS 199.894(5)). A provider caring for four to six unrelated children must apply for state certification of the home; one caring for three or fewer may apply by choice (KRS 199.8982(1)(a)). Certification requires smoke detectors, a telephone, an adequate water supply, sufficient lighting and space, and a safe environment in the residence (KRS 199.8982(1)(a)). The state certifies the home after an unannounced inspection, and the provider must display the certificate in the residence (KRS 199.8982(1)(b)-(c)). Local governments may not add licensing, certification or training rules for these homes, but general local ordinances still apply (KRS 199.8982(4)(b)). A local zoning code must name family child-care homes so its board of adjustments can consider conditional use permits for them in residential zones (KRS 199.8982(4)(c)). None of this gives the tenant a right against you. Where your city or county has adopted Kentucky's Uniform Residential Landlord and Tenant Act ("Where Kentucky's Landlord-Tenant Act Applies"), a tenant must, unless otherwise agreed, occupy the unit only as a dwelling unit (KRS 383.620). Where it has not, the lease decides. The library's "Residential Use Only" clause bars business use. The optional "Home-Based Business (Landlord's Permission)" clause lets you allow child care on conditions, including licenses, insurance and children coming to the property ("Home Businesses in a Rental").

title: Hunting and Fishing on Rented Land
bodyText:
No Kentucky statute says whether hunting, fishing or trapping rights pass to a tenant with a lease of land or stay with the owner, in either tier. The Kentucky Revised Statutes, the Kentucky Constitution, the 2025 and 2026 Acts and the state regulations on building and fire safety, public health, utilities, environment and human rights and those of the Attorney General and the Real Estate Commission contain no such rule. The law does say who may give permission.

No one may enter another's land to shoot, hunt, trap or fish without the oral or written permission of the landowner, tenant, or person with authority to grant it (KRS 150.092(1)). For this rule a tenant means a resident sharecropper, lessee or other person who works the farm or land and lives on it (KRS 150.010(47)). A tenant who only rents the house may still have authority over land the lease gives them; the text does not settle it. A first violation carries a fine of $100 to $300, and the violator owes the landowner or tenant the replacement cost of damaged property (KRS 150.990(15)). A resident owner of farmland, and tenants or their dependent children living on it, may hunt and fish there in open season without a license (KRS 150.170(4)).

An owner, lessee or occupant who lets someone hunt, fish or trap owes that person no duty to keep the land safe and is not liable for that person's negligent acts (KRS 150.645(1)). That shield does not cover a willful and malicious failure to guard or warn, or permission given for a fee (KRS 150.645(1)). On unimproved, unfenced land, criminal trespass requires notice against trespass given personally by the owner or other authorized person, or posted conspicuously (KRS 511.090(4)). Purple paint marks of the size and spacing the statute sets count as notice against trespass (KRS 511.070(2)). The constitutional right to hunt and fish does not change the law of trespass or property rights (Ky. Const. § 255A).

To control hunting on rented land, use the lease. The library's optional "Hunting, Trapping and Fishing" clause bars the tenant from hunting, trapping or fishing, or letting anyone else do so, without your written consent. The library does not offer a clause letting you or your guests enter the rented land to hunt. Where your city or county has adopted Kentucky's Uniform Residential Landlord and Tenant Act ("Where Kentucky's Landlord-Tenant Act Applies"), a landlord has no right of access beyond the cases the Act lists (KRS 383.615(4)). A reserved hunting entry may conflict with that, and the text does not say. Where it has not, no statute limits such a reservation; you may add your own clause, with legal advice. Leases of farmland for farming, with crop liens and crop-share rent, have their own rules (KRS 383.110 to 383.130).

title: Fees for Services Not Provided
bodyText: No Kentucky statute specifically bars a lease fee for a service you do not provide, in any locality. Kentucky's Consumer Protection Act makes unfair, false, misleading or deceptive acts in trade or commerce unlawful, and unfair there means unconscionable (KRS 367.170). Whether a tenant can sue under that Act over a residential lease is unsettled ("Consumer Protection Act and Leases"). Where your city or county has adopted Kentucky's Uniform Residential Landlord and Tenant Act ("Where Kentucky's Landlord-Tenant Act Applies"), a lease may include terms the Act and other rules of law do not prohibit (KRS 383.565(1)). A fee there counts as rent (KRS 383.545(10); "Fees Count as Rent"), and a court may refuse to enforce a provision that was unconscionable when made (KRS 383.555(1)(a)). Where the Act has not been adopted, the lease and contract law govern. In every locality the cautious course is to charge a fee only for a service you actually provide, and to describe the service and the fee in the lease ("Disclosing Fees"). The Kentucky Revised Statutes, the Kentucky Constitution, the 2025 and 2026 Acts and the state regulations on building and fire safety, public health, utilities, environment and human rights and those of the Attorney General and the Real Estate Commission contain no rule on fees for services not provided.

title: Kentucky's Fire Code
bodyText:
Kentucky's fire code is the Kentucky Standards of Safety, a state regulation adopted under KRS 227.300 (815 KAR 10:060). It applies to all buildings except one- and two-family dwellings, so it reaches apartment buildings and other multi-unit rentals (815 KAR 10:060, Section 2(1)). In finding and ordering the correction of a distinct fire hazard, fire officials apply the NFPA 1 Uniform Fire Code (2018), the NFPA 101 Life Safety Code (2018), the National Electrical Code (2017) and the Kentucky Building Code (815 KAR 10:060, Section 3(4)(c)). The State Fire Marshal enforces it unless your city or county has its own fire inspection program, and local governments must enforce it as a minimum standard (815 KAR 10:060, Section 2(2); KRS 227.320).

The State Fire Marshal's powers under chapter 227 do not reach a single-family dwelling, except fire investigation, unless a local ordinance extends them (KRS 227.225). Distinct fire hazards include blocked exits, fire protection that does not work, accumulated combustible material and combustibles too close to a stove or heater (815 KAR 10:060, Section 3(4)(a)). An official who finds one serves a written notice of deficiency on you or your agent, with a correction date no more than 60 days away (815 KAR 10:060, Section 5). A willful violation of the fire code or a fire official's order can bring an administrative fine of up to $1,000, or suspension or revocation of a certificate of occupancy or other license or permit, after notice and a hearing (KRS 227.331(2)).

Keep fire protection systems maintained, have alarm and suppression systems inspected and tested every year, and test single station smoke alarms you inspect yourself on the regulation's schedule, keeping a log on site (815 KAR 10:060, Sections 3(6) and 7(2)). In every locality, an owner must furnish reasonably adequate protection against fire loss and may not let the public into property the owner controls that is not reasonably safe from fire loss (KRS 227.400(1)-(2)).

Where your city or county has adopted Kentucky's Uniform Residential Landlord and Tenant Act ("Where Kentucky's Landlord-Tenant Act Applies"), you must comply with building and housing codes materially affecting health and safety (KRS 383.595(1)(a)), and your tenant must comply with the code duties placed on tenants (KRS 383.605(1)). Where it has not, the codes bind you directly and the lease governs the tenant's duties to you. For the model codes' detailed requirements, ask your fire marshal or local fire chief. See "Which Code Editions Apply" for the editions, "Fire Sprinklers in Rental Buildings", "Smoke and Carbon Monoxide Alarms", and the optional "Fire Safety" clause.

title: Fire Sprinklers in Rental Buildings
bodyText: No Kentucky statute requires a residential landlord to add or retrofit sprinklers in an existing building, in either tier. Whether a building needs sprinklers depends on the building code in force when it was built. The Kentucky Building Code adopts the 2015 International Building Code, with Kentucky amendments, for every building except one- and two-family dwellings and townhouses (815 KAR 7:120, Section 2). Those homes follow the Kentucky Residential Code, built on the 2015 International Residential Code (815 KAR 7:125, Section 2). Ask your building official what applies to your building. For buildings other than one- and two-family dwellings, the state fire code protects an existing building's original approvals. The building code standards in effect when it was built, with a lawful certificate of occupancy, control over different fire code standards for fire protection and built-in fire protection equipment (815 KAR 10:060, Sections 2(1) and 3(1)). A building put up before the statewide code is kept as built and approved (815 KAR 10:060, Section 3(3)(a)). Fixing a distinct fire hazard cannot require more construction than the current code requires of a new building (815 KAR 10:060, Section 3(5)). A change of use needs plan review and approval (815 KAR 10:060, Section 3(2)). If your building has sprinklers, you must keep them maintained under the applicable NFPA code and the manufacturer's instructions, and you may not remove them without approval (815 KAR 10:060, Section 3(6)). A certified person must inspect and test them every year and give you a report, with a copy to the local fire chief within 10 working days (815 KAR 10:060, Section 7(2)). Only a licensed sprinkler contractor may install, repair or maintain a system, except small domestic-supply systems of ten heads or fewer (KRS 198B.560). Where your city or county has adopted Kentucky's Uniform Residential Landlord and Tenant Act ("Where Kentucky's Landlord-Tenant Act Applies"), you must comply with building and housing codes materially affecting health and safety and keep facilities you supply in good and safe working order (KRS 383.595(1)(a), (d)). Where it has not, the codes bind you directly. In every locality, an owner must furnish reasonably adequate protection against fire loss (KRS 227.400(1)). See "Kentucky's Fire Code". Insurers must offer a premium credit for buildings with automatic sprinklers (KRS 304.20-380). On-campus housing run by colleges has its own sprinkler disclosure rule (KRS 164.9492). The Kentucky Revised Statutes, the Kentucky Constitution, the 2025 and 2026 Acts and the state regulations on building and fire safety, public health, utilities, environment and human rights and those of the Attorney General and the Real Estate Commission contain no sprinkler retrofit duty for landlords.

title: No Statutory Relief From Lease Forfeiture
bodyText: No Kentucky statute lets a court relieve a residential tenant from the forfeiture of a lease, or reinstate a lease that ended for unpaid rent or another breach. The Kentucky Revised Statutes, the Kentucky Constitution, the 2025 and 2026 Acts and the state regulations on building and fire safety, public health, utilities, environment and human rights and those of the Attorney General and the Real Estate Commission contain no such rule. Where your city or county has adopted Kentucky's Uniform Residential Landlord and Tenant Act ("Where Kentucky's Landlord-Tenant Act Applies"), a tenant can save the lease only before it ends. For unpaid rent the tenant has seven days after your written notice to pay (KRS 383.660(2)). For another material breach that can be remedied by repairs, paying damages or otherwise, the lease does not terminate if the tenant adequately remedies it before the date in your notice (KRS 383.660(1); "Cure Periods"). Kentucky's older statutes declare some forfeitures but give no relief from them. Unless you consent in writing, an assignment or transfer of all or part of the term by a tenant at will or by sufferance, or by one with a term under two years, works a forfeiture (KRS 383.180(2)). Where the Act has not been adopted, you may then recover possession after ten days of written notice to quit (KRS 383.180(2)). Where it has, you may recover possession only as the Act permits, so treat an assignment the lease bars as a breach and give the Act's notice (KRS 383.690, 383.660(1)); no statute settles whether the forfeiture itself applies there. In every locality, a tenant for years who commits waste without written permission loses the thing wasted and pays treble damages (KRS 381.350). Once a lease has ended, the tenant's ways to stay are an appeal with the rent deposit (KRS 383.255) or your agreement ("No Right to Pay and Stop an Eviction"). Whether a court would grant equitable relief from a forfeiture is case law. If you agree to reinstate a lease, put it in writing after the breach, since accepting rent with knowledge of a default can waive termination where the Act applies (KRS 383.675).

title: Which Code Editions Apply
bodyText: Kentucky's building and fire codes adopt named, dated editions of the model codes, and those editions stay in force until the regulation itself is amended. A state regulation that incorporates outside material must give its title and edition date (KRS 13A.2251(1)(a)). Changing that material takes an amendment to the regulation with a new edition date (KRS 13A.2255(1)(a)). So a newer edition published by the code's author does not apply in Kentucky until the state adopts it. Building Code (815 KAR 7:120, Sections 2 and 5): the 2015 International Building Code, with the 2018 Kentucky Building Code, Fourth Edition, February 2024, whose Kentucky amendments control where they conflict. It covers every building except one- and two-family dwellings, townhouses and manufactured homes. Residential Code (815 KAR 7:125, Sections 2 and 3): the 2015 International Residential Code for One and Two Family Dwellings, with the 2018 Kentucky Residential Code, Third Edition, August 2024, for single-family homes, two-family dwellings and townhouses. Fire code (815 KAR 10:060, Sections 3(4)(c) and 8): the NFPA 1 Uniform Fire Code, 2018 edition, and the NFPA standards listed in its Chapter 2; the NFPA 101 Life Safety Code, 2018 edition; the National Electrical Code (NFPA 70), 2017 edition; and NFPA 1124, 2006 edition, for consumer fireworks sales. The fire code uses 2018 NFPA editions while the building code is built on the 2015 International Building Code; the fire code's abatement rule points to the current Kentucky Building Code (815 KAR 10:060, Section 3(5)). Two references are not tied to a fixed edition. Sprinkler inspections follow NFPA 25 in the edition the commissioner prescribes (KRS 198B.6411). A neighborhood redevelopment zone must adopt the BOCA Basic Property Maintenance Code without any edition named (KRS 99A.030(1)). Get the model codes themselves, and the editions of the NFPA standards listed in NFPA 1's Chapter 2, from the Department of Housing, Buildings and Construction, which the regulations name as the place to inspect them. See "Kentucky's Fire Code" and "Fire Sprinklers in Rental Buildings".

title: Renting a Home Furnished
bodyText:
No Kentucky statute sets special rules for renting a home furnished, in either tier. The Kentucky Revised Statutes, the Kentucky Constitution, the 2025 and 2026 Acts and the state regulations on building and fire safety, public health, utilities, environment and human rights and those of the Attorney General and the Real Estate Commission contain no such rule.

So what furniture you supply, its condition and its return are for the lease. The optional furnishings clause lists the items and their condition and has the tenant return them, except for normal wear and tear. Where your city or county has adopted Kentucky's Uniform Residential Landlord and Tenant Act ("Where Kentucky's Landlord-Tenant Act Applies"), the tenant must not deliberately or negligently destroy, damage or remove any part of the premises (KRS 383.605(6)). There a security deposit secures you against damage to the premises beyond ordinary wear and tear (KRS 383.545(13)).

Before taking a deposit, you must give the tenant a signed listing of existing damage to the unit, and at move-out a listing of damage you will charge (KRS 383.580(2), (3); "Condition of the Property at Move-In" clause). If you may charge the deposit for damaged furniture, put the furniture and its condition in those listings. Without both listings and the separate deposit account, you may not keep any part of the deposit (KRS 383.580(4); "Security Deposit" clause). Where the Act has not been adopted, no statute governs deposits or furnishings; the lease governs.

Kentucky caps neither security deposits nor a separate furniture deposit ("No Security Deposit Cap"). Appliances you supply are listed separately ("Appliances & Equipment Included" clause), and where the Act applies you must keep them in good and safe working order (KRS 383.595(1)(d)).

title: No Good-Cause Eviction Notice
bodyText: Kentucky has no good-cause or just-cause eviction law. So there is no notice telling a tenant whether a unit is covered by one, no statutory form for it, and no reason you must state when you decline to renew. The Kentucky Revised Statutes, the Kentucky Constitution, the 2025 and 2026 Acts and the state regulations on building and fire safety, public health, utilities, environment and human rights and those of the Attorney General and the Real Estate Commission contain no such rule. To end a periodic tenancy you give the notice the law and the lease require ("Ending a Periodic Tenancy"). A fixed term ends on its last day ("No Just-Cause Eviction Rule"). Limits still apply: no retaliation where your city or county has adopted Kentucky's Uniform Residential Landlord and Tenant Act, no ending or refusing to renew because a tenant is protected by a protective order, for leases created or renewed on or after June 29, 2017 (KRS 383.300(3)(a); "No Adverse Action Against Protected Tenants"), and fair housing law everywhere. No local government may adopt or enforce a landlord-tenant ordinance that conflicts with state law (KRS 383.198). Where a city or county has adopted the Act, it may enact no other ordinance on the subjects the Act covers (KRS 383.500; "Local Landlord-Tenant Ordinances"). Federal rules for some subsidized housing, such as a Housing Choice Voucher tenancy ("Federal Rules for a Housing Choice Voucher Lease"), can require cause to end a tenancy.

title: Passing Government Fines to Tenants
bodyText: No Kentucky statute says whether a lease may pass a government fine on to a tenant, or makes a tenant liable to the owner for one, in any locality. The library's "Local Government Fees" clause passes through local registration or licensing fees only, and excludes fines, penalties and emergency response fees. Statewide, a local government, special district or other provider may not bill you an emergency response fee for a response arising out of a residential tenant's or guest's actions (KRS 65.111(2)(a)). That bar does not apply where the response resulted from your failure to keep the building in compliance with housing, building, fire, health or nuisance codes (KRS 65.111(2)(a)). The provider may still bill a responsible party (KRS 65.111(2)(b)). This version took effect June 27, 2025 (2025 Ky. Acts ch. 56, sec. 7). No fine or fee may be assessed on a non-occupying residential owner, and no lien placed on the property, for an occupant's failure to contract for or pay for solid waste pick-up, unless the owner agreed to pay for it; the occupant may be fined instead (KRS 109.310(6); "Tenant Utility Bills as Liens"). For local nuisance violations, the owner is personally liable for the civil fines and abatement costs secured by the local government lien (KRS 65.8840(9), (11)). Where your city or county has adopted Kentucky's Uniform Residential Landlord and Tenant Act ("Where Kentucky's Landlord-Tenant Act Applies"), a lease may not make the tenant indemnify you for a liability of yours arising under law, or its costs (KRS 383.570(1)(d)). A fine the law imposes on you is probably such a liability, so a clause making the tenant reimburse it may be unenforceable there. Instead, the tenant must comply with code duties imposed on tenants and must not damage the premises (KRS 383.605(1), (6)). You may recover damages for the tenant's breach of the lease or of those duties (KRS 383.660(3)), which can include a fine the breach caused. Where the Act has not been adopted, no statute bars a lease term making the tenant repay a fine the tenant caused. In every locality, a lease may not penalize a tenant for calling police or seeking emergency help (KRS 383.302; leases created or renewed on or after June 29, 2017; "Penalties for Unlawful Lease Terms"). So never pass on a fine or fee tied to such a call. The library does not offer a clause making the tenant repay fines the tenant causes, because where the Act applies it may be an unenforceable indemnity. If you want one, add your own with legal advice, and exclude any fine or fee tied to a call for police or emergency help. The Kentucky Revised Statutes, the Kentucky Constitution, the 2025 and 2026 Acts and the state regulations on building and fire safety, public health, utilities, environment and human rights and those of the Attorney General and the Real Estate Commission contain no rule on passing government fines to tenants.

title: How Serious a Repair Problem Must Be
bodyText: Where your city or county has adopted Kentucky's Uniform Residential Landlord and Tenant Act ("Where Kentucky's Landlord-Tenant Act Applies"), how serious a problem must be depends on the remedy the tenant uses. To end the lease on written notice, the tenant needs a material breach of the lease, or a breach of your repair duties that materially affects health and safety (KRS 383.625(1)). To sue for damages or an injunction, any breach of the lease or of those duties is enough; no materiality test applies (KRS 383.625(2)). To repair and deduct, you must have willfully and materially breached the lease, or breached your repair duties in a way that materially affects health and safety, and the reasonable cost must be under $100 or half a month's rent, whichever is more (KRS 383.635(1)). For heat, water, hot water, electricity, gas or another essential service, the test is a willful failure to supply it, not materiality (KRS 383.640(1)). Your first repair duty is to comply with building and housing codes materially affecting health and safety, and that duty controls where it asks more than the others (KRS 383.595(1)(a), (2)). Retaliation protection covers a tenant who complained to a code agency about a violation materially affecting health and safety (KRS 383.705(1)(a)). It also covers a tenant who complained to you of any breach of your repair duties, with no materiality test (KRS 383.705(1)(b)). The same words run the other way: you may give notice to end the lease for the tenant's material breach (KRS 383.660(1)). No Kentucky statute defines material, lists conditions that always count, or excludes minor defects; that is decided on the facts and the local housing code. Where the Act has not been adopted, no statute gives the tenant a repair remedy, so there is no statutory materiality test; the lease and case law govern ("Tenant Remedies for Repairs and Services"). In every locality the local-enforcement standard is an owner letting a structure become unfit and unsafe for human habitation, or letting conditions exist that are dangerous or injurious to the health or safety of occupants (KRS 65.8840(5)). See "Landlord's Repair Duties".

title: What an Agreement Can and Cannot Change About Habitability Duties
bodyText: Where your city or county has adopted Kentucky's Uniform Residential Landlord and Tenant Act ("Where Kentucky's Landlord-Tenant Act Applies"), an agreement can change who performs some of your duties, but not the duties themselves ("Habitability Duties Cannot Be Waived"). The water, hot-water and heat duty does not apply where the building is not required by law to be equipped for it, or where heat or hot water for the unit comes from an installation in the exclusive control of the tenant with its own direct utility connection (KRS 383.595(1)(e)). Those exceptions are facts about the building, not terms a lease can create. Where the duty to meet building and housing codes materially affecting health and safety is greater than any other listed duty, it controls (KRS 383.595(2)). In a single family residence you and the tenant may agree in writing that the tenant supplies the water, hot water and heat and performs specified repairs, maintenance tasks, alterations and remodeling, if made in good faith and not to evade your duties (KRS 383.595(3)). In any other unit the tenant can take on only specified repairs, maintenance, alterations or remodeling, in a separate writing signed by both of you and supported by adequate consideration. That writing cannot cover work needed to meet the health-and-safety codes and cannot reduce what you owe other tenants (KRS 383.595(4)). Kentucky has no special rule for a property with no well or utility water; the supply duty is shifted, if at all, only in those ways. See "Shifting Maintenance Tasks to the Tenant" and the separate "Tenant Maintenance Agreement (Separate Document)" clause agreement. Where the Act has not been adopted, no statute sets a habitability duty, so the lease sets the split of repair work. There, a promise by the tenant to repair does not oblige the tenant to rebuild after a fire or other casualty that was not the tenant's fault, unless the written lease expressly says so (KRS 383.170). In every locality the owner's duty not to let a structure become unfit and unsafe for human habitation stays with the owner, whatever the lease says, because a local government enforces it against the owner (KRS 65.8840(5), (7)).

title: No Presumption of a Habitability Breach
bodyText: No Kentucky statute presumes that you breached a repair or habitability duty, that a unit is unfit, or that you took too long to make a repair. The Kentucky Revised Statutes, the Kentucky Constitution, the 2025 and 2026 Acts and the state regulations on building and fire safety, public health, utilities, environment and human rights and those of the Attorney General and the Real Estate Commission contain no such presumption. So the ordinary burden applies: a tenant who claims a breach must prove it. Where your city or county has adopted Kentucky's Uniform Residential Landlord and Tenant Act ("Where Kentucky's Landlord-Tenant Act Applies"), the tenant must also give you the written notices the remedies require ("Tenant Remedies for Repairs and Services"). The Act has one presumption that touches repairs, and it is about retaliation, not condition. If the tenant complained to a code agency or to you within one year before you raised the rent, cut services or sued or threatened to sue for possession, a court presumes that you acted in retaliation (KRS 383.705(2)). That presumption does not arise if the complaint came after notice of a proposed rent increase or cut in services, and evidence supporting a finding that you did not retaliate overcomes it (KRS 383.705(2); "Retaliation"). The Act also makes the signed move-in and move-out damage lists conclusive evidence of their accuracy, except for latent defects at move-in, but that rule decides deposit charges, not habitability (KRS 383.580(2)-(3); "Condition of the Property at Move-In" clause). Where the Act has not been adopted, no statute sets either rule. Practical point: keep repair requests, your responses and dated photos, since in a dispute the evidence decides.

title: No Required Habitability Statement in the Lease
bodyText: No Kentucky statute requires your lease to state that the unit is, or will be delivered, fit for habitation. The Kentucky Revised Statutes, the Kentucky Constitution, the 2025 and 2026 Acts and the state regulations on building and fire safety, public health, utilities, environment and human rights and those of the Attorney General and the Real Estate Commission contain no such requirement. Where your city or county has adopted Kentucky's Uniform Residential Landlord and Tenant Act ("Where Kentucky's Landlord-Tenant Act Applies"), the duty applies whether or not the lease mentions it. At the start of the term you must deliver possession in compliance with the lease and your repair duties (KRS 383.590; "Landlord's Repair Duties"). The writings the Act does require are the manager and owner disclosure (KRS 383.585; "Manager and Owner Disclosure" clause) and, before taking a security deposit, the signed list of existing damage (KRS 383.580(2); "Condition of the Property at Move-In" clause). Where the Act has not been adopted, no statute requires either a fitness statement or those writings. In every locality, anything the lease does promise about condition is a term you can be held to; in a locality with the Act, a material breach of the lease is grounds for the tenant to end it on notice (KRS 383.625(1)). So describe the actual condition and your repair duties accurately, and avoid broad promises such as that the unit meets every code. See "Other Required Lease Notices".

title: Habitability Duties Cannot Be Waived
bodyText: Where your city or county has adopted Kentucky's Uniform Residential Landlord and Tenant Act ("Where Kentucky's Landlord-Tenant Act Applies"), a lease cannot waive your habitability duties. Those duties are to meet building and housing codes materially affecting health and safety, make repairs to keep the premises fit and habitable, keep common areas clean and safe, keep supplied facilities and appliances working, and supply water, hot water and heat (KRS 383.595(1); "Landlord's Repair Duties"). No lease may let you collect rent free of those duties (KRS 383.575). A term by which the tenant waives or forgoes a right or remedy under the Act, such as the repair remedies, is unenforceable (KRS 383.570(1)(a), (2)). So an as-is clause, a release of your repair duties or a promise not to use the tenant's repair remedies does not work there. What the Act allows is moving who does some of the work, not removing the standard. In a single family residence the tenant may agree in writing to supply the water, hot water and heat and to do specified repairs and maintenance, if done in good faith and not to evade your duties (KRS 383.595(3)). In any other unit only specified repairs, maintenance, alterations or remodeling can move, by a separate signed writing with adequate consideration, never work needed to meet the health-and-safety codes (KRS 383.595(4)). Kentucky has no rule letting a tenant accept named defects for a rent reduction. Where the Act has not been adopted, no statute puts a general habitability or repair duty on you, so there is no statutory duty for a lease to waive; a waiver of a rule that does not exist is empty, not a lawful choice. Whether Kentucky courts imply a warranty of habitability, and whether a lease could waive it, is case law. In every locality an owner must not let a structure become unfit and unsafe for human habitation, a duty local governments enforce with fines and liens; nothing in that statute turns on the lease (KRS 65.8840(5), (7), (9)). The cautious course everywhere is to leave as-is and habitability-waiver language out of the lease, state your repair duties plainly, and use "Tenant Maintenance Agreement (Separate Document)" clause or the lease's own task sections to shift named tasks ("Shifting Maintenance Tasks to the Tenant").

title: Contamination Disclosures
bodyText: Kentucky's only contamination disclosure to tenants is for methamphetamine; see "Methamphetamine Contamination" and the clause "Methamphetamine Contamination Disclosure". If a methamphetamine contamination notice has been posted on your property, you must disclose in writing to any potential tenant that it is contaminated and has not been decontaminated (KRS 224.1-410(10)). The duty ends once the Energy and Environment Cabinet releases the property after decontamination (KRS 224.1-410(10); 902 KAR 47:200, Section 5). The disclosure must give the property address, the location in the property used to make methamphetamine, and a copy of the posted notice. You sign and date the disclosure statement and keep a copy for as long as you own the property (902 KAR 47:200, Section 4(1), (2)). On request, you must give the tenant copies of documents about the contamination you received from law enforcement or the state or local agencies (902 KAR 47:200, Section 4(4)). Failing to disclose is a Class D felony (902 KAR 47:200, Section 4(6)). Cleaned-up sites are different. When the cabinet approves an environmental covenant limiting how a remediated property may be used, a copy must be given to each person in possession of the property (KRS 224.80-160(1)(c)). The covenant runs with the land (KRS 224.80-140(1)), and it may require notice when an interest in the property is transferred (KRS 224.80-130(2)(a)). If your property is subject to one, read it before you lease; the cabinet keeps a public registry (KRS 224.80-210). No other Kentucky statute or regulation requires you to disclose hazardous substances, petroleum, a brownfield or other contamination to a tenant. The Kentucky Revised Statutes, the Kentucky Constitution, the 2025 and 2026 Acts and the state regulations on building and fire safety, public health, utilities, environment and human rights and those of the Attorney General and the Real Estate Commission contain no other such rule. For mold, radon, lead and asbestos, see "Mold Disclosure", "Radon Disclosure", "Lead Hazards and Children" and "Asbestos in Rental Buildings". Where your city or county has adopted Kentucky's Uniform Residential Landlord and Tenant Act ("Where Kentucky's Landlord-Tenant Act Applies"), your building and housing code and habitability duties also apply (KRS 383.595(1)(a), (b)).

title: Local Health Department Rules for Rentals
bodyText: Kentucky's state health regulations contain no rental housing code. No statute or regulation requires you to give tenants your local health department's rules or to refer tenants to it, in either tier. The Kentucky Revised Statutes, the Kentucky Constitution, the 2025 and 2026 Acts and the state regulations on building and fire safety, public health, utilities, environment and human rights and those of the Attorney General and the Real Estate Commission contain no such duty. The state hotel and motel code does not reach apartments, single- or multi-family homes or vacation rental cabins (902 KAR 7:010, Section 2(2)). Local health departments still have power over rentals. A county, city-county or district board of health may adopt regulations needed to protect health, if they do not conflict with the state health cabinet's regulations (KRS 212.230(1)(c)). The cabinet or the local board may order the owner or occupant of private property in writing to remove a nuisance, source of filth or cause of sickness within 24 hours or a reasonable time it sets (KRS 212.210(1)). Not complying is fined $10 to $100, and each day is a separate offense (KRS 212.990(1)). In most counties, violating a local board's regulation is fined $10 to $100 for each day it continues (KRS 212.990(2)). A local health department may order compliance with state and local health rules, and its officers may enter premises when necessary to inspect (KRS 212.245(6)-(7)). For a building with two or more apartment units, the local board must require the owner to provide approved waste receptacles where a refuse area is designated (KRS 212.210(4)). A local lead program's rules must be the same as the state's (KRS 211.901(6); "Kentucky Lead Notices and Orders"). Separately, every owner must not let a structure become unfit and unsafe for habitation, a duty local governments enforce by ordinance (KRS 65.8840(5), (7), as amended effective April 14, 2026; "Rental Inspections"). Where your city or county has adopted Kentucky's Uniform Residential Landlord and Tenant Act ("Where Kentucky's Landlord-Tenant Act Applies"), you must comply with building and housing codes materially affecting health and safety (KRS 383.595(1)(a)). Those codes include any governmental regulation concerning fitness for habitation (KRS 383.545(2)). Where it has not, the health orders above still bind you as owner. No local landlord-tenant ordinance may conflict with state law (KRS 383.198; "Local Landlord-Tenant Ordinances"). Ask your local health department what it enforces.

title: Home Businesses in a Rental
bodyText:
No Kentucky statute gives a tenant a right to run a business from a rental home, or stops a lease from banning or limiting one, in either tier. The Kentucky Revised Statutes, the Kentucky Constitution, the 2025 and 2026 Acts and the state regulations on building and fire safety, public health, utilities, environment and human rights and those of the Attorney General and the Real Estate Commission contain no such rule.

So business use is for the lease. "Residential Use Only" clause bars non-residential use, and "Home-Based Business (Landlord's Permission)" clause lets you allow a named business on your conditions. Whether a home business is allowed at the address is for local zoning under chapter 100 KRS, which may require a home occupation permit.

No state statute limits those zoning rules, and no local landlord-tenant ordinance may conflict with state law (KRS 383.198; "Local Landlord-Tenant Ordinances"). One state rule reaches food made at home. A home-based processor may sell labeled home-produced foods directly to consumers, including from the processor's home, if it registers with the Cabinet for Health and Family Services (KRS 217.136(5), (11)). The cabinet may inspect its processing facilities each year (KRS 217.136(7)). That rule does not override your lease.

Where your city or county has adopted Kentucky's Uniform Residential Landlord and Tenant Act ("Where Kentucky's Landlord-Tenant Act Applies"), the lease may include terms the Act and other law do not bar (KRS 383.565(1)). There a business-use clause may not have the tenant indemnify you or limit your liability under law (KRS 383.570(1)(d)). Where the Act has not been adopted, the lease governs. Child care run from the home is a separate topic, family child care.

title: No Duty to Disclose Inspection or Condemnation Orders
bodyText: No Kentucky statute or regulation requires you to give a tenant or prospective tenant copies of inspection reports, code violation notices, or condemnation or vacate orders. The Kentucky Revised Statutes, the Kentucky Constitution, the 2025 and 2026 Acts and the state regulations on building and fire safety, public health, utilities, environment and human rights and those of the Attorney General and the Real Estate Commission contain no such rule. One posted notice must be disclosed: where a methamphetamine contamination notice has been posted, you must tell any potential tenant in writing that the property is contaminated and not yet decontaminated (KRS 224.1-410(10); "Methamphetamine Contamination"). The closest other rule is for lead. Where the health cabinet finds lead-based hazards in a home where a child under six lives, it notifies both the owner and the occupant (KRS 211.905(2)(a)). If you do not fix the hazards within 60 days, the cabinet posts the unit as unfit for human habitation for children under six, and the posting stays until you comply (KRS 211.905(4)). A finding that a child under six is in immediate danger is cause for releasing the occupant from the lease without prejudice (KRS 211.905(5)). See "Unfit or Condemned Units" and "Lead Hazards and Children". Local code enforcement runs against owners: an owner must not let a structure become unfit and unsafe for habitation (KRS 65.8840(5)). Notices and hearings under that section go to the owner and lienholders, not tenants (KRS 65.8840(7), (8)). In buildings other than one- and two-family dwellings, a building not occupied for a year or more must be inspected by the State Fire Marshal or a designee before it is occupied again (815 KAR 10:060, Section 3(3)(c)). Where your city or county has adopted Kentucky's Uniform Residential Landlord and Tenant Act ("Where Kentucky's Landlord-Tenant Act Applies"), you must comply with building and housing codes materially affecting health and safety (KRS 383.595(1)(a)); see "Landlord's Repair Duties". Where it has not, the lease and local codes govern. Your city's own housing code may require more. Telling a prospective tenant in writing about any open order that affects the unit is the cautious course.

title: Inspection Notices and the Deposit Penalty
bodyText: No Kentucky statute requires you to notify a tenant of a move-in or move-out inspection, or of a right to attend one, and none sets a penalty for skipping such a notice. Where your city or county has adopted Kentucky's Uniform Residential Landlord and Tenant Act ("Where Kentucky's Landlord-Tenant Act Applies"), the inspection duties are the two signed damage lists (KRS 383.580(2)-(3); "Move-In and Move-Out Damage Lists"). At move-out you inspect and list any damage charged to the deposit, and the tenant then has the right to inspect to check the list (KRS 383.580(3)). The penalty attaches to the lists and the account, not to a notice. You are not entitled to keep any part of the deposit if it was not kept in a separate account and the move-in and move-out lists were not provided (KRS 383.580(4)). The statute joins the two failures with "and"; to be safe, meet both duties ("Losing the Right to Keep a Deposit"). A tenant who disputes the move-out list may sue in District Court only over items the tenant dissented from in writing (KRS 383.580(5)). A tenant who neither signs the list nor dissents cannot recover damages under the deposit statute (KRS 383.580(5)). That limit works best when the tenant was actually offered the list and the chance to inspect, so tell the tenant when the list is ready. If the tenant still lives in the home, an inspection is an entry and needs at least two days' notice, except in an emergency or where that is impracticable (KRS 383.615(3); "Landlord's Right of Entry" clause). Where the Act has not been adopted, no statute requires damage lists, inspection notices or a deposit penalty; your lease governs ("Where to Keep the Security Deposit"). The Kentucky Revised Statutes, the Kentucky Constitution, the 2025 and 2026 Acts and the state regulations on building and fire safety, public health, utilities, environment and human rights and those of the Attorney General and the Real Estate Commission contain no inspection-notice rule or penalty.

title: No Key-Control Mandate
bodyText: No Kentucky statute or regulation requires a key-control policy, a master-key log, background checks of staff who handle tenant keys, or rekeying between tenants, in either tier. The Kentucky Revised Statutes, the Kentucky Constitution, the 2025 and 2026 Acts and the state regulations on building and fire safety, public health, utilities, environment and human rights and those of the Attorney General and the Real Estate Commission contain none. So how you issue, track and recover keys is for your own policy and the lease (`keys` covers key receipts and return; "Locks and Security Devices" covers locks). One statute limits a lease rule requiring your consent to a lock change. For leases created or renewed on or after June 29, 2017, a tenant protected by a domestic violence or interpersonal protective order may rekey or replace a lock at their own expense after telling you (KRS 383.300(1)(a), (4)(a)1.). The tenant must give you a key to the new lock if you ask, and you may refuse a key to the restrained person even if that person is on the lease (KRS 383.300(4)(a)2., (4)(b); "Lock Changes by Protected Tenants"). Where your city or county has adopted Kentucky's Uniform Residential Landlord and Tenant Act ("Where Kentucky's Landlord-Tenant Act Applies"), entry with a key still follows the Act's access rules ("Landlord's Right of Entry" clause); where it has not, the lease governs entry.

title: What a Tenant Can Do When You Breach
bodyText:
Where your city or county has adopted Kentucky's Uniform Residential Landlord and Tenant Act ("Where Kentucky's Landlord-Tenant Act Applies"), a tenant has these remedies when you breach, set out in full in "Tenant Remedies for Repairs and Services". For a material breach of the lease, or a breach of your repair duties materially affecting health and safety, the tenant may give written notice ending the lease at least 30 days later unless you fix it within 14 days (KRS 383.625(1)). Any breach supports damages and an injunction (KRS 383.625(2)). A small health-and-safety repair you willfully fail to make may be done by the tenant and deducted from rent, within the limit in KRS 383.635.

If you willfully fail to supply heat, water, hot water, electricity, gas or another essential service, the tenant may buy it and deduct the cost, recover reduced rental value, or move to substitute housing rent-free and recover attorney fees; choosing this route rules out the other repair remedies for that breach (KRS 383.640). If you do not deliver possession at the start, rent abates and the tenant may end the lease on five days' written notice or sue for possession and damages (KRS 383.630(1)).

If the failure is willful and not in good faith, the tenant may recover up to three months' periodic rent or three times actual damages, whichever is greater, and attorney fees (KRS 383.630(2)). Unlawfully removing or excluding the tenant, or willfully cutting essential services, lets the tenant recover possession or end the lease and recover up to three months' periodic rent and attorney fees (KRS 383.655). In your nonpayment or rent action the tenant may counterclaim, and the court may order rent paid into court (KRS 383.645). Termination, repair-and-deduct and the essential-services remedies are not available for a condition caused by the tenant, a family member or another person on the premises with the consent of the tenant (KRS 383.625(1)(c), 383.635(2), 383.640(4)).

No Kentucky statute lets a tenant withhold rent or pay it into an escrow account on the tenant's own decision because of a repair problem, including for lead hazards. The Kentucky Revised Statutes, the Kentucky Constitution, the 2025 and 2026 Acts and the state regulations on building and fire safety, public health, utilities, environment and human rights and those of the Attorney General and the Real Estate Commission contain no such rule. Where the Act has not been adopted, no statute gives a tenant a remedy for your failure to repair; the lease and case law govern.

Statewide, a health cabinet finding that a child under six is in immediate danger from lead hazards is cause for releasing the occupant from the lease (KRS 211.905(5)).

title: Landlord Liability Insurance
bodyText: No Kentucky statute requires a residential landlord to carry liability or property insurance, to show tenants proof of insurance, or to file insurance with a registration, in either tier. The Kentucky Revised Statutes, the Kentucky Constitution, the 2025 and 2026 Acts and the state regulations on building and fire safety, public health, utilities, environment and human rights and those of the Attorney General and the Real Estate Commission contain no such rule. Your lender, a homeowners or condominium association, or a housing program contract may still require coverage. An association formed after June 29, 2023, must insure its own common areas unless its declaration provides otherwise; that duty falls on the association, not on you (KRS 381.790(2)). Carrying insurance is prudent, because a lease cannot do much to shift your liability. Where your city or county has adopted Kentucky's Uniform Residential Landlord and Tenant Act ("Where Kentucky's Landlord-Tenant Act Applies"), a lease may not have the tenant agree to excuse or limit any liability of yours arising under law, or to indemnify you for it. Such a term is unenforceable (KRS 383.570(1)(d), (2); "Liability Waivers"). Where the Act has not been adopted, no statute governs such terms, and whether a court enforces one is case law. Requiring the tenant to carry renter's insurance is a separate question ("Renter's Insurance Requirements"). Contractors you hire may have their own insurance duties; for example, a plumbing business must carry general liability insurance of at least $250,000 (KRS 318.030(2)(a)). Local rental registration or licensing ordinances may add conditions.

title: Your Remedies When a Tenancy Ends for Breach
bodyText: Your remedies when a Kentucky tenancy ends for the tenant's breach depend on whether your city or county has adopted the Uniform Residential Landlord and Tenant Act ("Where Kentucky's Landlord-Tenant Act Applies"). In every locality, recover possession only through a forcible detainer case in District Court ("The Eviction (Forcible Detainer) Process"), never by a lockout ("No Lockouts or Utility Shutoffs"). The eviction case does not bar a separate action for trespass, waste, rent or mesne profits (KRS 383.280). Where the Act applies, once the lease is terminated you may claim possession and rent, and separately your actual damages for the breach (KRS 383.685). Attorney's fees come only where a statute allows them, such as for a tenant's willful noncompliance (KRS 383.660(3); "Attorney Fees in Landlord-Tenant Cases"). You may also recover damages and get an injunction for a tenant's noncompliance without ending the lease (KRS 383.660(3)). Other remedies there: repair and bill for a tenant's failure to maintain ("Fixing Tenant Damage Yourself"); an injunction or termination, with damages and fees, when a tenant refuses lawful access (KRS 383.700(1)); and extra damages for a willful holdover ("Holdover Rent"). You must mitigate your damages and try to re-rent an abandoned unit (KRS 383.520(1), 383.670(3); "Re-Renting After a Tenant Leaves Early"). In a nonpayment case the tenant may counterclaim, and the court may order rent paid into court (KRS 383.645; "Counterclaims and Rent Paid Into Court"). Seizing a tenant's goods for rent (distraint) is abolished there (KRS 383.680(2)). In every locality, unpaid rent may be recovered by action and bears 6% interest a year from when it is due (KRS 383.010(1)). Without a written lease you may recover reasonable satisfaction for the use of the property (KRS 383.090). Where the Act has not been adopted, the older statutes also give a lien on the tenant's personal property for up to four months' rent (KRS 383.070(2)), enforced through a court attachment after you post a bond (KRS 383.030(1)). A resident tenant's household furnishings, jewelry, clothing and ornaments up to $3,000 in value, and other listed property, are exempt from attachment (KRS 427.010(1); "The Landlord's Lien for Rent"). There, the lease and case law govern your damages and whether you must mitigate, so try to re-rent ("Re-Renting After a Tenant Leaves Early"). Apply the deposit as "Security Deposit" clause allows. Which court: District Court hears civil claims of $5,000 or less, not counting interest and costs (KRS 24A.120(1)). Its small claims division hears claims of $2,500 or less (KRS 24A.230(1)). Larger claims go to Circuit Court (KRS 23A.010(1)). No Kentucky statute allows or bars a lease term making all rent for the rest of the term due at once (acceleration). Because of the mitigation duty where the Act applies, and penalty case law, claim rent accrued to date plus actual, mitigated losses rather than the whole remaining term.

title: No Late Fee Cap
bodyText: No Kentucky statute caps a late fee on a residential lease or sets a grace period, in any locality ("Late Fees in Kentucky"). The library's Kentucky late-fee clause is "Late Fee" clause, with your own amount and grace period. Kentucky's one rental late-fee rule covers self-service storage units only, not homes (KRS 359.215; KRS 359.200). Other statutory late-fee caps found apply to utilities, loans and licences, not to leases. Unpaid rent also bears 6% interest a year from its due date by statute (KRS 383.010(1)). A court could refuse to enforce a very large fee as a penalty; that is case law. The cautious course is a fee reasonably related to what late payment costs you, stated in the lease. The Kentucky Revised Statutes, the Kentucky Constitution, the 2025 and 2026 Acts and the state regulations on building and fire safety, public health, utilities, environment and human rights and those of the Attorney General and the Real Estate Commission contain no late-fee cap for residential leases.

title: Working With Police
bodyText: No Kentucky statute requires a landlord to cooperate with police, give officers tenant information, or join a crime-free housing program. None regulates crime-free or drug-free lease addenda ("Drug-Free Housing Addenda"). The Kentucky Revised Statutes, the Kentucky Constitution, the 2025 and 2026 Acts and the state regulations on building and fire safety, public health, utilities, environment and human rights and those of the Attorney General and the Real Estate Commission contain no such duty or program. The Uniform Residential Landlord and Tenant Act, where your city or county has adopted it ("Where Kentucky's Landlord-Tenant Act Applies"), adds nothing on police cooperation. Where it has not, the older statutes (KRS 383.010 to 383.302) add nothing either. What Kentucky does have applies in every locality. A lease may not let you end the tenancy or penalize the tenant for asking for help from police or other emergency help.
