This applies to leases created or renewed on or after June 29, 2017 (KRS 383.302; "Calls for Police or Emergency Help"). The library's "Criminal Activity" clause carves those calls out. A local government or other provider may not bill you an emergency response fee for a response arising out of a tenant's or guest's actions, unless your failure to keep the building up to code caused it (KRS 65.111(2)(a); "Passing Government Fines to Tenants"). You or your agent may ask a law enforcement officer to remove a person who never was a tenant and never had an agreement to occupy, using the statutory petition. The property must not have been open to the public when the person entered, you must have told the person to leave, the person must not be your immediate family member, and no case between you may be pending. That procedure never applies to a current or former tenant (KRS 383.290(2), (9); "Squatters and Unauthorized Occupants"). Police may, by written agreement with a residential property owner, patrol private roads and parking lots to enforce traffic laws, but not your private rules (KRS 61.362(1)-(2)). An officer needs a warrant to enter open land you own or lease for covert surveillance, unless the owner, lessee or lawful occupant permits it or another exception applies (KRS 15.519(2)). Reporting duties bind you as any person does. Anyone who knows or has reasonable cause to believe a child is dependent, neglected or abused must report it immediately to police or the state (KRS 620.030(1)). Anyone with reasonable cause to suspect abuse, neglect or exploitation of an adult must report it to the cabinet (KRS 209.030(2)-(3)).

title: No Lead-Safe Certificate, but Lead Work Needs Certified People
bodyText: Kentucky has no lead-safe certificate for rental housing. No statute or regulation requires you to get a certificate that a unit is lead-safe or lead-free, to register an older rental building, or to attach a lead certificate to the lease, in either tier. The Kentucky Revised Statutes, the Kentucky Constitution, the 2025 and 2026 Acts and the state regulations on building and fire safety, public health, utilities, environment and human rights and those of the Attorney General and the Real Estate Commission contain no such rule. What Kentucky certifies is the people who do lead work. Anyone who performs or offers to perform lead-hazard inspections, risk assessments or abatement in housing built before 1978 must be certified by the Department for Public Health (KRS 211.9061(3)-(5), 211.9063(1)). Each abatement job also needs a permit before work starts (KRS 211.9063(5); 902 KAR 48:040, Section 8(1)). Doing that work without certification is a Class A misdemeanor (KRS 211.990(5)). Abatement means work meant to permanently eliminate lead hazards. Ordinary renovation, remodeling and temporary interim controls are not abatement (KRS 211.9061(4)(b)). The certification sections state no exception for an owner working on their own rental, so check with the Department for Public Health before doing abatement yourself. Pre-1978 housing for the elderly or people with disabilities is outside these rules if no child under six lives there or is expected to (KRS 211.9061(5)). If the state health cabinet orders lead hazards fixed after a young child's blood test, see "Lead Hazards and Children" and "Kentucky Lead Notices and Orders". The federal lead paint disclosure still applies to pre-1978 housing ("Lead-Based Paint Disclosure" clause). A local board of health may run its own lead program only with rules that are the same as the state's (KRS 211.901(6)).

title: Kentucky Lead Notices and Orders
bodyText:
Kentucky law adds no lead notice, pamphlet or certificate that you must give a tenant with the lease, in either tier. The lead disclosure you give at leasing is the federal one for housing built before 1978 ("Lead-Based Paint Disclosure" clause). The Kentucky Revised Statutes, the Kentucky Constitution, the 2025 and 2026 Acts and the state regulations on building and fire safety, public health, utilities, environment and human rights and those of the Attorney General and the Real Estate Commission contain no state lead notice for leases.

Kentucky's lead notices come from the health authorities after a child 72 months old or younger is found to have a confirmed elevated blood lead level. The state health cabinet then inspects the home. If lead hazards are present and young children live there, it notifies you and the occupant (KRS 211.905(1)-(2)). It orders you in writing to remove, replace or securely and permanently cover lead hazards children can reach, within 60 days (KRS 211.905(2)(c)).

If you do not, it posts a notice on the unit declaring it unfit for children under 72 months, and the posting stays until you comply (KRS 211.905(4)). Letting children under six occupy a posted unit is fined $25 for each day (KRS 211.994). A cabinet finding that such a child is in immediate danger lets the occupant be released from the rental agreement without prejudice (KRS 211.905(5); "Lead Hazards and Children").

Where a local board of health runs a lead program, its rules must be the same as the state's (KRS 211.901(6)), and a state regulation sets what they must contain (902 KAR 4:090). Under those rules the local health director orders a lead hazard fixed within no more than 30 days (902 KAR 4:090, Section 4(1)). If the occupant who lived there when the order was issued moves out, the unit may not be let or occupied by anyone else until the order is met (902 KAR 4:090, Section 4(3)).

So before re-renting a unit under a lead order, confirm the order has been cleared. Lead-hazard work must be done by certified people ("No Lead-Safe Certificate, but Lead Work Needs Certified People").

title: No Initials Requirement
bodyText: No Kentucky statute requires a tenant to initial, separately sign or separately acknowledge a lease term for it to bind, including a notice period longer than the law requires, with one exception where the Uniform Residential Landlord and Tenant Act applies. There, an agreement that the tenant of a unit other than a single family residence will do specified repairs, maintenance, alterations or remodeling must be in a separate writing signed by both of you and supported by adequate consideration (KRS 383.595(4)(a); "Moving Repair and Maintenance Work to the Tenant"). The Kentucky Revised Statutes, the Kentucky Constitution, the 2025 and 2026 Acts and the state regulations on building and fire safety, public health, utilities, environment and human rights and those of the Attorney General and the Real Estate Commission contain no other such rule. The tenant's signature on the lease is all the statutes ask for, and they set no type size or conspicuousness rule for a residential lease ("Plain Language and Translation"). Where your city or county has adopted Kentucky's Uniform Residential Landlord and Tenant Act ("Where Kentucky's Landlord-Tenant Act Applies"), the move-in and move-out damage lists must be signed by both of you (KRS 383.580(2)-(3); "Move-In and Move-Out Damage Lists"). There you must also disclose in writing, at or before the start of the tenancy, the names and addresses of the manager and of an owner or agent for notices (KRS 383.585(1); "Manager and Owner Disclosure" clause). Other start-of-lease notices are listed in "Other Required Lease Notices". Before lengthening the notice a tenant must give, note that where the Act applies either side may end a month-to-month tenancy on at least 30 days' written notice (KRS 383.695(2)). A lease term making the tenant give more notice could be challenged as a waiver of a right under the Act, which is unenforceable (KRS 383.570(1)(a), (2)). The statute does not settle it, and initials would not cure it. Initialing that a statute does require appears only in other settings, such as the 2025 petition to remove squatters (KRS 383.290(3)) and a real estate licensee's listing and purchase contracts (201 KAR 11:121).

title: Recording a Lease Is Optional
bodyText: No Kentucky statute or regulation requires you to record a residential lease, register it with a state or local office, or file a list of your tenants, in either tier. The Kentucky Revised Statutes, the Kentucky Constitution, the 2025 and 2026 Acts and the state regulations on building and fire safety, public health, utilities, environment and human rights and those of the Attorney General and the Real Estate Commission contain no such duty. Recording is optional. The county clerk takes a lease lodged for record, indexes the parties and records it (KRS 382.200(1)), in the county where the property lies (KRS 382.110(1)). Recording matters mainly for a long lease. A deed conveying an interest in real property for longer than five years is not good against a later buyer for value without notice, or a creditor, unless it is acknowledged or proved and lodged for record (KRS 382.080(1)). Whether that rule reaches a residential lease of more than five years is a case-law question; take legal advice before relying on an unrecorded long lease. A term of more than one year in real property may not be conveyed 'except by deed or will' (KRS 382.010), which supports treating a long lease as a deed under KRS 382.080. A lease of five years or less is outside KRS 382.080. Whether the general rule for unacknowledged deeds (KRS 382.270(1)) reaches a lease of more than one year is also case law, so acknowledging and recording such a lease is the cautious course. A lease longer than one year must be in writing ("Written Leases and Long Terms"). Registering yourself as a landlord is a separate subject: Kentucky has no statewide landlord registration, though local programs may exist. No local landlord-tenant ordinance may conflict with state law (KRS 383.198; "Local Landlord-Tenant Ordinances").

title: Lease Length, Formalities and Spouses
bodyText: Kentucky sets no maximum term for a residential lease. No statute requires a seal, a notary, or your spouse's signature on a lease of any length the library offers, in either tier. The Kentucky Revised Statutes, the Kentucky Constitution, the 2025 and 2026 Acts and the state regulations on building and fire safety, public health, utilities, environment and human rights and those of the Attorney General and the Real Estate Commission contain no such rule. Four rules turn on length. An estate for a term of more than one year in real property may not be conveyed 'except by deed or will' (KRS 382.010); what that demands of a written lease beyond a signed writing is case law, so use a written lease signed by both of you for any term over a year. A lease for longer than one year, or an agreement that cannot be performed within a year of signing, must be in writing and signed by the party to be charged (KRS 371.010(6)-(7); "Written Leases and Long Terms"). A deed conveying an interest in real property for longer than five years is not good against a later buyer for value without notice, or a creditor, unless acknowledged or proved and lodged for record (KRS 382.080(1)). Whether that reaches a residential lease of more than five years is a case-law question; recording is optional and explained in "Recording a Lease Is Optional". Where your city or county has not adopted Kentucky's Uniform Residential Landlord and Tenant Act, a tenant holding over after a term of a year or more can, after 90 days without a court case, hold year to year (KRS 383.160(1)); see "Holdover" clause. Where it has adopted the Act ("Where Kentucky's Landlord-Tenant Act Applies"), the lease may set any term not prohibited by law (KRS 383.565(1)). Without a definite term the tenancy is week-to-week for a roomer paying weekly, otherwise month-to-month (KRS 383.565(3)). Your spouse's interests do not change this. Since July 15, 2026, when a spouse dies intestate, the survivor's dower is a life estate in one-third of real estate the other spouse owned in fee during the marriage but not at death, unless relinquished (KRS 392.020(1)(a)). A lease does not transfer ownership, so dower does not require your spouse to sign it; whether a later dower claim binds an existing tenant is case law. A waiver of the homestead exemption must be signed by the debtor and spouse and recorded like a deed (KRS 427.100; "Exemption Waivers"), but a lease waives nothing and needs no such signing. Kentucky has abolished the rule against perpetuities, so a long term or renewal option is not void for remoteness (KRS 381.224). Some lessors have their own limits. A guardian may not lease a ward's real property for longer than seven years without court approval (KRS 387.125(7)); see "Leases From a Life Tenant or Other Limited Owner".

title: Month-to-Month and Fixed-Term Leases Compared
bodyText: No Kentucky statute requires you to offer both month-to-month and fixed-term leases, to give a month-to-month tenant the same terms as a tenant with a fixed term, or to limit how much more you charge for one than the other, in either tier. The Kentucky Revised Statutes, the Kentucky Constitution, the 2025 and 2026 Acts and the state regulations on building and fire safety, public health, utilities, environment and human rights and those of the Attorney General and the Real Estate Commission contain no such rule. Only the General Assembly may enact rent control on private property, so a city or county cannot set such a limit either (KRS 65.875; "Local Landlord-Tenant Ordinances"). Where your city or county has adopted Kentucky's Uniform Residential Landlord and Tenant Act ("Where Kentucky's Landlord-Tenant Act Applies"), a lease that does not fix a definite term creates a week-to-week tenancy for a roomer who pays weekly rent and a month-to-month tenancy otherwise (KRS 383.565(3)). Either side may end a month-to-month tenancy by written notice at least 30 days before the periodic rental date, and a week-to-week tenancy by written notice at least 7 days before the termination date (KRS 383.695(1), (2); "Ending a Periodic Tenancy"). Where the Act has not been adopted, you may end a tenancy at will or by sufferance by giving the tenant one month of written notice (KRS 383.195). Different terms or rents for different lease types are lawful, but they must not track a protected class under fair housing law ("Kentucky Fair Housing Classes"). For rent increases, see "Rent Increases".

title: Type Size in Leases
bodyText: No Kentucky statute sets a minimum type size for a residential lease, and none bars a small-print lease from evidence, in either tier. The Kentucky Revised Statutes, the Kentucky Constitution, the 2025 and 2026 Acts and the state regulations on building and fire safety, public health, utilities, environment and human rights and those of the Attorney General and the Real Estate Commission contain no such rule. Two print rules come close. An assisted living community's lease agreement must be in type no smaller than 12 point (KRS 194A.713). A self-service storage rental agreement must state the operator's lien in bold type (KRS 359.220(2)). Neither reaches an ordinary residential lease. Use a readable size anyway, since no statute sets plain-language rules for leases either ("Plain Language and Translation"). Where your city or county has adopted Kentucky's Uniform Residential Landlord and Tenant Act ("Where Kentucky's Landlord-Tenant Act Applies"), a court may refuse to enforce an unconscionable term (KRS 383.555).

title: Time Limits to Sue for Rent or Damage
bodyText: Kentucky's general time limits for lawsuits apply to rent and damage claims in every locality, whether or not your city or county has adopted the Uniform Residential Landlord and Tenant Act ("Where Kentucky's Landlord-Tenant Act Applies"). Neither tier sets its own period, except the eviction limit below. A suit on a written lease signed after July 15, 2014 must be brought within 10 years after the claim accrued (KRS 413.160). For a written lease signed on or before that date, the limit is 15 years (KRS 413.090(2)). A suit on an oral lease must be brought within 5 years (KRS 413.120(1)). A trespass claim for damage to real or personal property has 5 years (KRS 413.120(4)). So does a claim for the profits of, or damages for, withholding the property, such as against a tenant who holds over (KRS 413.120(5)). A claim for taking, keeping or injuring personal property, such as furnishings you supplied, has 2 years (KRS 413.125). A damage claim can also be framed as a breach of the lease; which period a court applies is a case-law question. A personal injury claim, such as a tenant's or guest's injury claim against you, has 1 year (KRS 413.140(1)(a)). An eviction (forcible detainer) case cannot be brought more than two years after the detainer complained of (KRS 383.285; "The Eviction (Forcible Detainer) Process"). A suit starts on the date the first summons is issued in good faith (KRS 413.250). If a Kentucky-resident tenant is out of the state when the claim accrues, the period runs from the tenant's return. Time spent absconding or hiding also does not count (KRS 413.190). A written agreement to extend a limitations period, made in good faith and at arm's length, is valid (KRS 413.265). No Kentucky statute says that a part payment or a new promise to pay restarts the period for a rent or damage claim, or lets a lease shorten it. The Kentucky Revised Statutes, the Kentucky Constitution, the 2025 and 2026 Acts and the state regulations on building and fire safety, public health, utilities, environment and human rights and those of the Attorney General and the Real Estate Commission contain no such rule. Those questions are left to case law. Don't count on a part payment to keep an old claim alive; sue well within the period. The library offers no clause shortening the time to sue; if you want one, add your own with legal advice. Your lien for rent has its own shorter limits ("The Landlord's Lien for Rent").

title: No Statute on Liquidated Damages in Leases
bodyText:
No Kentucky statute says when a lease clause fixing damages in advance is valid liquidated damages and when it is an unenforceable penalty. The Kentucky Revised Statutes, the Kentucky Constitution, the 2025 and 2026 Acts and the state regulations on building and fire safety, public health, utilities, environment and human rights and those of the Attorney General and the Real Estate Commission contain none for leases of homes. The liquidated-damages rules in Kentucky's commercial code cover sales and leases of goods, meaning movable things, not the lease of a home (KRS 355.2-718; KRS 355.2A-103(1)(k), 355.2A-504).

Other statutes that allow or award liquidated damages deal with public contracts, wages, cooperatives, construction and consumer credit, not housing. The penalty doctrine itself is case law. A few statutes still shape a fixed charge. Where your city or county has adopted Kentucky's Uniform Residential Landlord and Tenant Act ("Where Kentucky's Landlord-Tenant Act Applies"), you may recover appropriate damages but must mitigate them (KRS 383.520(1)). The Act also sets its own measures, such as up to three months' rent or three times actual damages for a willful, bad-faith holdover (KRS 383.695(4); "Holdover Rent").

In every locality, a protected tenant who ends a lease under the domestic violence statute pays rent only to the termination date, and no other rent or fees due solely to the early termination (KRS 383.300(5)(c); "Early Termination by Protected Tenants"). The cautious course is to set any fixed charge, such as an early termination fee, at a figure that reasonably estimates your likely loss, and to keep proof of your actual losses.

The library's early termination clause for Kentucky is "Early Termination" clause, a flat fee of one month's rent; whether even that fee would survive a penalty challenge is the same unsettled question. See also "Late Fee" clause and "No Specific Ban on Eviction Penalty Clauses".

title: No Lockouts for Unpaid Rent
bodyText: Where your city or county has adopted Kentucky's Uniform Residential Landlord and Tenant Act ("Where Kentucky's Landlord-Tenant Act Applies"), you may not lock out a tenant, change the locks, or cut off heat, water, electricity, gas or another essential service to make a tenant pay rent or leave. You may recover possession only through the court process, except after abandonment or surrender (KRS 383.690). If you unlawfully remove or exclude a tenant, or willfully interrupt an essential service, the tenant may recover possession or end the lease. In either case the tenant may recover up to three months' periodic rent and a reasonable attorney's fee, and if the lease ends you must return all prepaid rent (KRS 383.655). A lease term allowing a lockout would waive these rights, and is unenforceable (KRS 383.570(1)(a), (2)). Where the Act has not been adopted, no statute allows a lockout for unpaid rent, and none bars it in those words. The Kentucky Revised Statutes, the Kentucky Constitution, the 2025 and 2026 Acts and the state regulations on building and fire safety, public health, utilities, environment and human rights and those of the Attorney General and the Real Estate Commission contain no such rule. But the forcible entry statutes call a landlord's entry on a tenant at will or by sufferance a forcible entry, even with the tenant's consent, and also any entry without the consent of the person in actual possession (KRS 383.200(2)). So in every locality the safe course is to recover possession only through a forcible detainer case ("The Eviction (Forcible Detainer) Process"). The 2025 police-removal procedure for unlawful occupants cannot be used against a current or former tenant (KRS 383.290(9); "Squatters and Unauthorized Occupants"). The library offers no lockout clause. See "No Lockouts or Utility Shutoffs".

title: Moving Repair and Maintenance Work to the Tenant
bodyText: Where your city or county has adopted Kentucky's Uniform Residential Landlord and Tenant Act ("Where Kentucky's Landlord-Tenant Act Applies"), repair and maintenance work can move to the tenant only in two ways, and the full rules are in "Shifting Maintenance Tasks to the Tenant". In a single family residence you and the tenant may agree in writing, including in the lease, that the tenant supplies water, hot water and heat and performs specified repairs, maintenance tasks, alterations and remodeling. The agreement must be made in good faith and not to evade your duties; the Act asks for no particular consideration there (KRS 383.595(3)). In any other unit the work must be specified, and the agreement binds only if it is made in good faith, not to evade your duties, and is in a separate writing signed by both of you and supported by adequate consideration, such as a rent reduction (KRS 383.595(4)(a)). It cannot cover work needed to meet building and housing codes materially affecting health and safety, and cannot reduce your duties to other tenants (KRS 383.595(4)(b)-(c)). A conspicuous lease paragraph alone is not enough for those units; use the separate Tenant Maintenance Agreement ("Tenant Maintenance Agreement (Separate Document)" clause). The Act has no duty to provide garbage receptacles or removal that a lease could shift; the tenant must already dispose of the unit's waste in a clean and safe manner (KRS 383.605(3)). Common areas stay your duty (KRS 383.595(1)(c)). Where the Act has not been adopted, no statute limits how a lease divides repair and maintenance work. The one rule there is that a promise by the tenant to repair does not oblige the tenant to rebuild after a fire or other casualty that was not the tenant's fault, unless the written lease expressly says so (KRS 383.170). In every locality, an agreement with the tenant does not move your duty as owner not to let the structure become unfit and unsafe for human habitation, which local governments enforce (KRS 65.8840(5)).

title: Meter Conservation and Efficiency Charges
bodyText: No Kentucky statute or regulation lets a utility attach an energy-efficiency or conservation repayment charge to the meter at a rental so that it follows the next customer. None requires you to tell a new tenant about such a charge or to credit it against rent, in either tier. Utilities may recover the cost of Public Service Commission-approved demand-side management programs through their rates (KRS 278.285(2)). The Commission assigns that cost only to the class or classes of customers that benefit (KRS 278.285(3)). Those are rate charges paid by the whole class, not a charge tied to one meter or one rental. A different tool exists for buildings of five or more units. A local government's energy project assessment district can finance an owner's energy improvement through an assessment added to the property tax bill (KRS 65.205(6), 65.207(4)). It is imposed only at the owner's request (KRS 65.208), and the statutes say nothing about tenants; whether you pass any of it on is a matter for the lease. If you bill tenants for water through your own submeters, you may charge no more than each tenant's share of the actual water bill, based on usage (401 KAR 8:020, Section 2; "Utility Allowances and Overage Charges"). No Kentucky rule adds a separate meter surcharge or a monthly reading statement for submetered water. The Kentucky Revised Statutes, the Kentucky Constitution, the 2025 and 2026 Acts and the state regulations on building and fire safety, public health, utilities, environment and human rights and those of the Attorney General and the Real Estate Commission contain no meter conservation charge rule.

title: No Separate Notice for Nonrefundable Fees
bodyText: No Kentucky statute requires a separate written notice when you collect a nonrefundable deposit or fee, in any locality. Kentucky's rules on nonrefundable move-in, cleaning and administrative fees are in "Nonrefundable Fees". Where your city or county has adopted Kentucky's Uniform Residential Landlord and Tenant Act ("Where Kentucky's Landlord-Tenant Act Applies"), every payment under the lease other than a security deposit is rent (KRS 383.545(10)). A security deposit there is an escrow payment securing you against damage beyond ordinary wear and tear (KRS 383.545(13)). So a payment you plan to keep whatever happens is a fee, not a deposit; call it a fee in the lease. Where the Act has not been adopted, no landlord-tenant statute governs deposits or fees, so the lease governs ("Where to Keep the Security Deposit"). In every locality, state any nonrefundable fee, its amount and what it is for in the lease, so the tenant agreed to it in writing. The Kentucky Revised Statutes, the Kentucky Constitution, the 2025 and 2026 Acts and the state regulations on building and fire safety, public health, utilities, environment and human rights and those of the Attorney General and the Real Estate Commission contain no separate-notice rule.

title: Notice-Service Fees Not Offered
bodyText: No Kentucky statute authorizes or bars a lease fee for preparing or serving a default or termination notice on a tenant, in any locality. The library does not offer a notice-service fee clause for Kentucky, for the same reasons it offers no collection fee ("Collection Fees"). Where your city or county has adopted Kentucky's Uniform Residential Landlord and Tenant Act ("Where Kentucky's Landlord-Tenant Act Applies"), a lease may not make the tenant agree to pay your attorney's fees, and such a term is unenforceable (KRS 383.570(1)(c), (2)). So a fee for a notice a lawyer prepares cannot be charged there. You may recover damages for the tenant's breach (KRS 383.660(3)), but a flat fee that is not your actual loss could be refused as a penalty or as unconscionable (KRS 383.555(1)(a)). Where the Act has not been adopted, no statute bars a notice fee, and the lease governs. A written agreement to pay reasonable attorney fees on default is enforceable there only to the extent the fees are actually paid or agreed to be paid, and not for a salaried employee (KRS 411.195; "Attorney Fees (Only Where the URLTA Is Not in Effect)" clause). Whether a flat notice fee is an unenforceable penalty is case law. A landlord who wants a notice fee can add their own clause after taking legal advice, limited to the actual cost of serving the notice. The only notice-service fee in Kentucky statute is the $20 a sheriff or constable may charge to serve a notice to vacate on someone unlawfully occupying property (KRS 383.290(5)(a)). That procedure never applies to a current or former tenant (KRS 383.290(9)). The Kentucky Revised Statutes, the Kentucky Constitution, the 2025 and 2026 Acts and the state regulations on building and fire safety, public health, utilities, environment and human rights and those of the Attorney General and the Real Estate Commission contain no rule on notice-service fees.

title: Waiving the Notice to Quit
bodyText: Some states let a lease waive or shorten the notice a landlord must give before ending a tenancy. This library does not offer that clause in Kentucky. Where your city or county has adopted Kentucky's Uniform Residential Landlord and Tenant Act ("Where Kentucky's Landlord-Tenant Act Applies"), a lease may not have the tenant waive or forgo rights or remedies under the Act, and such a term is unenforceable (KRS 383.570(1)(a), (2)). That reaches the Act's notices: 7 days' written notice for unpaid rent, the written notice for other material breaches, and the notices that end a periodic tenancy (KRS 383.660(1)-(2), 383.695(1)-(3)). Where it has not, one month's written notice ends a tenancy at will or by sufferance (KRS 383.195). There, too, 10 days' written notice to quit follows an assignment made without your written consent by a tenant at will or by sufferance, or by one with a term under two years (KRS 383.180(2)); where the Act applies, you may recover possession only as the Act permits (KRS 383.690). Neither section says whether a lease may waive or shorten its notice. The Kentucky Revised Statutes, the Kentucky Constitution, the 2025 and 2026 Acts and the state regulations on building and fire safety, public health, utilities, environment and human rights and those of the Attorney General and the Real Estate Commission contain no statute that does. This library's lease gives the 7-day notice for unpaid rent in every locality ("Default by Tenant" clause; "Notice for Unpaid Rent"). If your property is outside the Act's localities and you want a waiver anyway, you can add your own clause, but take legal advice first: whether a court would enforce it is unsettled.

title: Extra Terms in a Notice to Vacate
bodyText: No Kentucky statute limits what a notice to vacate may say, regulates a move-out form that adds terms, requires a warning on one, or bars alterations while a notice is pending. The Kentucky Revised Statutes, the Kentucky Constitution, the 2025 and 2026 Acts and the state regulations on building and fire safety, public health, utilities, environment and human rights and those of the Attorney General and the Real Estate Commission contain no such rule. Kentucky prescribes no form for your notice to vacate. It only has to give the notice the lease and the law require ("Notice for Unpaid Rent", "Ending a Periodic Tenancy"), and the sworn complaint states the date you gave it (AOC-216). Where your city or county has adopted Kentucky's Uniform Residential Landlord and Tenant Act ("Where Kentucky's Landlord-Tenant Act Applies"), the rental agreement includes all agreements, written or oral, on the terms of use and occupancy (KRS 383.545(11)). So new terms a tenant signs at move-out may be treated as part of the rental agreement, and a term there waiving the tenant's rights under the Act would be unenforceable (KRS 383.570(1)(a), (2)). A separate settlement in which a tenant gives up a claim or right can be enforced, but a court may refuse to enforce it if it was unconscionable when made (KRS 383.555(1)(b)). While the tenant is still in possession there, you must keep the unit fit and habitable (KRS 383.595(1)(b)), and you may not retaliate for code complaints ("Retaliation"). Where the Act has not been adopted, a move-out form is an ordinary contract. In every locality, for leases created or renewed on or after June 29, 2017, a court will refuse possession if the notice to vacate is substantially based on acts that violated a protected tenant's protective order (KRS 383.300(1)(a), (3)(b); "No Adverse Action Against Protected Tenants"). The safe course: keep the notice to the facts the law requires. Put any new terms in a separate document, and don't make the tenant's notice depend on signing it.

title: Optional Lease Terms in Kentucky
bodyText: Kentucky lets a lease include terms the law does not prohibit, and several rules apply only unless the parties agree otherwise. These are the optional terms the library offers for Kentucky; none is a default. Where your city or county has adopted Kentucky's Uniform Residential Landlord and Tenant Act ("Where Kentucky's Landlord-Tenant Act Applies"), the lease may set rent, the term and the parties' rights and duties (KRS 383.565(1)). There the lease may change where and when rent is paid and whether it is apportioned day to day (KRS 383.565(2); "Rent Payment" clause, "Rent Paid in Installments" clause). It may require notice of an absence of more than seven days (KRS 383.620; "Notice of Extended Absence" clause). Unless otherwise agreed, the tenant must use the unit only as a dwelling (KRS 383.620; the standard clause is "Residential Use Only" clause); the lease may allow other uses, such as a home business ("Home-Based Business (Landlord's Permission)" clause). A good-faith written agreement may shift specified repairs to the tenant (KRS 383.595(3)-(4); "Tenant Maintenance Agreement (Separate Document)" clause). A sale to a good-faith buyer, or the end of a manager's role, releases the old landlord or manager after written notice unless otherwise agreed (KRS 383.600). Where the Act has not been adopted, two opt-in clauses are offered: "Attorney Fees (Only Where the URLTA Is Not in Effect)" clause and "Showings Near the End of the Lease (Only Where the URLTA Is Not in Effect)" clause. Kentucky clauses: Mid-Term Rent Increase; Local Government Fees; Tenant Maintenance Agreement ("Tenant Maintenance Agreement (Separate Document)" clause); Casualty ("Fire or Casualty Damage" clause); Damage Caused by Tenant; Criminal Activity; Methamphetamine Contamination Disclosure; No Liens for Tenant Improvements. Added: Association Documents Given to Tenant; Common-Area Lighting on Tenant's Meter; Fire Safety; Home-Based Business ("Home-Based Business (Landlord's Permission)" clause). Also added: Utility Allowance with Tenant-Paid Overage; Transfer of Utility Accounts. Shared clauses tagged for Kentucky: Condemnation; Animal Care in Tenant's Absence; Pest Reporting and Treatment; Energy Usage Data Authorization. Also tagged: Owner Occupancy; Tax and Insurance Increases; Authorization for Utility Notices to Landlord; Hunting, Trapping and Fishing. Also tagged: Rent Paid in Installments; Accessory Dwelling Unit ("The Premises Is an Accessory Dwelling Unit" clause); Cold Weather Notice Before Vacating; No Admitting a Barred Person; Tenant's Emergency Contact; Furnishings; Cooling Equipment and Window Units; Prohibited Acts by Tenant; Online Tenant Portal. Declined options, each explained in its own row: arbitration ("Binding Arbitration Clauses"; mediation, "Mediation and Dispute Resolution"), notice fees ("Notice-Service Fees Not Offered"), notice-to-quit waivers ("Waiving the Notice to Quit"), appliance exclusions ("Appliances You Do Not Want to Supply"), and exemption waivers or liens. Also declined: a premium holdover rate ("Holdover Rent"), a contract interest rate ("Interest on Unpaid Rent"), a jury waiver ("Jury Waivers"), a collection fee ("Collection Fees"), an abandoned-property procedure ("Belongings Left Behind"), a guaranty ("Lease Guaranties") and a clause passing tenant-caused fines on to the tenant ("Passing Government Fines to Tenants"). A reserved right for you to enter rented land to hunt is also declined ("Hunting and Fishing on Rented Land"). No spouse's signature, notarization or recording is required for any of these terms, or for any lease length the library offers ("Lease Length, Formalities and Spouses"). Options to buy: no Kentucky statute governs a lease with an option to purchase a home, or a rent-to-own home contract. The Kentucky Revised Statutes, the Kentucky Constitution, the 2025 and 2026 Acts and the state regulations on building and fire safety, public health, utilities, environment and human rights and those of the Attorney General and the Real Estate Commission contain none. The seller's disclosure form applies to sales and purchases of single-family homes where a real estate licensee is paid (KRS 324.360(1)). Whether it reaches an option when granted or only when exercised is not settled. A contract for the sale of real estate must be in writing and signed (KRS 371.010(6)), so put any option in the signed lease. Kentucky's rental-purchase law covers personal property, not homes (KRS 367.976(3)).

title: No Ordnance, Demolition or Shared Meter Disclosure
bodyText: Kentucky has none of these three disclosures. No Kentucky statute or regulation requires you to tell a prospective tenant about a former military ordnance site near the property, about an application to demolish the building, or that a utility meter serving the unit also serves other areas or units. The Kentucky Revised Statutes, the Kentucky Constitution, the 2025 and 2026 Acts and the state regulations on building and fire safety, public health, utilities, environment and human rights and those of the Attorney General and the Real Estate Commission contain no such rule. Demolition. Where your city or county has adopted Kentucky's Uniform Residential Landlord and Tenant Act ("Where Kentucky's Landlord-Tenant Act Applies"), the retaliation rule does not stop an action for possession in one case. That case is when complying with the building or housing code requires alteration, remodeling or demolition that would effectively deprive the tenant of use of the unit (KRS 383.705(3)(c)). The tenant keeps any damages claim for your own breach (KRS 383.705(4)). Where the Act has not been adopted, no statute addresses ending a tenancy for demolition; the lease and the ordinary notice rules govern ("Ending a Periodic Tenancy"). Before renovating or demolishing, check the asbestos notification rules ("Asbestos in Rental Buildings"). Meters: each unit in a nontransient multi-unit residential building whose building permit was applied for after May 31, 1981 must have its own electric meter (807 KAR 5:046, Section 2). See "Electric and Gas Submetering and Resale" and "Splitting Shared Utilities". If a meter the tenant pays for also serves shared areas, say so in the lease; "Common-Area Lighting on Tenant's Meter" clause does that for shared-area lights.

title: Elevators, Boilers, Pools and Other Facilities
bodyText: Beyond the general repair duty, three Kentucky safety laws reach facilities common in rental buildings: elevators, boilers and pools. Where your city or county has adopted Kentucky's Uniform Residential Landlord and Tenant Act ("Where Kentucky's Landlord-Tenant Act Applies"), you must keep in good and safe working order the facilities and appliances you supply or are required to supply (KRS 383.595(1)(d)). That covers electrical, plumbing, sanitary, heating, ventilating and air-conditioning facilities, and elevators. You must also keep common areas clean and safe (KRS 383.595(1)(c)), and the tenant must use those facilities in a reasonable manner (KRS 383.605(5)). The premises include grounds, areas and facilities held out for the use of tenants generally or promised to the tenant (KRS 383.545(9)), so a laundry room, pool or garage you offer is covered. Where the Act has not been adopted, the lease and local codes govern; see "Landlord's Repair Duties". Elevators, in every locality: the owner or user must register each elevator with the Department of Housing, Buildings and Construction (KRS 198B.460(1)). Each passenger or freight elevator must be inspected every 12 months (KRS 198B.470(1)). An elevator or lift used only by the occupants of one dwelling unit is exempt from that yearly inspection, but not one used by or accessible to the occupants of more than one unit (KRS 198B.470(2)(g)). An inspected elevator may not be operated without a conspicuously posted certificate of operation (KRS 198B.480(5)). Boilers: a low-pressure steam or hot water heating boiler, or a hot water supply boiler, needs a state certificate of inspection every two years, posted in the boiler room (KRS 236.110(1)(b), 236.120(1)). Small heating boilers located in private residences are exempt (KRS 236.060(3)(c), (d)). The chapter does not define private residences, so ask the Department whether a central boiler serving several units is covered. Pools: a shared pool, such as an apartment complex pool, is a public swimming and bathing facility; only a pool at a private single-family residence used by its occupant and guests is excluded (902 KAR 10:120, Section 1). It needs an annual permit from the Department for Public Health, paid by May 1, and must meet the state pool rules (902 KAR 10:120, Section 2; 902 KAR 10:123; 902 KAR 10:125). No Kentucky statute or regulation held sets rules for automatic garage door or gate openers in rentals. The Kentucky Revised Statutes, the Kentucky Constitution, the 2025 and 2026 Acts and the state regulations on building and fire safety, public health, utilities, environment and human rights and those of the Attorney General and the Real Estate Commission contain no such rule. If you supply one, it is a facility you must keep in good and safe working order where the Act applies (KRS 383.595(1)(d)). For radiators and window guards, see "No Radiator Cover Requirement" and "No Window Guard Requirement"; for the fire code, see "Kentucky's Fire Code".

title: No Owner Move-In Rule
bodyText:
No Kentucky statute gives you, or limits, a right to end a tenancy so that you or a family member can move in. There is no owner-use ground, holding period, relocation payment or duty to re-offer the unit. The Kentucky Revised Statutes, the Kentucky Constitution, the 2025 and 2026 Acts and the state regulations on building and fire safety, public health, utilities, environment and human rights and those of the Attorney General and the Real Estate Commission contain no such rule.

For a periodic tenancy you need no reservation: you may end it with the required notice and no reason ("Ending a Periodic Tenancy", "No Just-Cause Eviction Rule"). For a fixed term you have no such right unless the lease reserves it. The library offers the optional owner-occupancy clause for that.

Where your city or county has adopted Kentucky's Uniform Residential Landlord and Tenant Act ("Where Kentucky's Landlord-Tenant Act Applies"), a lease may include any term the Act or other law does not prohibit (KRS 383.565(1)). If the tenant stays past the termination date there, you may bring an action for possession (KRS 383.695(4)). Where it has not, the clause is an ordinary contract term, and you recover possession through a forcible detainer case ("The Eviction (Forcible Detainer) Process").

Two cautions. Where the Act applies, a landlord may not retaliate by bringing an action for possession after a tenant's code complaint, repair complaint or union activity, and a complaint within a year before raises a presumption of retaliation (KRS 383.705(1)-(2); "Retaliation"). In every locality, for a lease created or renewed on or after June 29, 2017, you may not end or refuse to renew it because a tenant is protected by a protective order (KRS 383.300(1)(a), (3)(a)). Don't confuse this with the Jefferson County owner-residence rule for leasing in single-family zones (KRS 383.199; "Jefferson County: Leasing in Single-Family Zones").

title: Parking Rules and Towing Signs
bodyText:
No Kentucky statute requires you to give tenants parking rules in a separate document, or to state in the lease whether parking is provided or what it costs, in either tier. None requires you to wait, or to post a notice on the car of a resident, before having it towed. The Kentucky Revised Statutes, the Kentucky Constitution, the 2025 and 2026 Acts and the state regulations on building and fire safety, public health, utilities, environment and human rights and those of the Attorney General and the Real Estate Commission contain no such rule. Towing has its own posting rules, which apply to a residential lot as to any private lot ("Towing from Rental Parking Lots").

Every operator of a privately owned parking lot that has unauthorized vehicles towed must post signs stating 'that the parking lot is privately owned and unauthorized vehicles will be towed away at the owner's expense' (KRS 189.725(2)). A property owner who sets up a tow-away zone must post there a sign clearly visible to the public, stating that the area is a tow-away zone, giving contact information and describing who may or may not park there (KRS 281.924(3)). The towing company then has its own notice duties to the owner of the vehicle (KRS 281.928). Put your parking rules in the lease or in written rules given at signing ("Parking & Vehicle Requirements" clause).

Where your city or county has adopted Kentucky's Uniform Residential Landlord and Tenant Act ("Where Kentucky's Landlord-Tenant Act Applies"), a rule binds the tenant only if it meets the Act's tests, including that the tenant has notice of it at signing or when it is adopted (KRS 383.610(1)). A later rule that works a substantial modification of the bargain is not valid unless the tenant consents in writing (KRS 383.610(2)). A parking fee the lease requires counts as rent there (KRS 383.545(10); "Fees Count as Rent"). Where the Act has not been adopted, the lease governs.

In every locality, a parking rule may not ban a firearm that a person may legally possess from a vehicle on the property (KRS 237.106(1); "Firearms in Vehicles on Rental Property"). If you park the cars of tenants for hire, taking possession of them and keeping their keys, the parking-lot statutes make you liable as a bailee for hire, and a contract limiting that liability is void (KRS 189.710, 189.720).

title: Rights a Kentucky Lease Cannot Waive
bodyText: Where your city or county has adopted Kentucky's Uniform Residential Landlord and Tenant Act ("Where Kentucky's Landlord-Tenant Act Applies"), a lease may not have the tenant waive or forgo any right or remedy the Act gives (KRS 383.570(1)(a)). The same section bars confession-of-judgment, attorney-fee and exculpation or indemnity terms (KRS 383.570(1)(b)-(d)). A barred term is unenforceable (KRS 383.570(2)); that section sets no money penalty for including one, unlike the police-call rule below. No lease, assignment, conveyance, trust deed or security instrument may let you collect rent free of your repair and habitability duties (KRS 383.575). The only agreements the Act allows that move repair or maintenance work to the tenant are the written ones in KRS 383.595(3)-(4) ("Shifting Maintenance Tasks to the Tenant"). A court may also refuse to enforce a term that was unconscionable when made, or an unconscionable settlement in which a party gave up a right under the Act (KRS 383.555(1)). Where the Act has not been adopted, no statute lists rights a lease cannot waive; the lease and the older statutes (KRS 383.010 to 383.302) govern. Whether a court there would enforce a particular waiver is a question of case law, so the cautious course is to leave waiver language out of the lease. Two rules apply in every locality. A lease may not let you end the tenancy or penalize a tenant for asking police or others for emergency help, and knowingly enforcing such a term exposes you to damages (KRS 383.302, leases created or renewed on or after June 29, 2017). A power of attorney to confess judgment given before a lawsuit is filed is void (KRS 372.140(1)). Kentucky has no special waiver rule for a home sold and leased back to the seller. See "Lease Terms Kentucky Voids", "Penalties for Unlawful Lease Terms" and "Unconscionable Terms".

title: No Pest Control Notice Requirement
bodyText: No Kentucky statute requires you, or a pest control company you hire, to give tenants notice before pesticide is applied in or around a rental. No held regulation does either. The Kentucky Revised Statutes, the Kentucky Constitution, the 2025 and 2026 Acts and the state regulations on building and fire safety, public health, utilities, environment and human rights and those of the Attorney General and the Real Estate Commission contain no such rule. Pesticide use is regulated by the Department of Agriculture, whose rules are in Title 302 of the Kentucky Administrative Regulations. By statute the Department must run a program regulating the application, and notice of application, of pesticides for lawn care and mosquito control (KRS 217B.050(6)). So a notice rule for lawn or mosquito treatments may exist in those regulations; ask your applicator. Structural pest management and fumigation require a state license, and a business offering them must register with the Department (KRS 217B.515(1), 217B.538(1)). Cities and counties may not adopt their own rules on pesticide use, including notification of use (KRS 217B.270(2)). Where your city or county has adopted Kentucky's Uniform Residential Landlord and Tenant Act ("Where Kentucky's Landlord-Tenant Act Applies"), entering a unit to treat it needs at least two days' notice, except in an emergency or where it is impracticable (KRS 383.615(3)); see "Landlord's Right of Entry" clause. Where it has not, the lease sets the entry notice. For treatment cooperation and costs, see "Bed Bug and Pest Treatment Cooperation". Telling tenants in writing what will be applied, when, and any label precautions such as staying out until it dries is the cautious course.

title: No Pet and Eviction Fact Sheet
bodyText: No Kentucky statute or regulation requires you to give a tenant who has a dog or cat a fact sheet or notice about pets and eviction, with the lease or at any later stage, in either tier. The Kentucky Revised Statutes, the Kentucky Constitution, the 2025 and 2026 Acts and the state regulations on building and fire safety, public health, utilities, environment and human rights and those of the Attorney General and the Real Estate Commission contain no such rule. No statute ties a tenant's animals to the eviction process either. The one state handout tied to renting is the Fair Housing Brochure of the Kentucky Commission on Human Rights, which a person engaged in real estate transactions must give customers at the time of rental (104 KAR 1:010, Section 4; "No State Rights Guide, but Give the Fair Housing Brochure"). Your pet terms come from the lease ("Pets" clause), and assistance animals follow fair housing law. When you end a tenancy, tell the tenant in writing to take every animal when they leave. Cruelty to animals in the second degree includes cruel or injurious mistreatment through abandonment (KRS 525.130(1)(a)). Torture of a dog or cat can include extreme pain or death that results from the animal being abandoned in a building for three days or more with no provision for its care (KRS 525.135(1)(a)). If an animal is left behind, call the local animal control officer, a peace officer or an animal shelter rather than keep it yourself, since a person who keeps or harbors a dog counts as its owner (KRS 258.095(5); "Caring for a Tenant's Animal").

title: No Plain-Language Lease Statute
bodyText: No Kentucky statute requires a residential lease to be written in plain language, to pass a readability test, or to carry a statement of consumer restrictions listing the tenant's waivers, in either tier. The Kentucky Revised Statutes, the Kentucky Constitution, the 2025 and 2026 Acts and the state regulations on building and fire safety, public health, utilities, environment and human rights and those of the Attorney General and the Real Estate Commission contain no such rule. Kentucky's readability rules are for insurance policies and some insurance disclosures (KRS 304.14-440), not leases; see "Plain Language and Translation". The Consumer Protection Act makes unfair, false, misleading or deceptive acts in trade or commerce unlawful, and unfair means unconscionable (KRS 367.170). Its private damages action belongs to a person who purchases or leases goods or services primarily for personal, family or household purposes (KRS 367.220(1)). Whether a residential lease counts as goods or services is a case-law question ("Consumer Protection Act and Leases"). Where your city or county has adopted Kentucky's Uniform Residential Landlord and Tenant Act ("Where Kentucky's Landlord-Tenant Act Applies"), certain lease terms are barred and unenforceable (KRS 383.570; "Lease Terms Kentucky Voids"). There a court may also refuse to enforce, or limit, a lease term it finds unconscionable when made (KRS 383.555(1)(a)). Where the Act has not been adopted, no statute lists barred lease terms; the lease and the older statutes (KRS 383.010 to 383.302) govern. In every locality a police or emergency-call penalty term is barred (KRS 383.302, leases created or renewed on or after June 29, 2017), and a power to confess judgment given before suit is void (KRS 372.140(1)).

title: No Candidate Access or Political Sign Right Against the Lease
bodyText: No Kentucky statute gives candidates or campaign workers a right to enter an apartment building or other rental property, or gives tenants a right to post political signs or literature despite the lease. The Kentucky Revised Statutes, the Kentucky Constitution, the 2025 and 2026 Acts and the state regulations on building and fire safety, public health, utilities, environment and human rights and those of the Attorney General and the Real Estate Commission contain none. The election law only says its polling-place electioneering ban does not stop a person with a leased or ownership interest in private property from displaying campaign signs there, even near a polling place (KRS 117.235(7)). That rule gives a tenant no right against your lease. If your rental is in a planned community with a homeowners association, the association's governing documents may not bar an owner or resident from displaying political yard signs on the property from 30 days before to seven days after an election (or longer if a local ordinance allows), though they may set reasonable placement, size and display rules (KRS 381.800(1), (2); "Condominium and Homeowners Association Rules for Rentals"). That limit binds the association, not your lease. The one statewide display right that overrides a lease is for the United States flag: whatever the lease says, a tenant may display a U.S. flag no larger than two feet by three feet from the residence (KRS 2.042; "Displaying the U.S. Flag"). Other sign, canvassing and access rules are for your lease ("No Alterations" clause covers attaching things to the property).

title: No Tenant Right to a Window or Portable Air Conditioner
bodyText:
No Kentucky statute or regulation gives a tenant a right to install or use a window, portable or through-the-wall air conditioner, in either tier. None sets a cooling or maximum indoor temperature standard for ordinary rental housing. Where your city or county has adopted Kentucky's Uniform Residential Landlord and Tenant Act ("Where Kentucky's Landlord-Tenant Act Applies"), you must keep any air-conditioning you supply, or are required to supply, in good and safe working order (KRS 383.595(1)(d)). The tenant must use it in a reasonable manner (KRS 383.605(5)). The Act's heat duty runs from October 1 to May 1 and says nothing about cooling (KRS 383.595(1)(e); "Heat and Hot Water"). Where the Act has not been adopted, no statute requires you to cool the home or keep up an air conditioner; the lease governs.

So whether a tenant may put in a window or portable unit is for your lease to decide. The library's optional "Cooling Equipment and Window Units" clause allows plug-in floor units and fans, needs your written consent for window and through-the-wall units, and sets installation and removal terms. Kentucky's HVAC licensing law does not apply to installing residential window air conditioning units (KRS 198B.674(4)). It does cover installing other cooling systems (KRS 198B.650(15)(a); KRS 198B.656(4)).

So if you agree to a through-the-wall unit, the cautious course is to require a licensed HVAC contractor. A tenant with a disability may still ask for a reasonable accommodation or modification (KRS 344.360(11)(a)-(b); "Accommodations and Modifications"). Some low-income households with an older adult, a young child or a member whose health needs cooling can get a one-time air-conditioning unit through a utility's voluntary energy assistance fund (KRS 278.287(8)). That law does not override your lease.

The Kentucky Revised Statutes, the Kentucky Constitution, the 2025 and 2026 Acts and the state regulations on building and fire safety, public health, utilities, environment and human rights and those of the Attorney General and the Real Estate Commission contain no tenant cooling-device right or rental cooling standard.

title: No Possession Bond
bodyText: Kentucky has no end-of-term possession bond, under which a tenant binds themselves to give up possession on the last day and authorizes a confessed judgment if they don't. The Kentucky Revised Statutes, the Kentucky Constitution, the 2025 and 2026 Acts and the state regulations on building and fire safety, public health, utilities, environment and human rights and those of the Attorney General and the Real Estate Commission contain no statute creating one. You can't write one into a lease. In every locality, a power of attorney to confess judgment given before a case is filed is void (KRS 372.140(1)). Where your city or county has adopted Kentucky's Uniform Residential Landlord and Tenant Act ("Where Kentucky's Landlord-Tenant Act Applies"), a lease also may not authorize anyone to confess judgment on a claim arising out of it (KRS 383.570(1)(b), (2)). See "Confession of Judgment". What Kentucky does have is a deposit on appeal. A party who appeals a forcible detainer judgment must deposit with the circuit court clerk the rent owed since the case began, and each month's rent as it comes due (KRS 383.255(1)). Once the appeal is perfected by that payment, further proceedings are stayed (KRS 383.255(2)). If the appellant then fails to prosecute the appeal, the appellant and any surety are liable for your damages for withholding possession and your reasonable expenses of defending the appeal (KRS 383.260). A tenant who stays after the term ends is handled by a forcible detainer case ("The Eviction (Forcible Detainer) Process") and the holdover rules.

title: Testing a Well That Serves Your Rental
bodyText: No Kentucky statute or regulation requires you to test a private well that serves your rental, or to give tenants well-test results. The Kentucky Revised Statutes, the Kentucky Constitution, the 2025 and 2026 Acts and the state regulations on building and fire safety, public health, utilities, environment and human rights and those of the Attorney General and the Real Estate Commission contain no such rule. When a well is drilled or modified, the certified driller must have it tested for bacteria and give you the written results (KRS 223.440(2); 401 KAR 6:310, Sections 1(7) and 9(6)). Keep those records. The owner or user of a private water supply can ask the Department for Public Health to test it for bacterial and chemical contamination (KRS 211.345). The sampling fee is $50, paid to the local health department (902 KAR 45:120, Sections 3 and 4). A well that serves several households is different. Under the state drinking water rules, a private water supply serves one to three residential households (401 KAR 8:010). A water system for drinking or domestic use that is neither private nor public is a semipublic water system, and public and semipublic systems are subject to those rules (401 KAR 8:010; 401 KAR 8:020, Section 1). So a well serving four or more households may be a regulated water system. Its operator must run it under the drinking water rules, issue a boil water advisory when one is warranted, and notify the local health department (401 KAR 8:020, Section 3(1), (9)). A system large enough to be a public water system must also give public notice of violations (401 KAR 8:075, Section 2). Ask the Division of Water whether your system is regulated. If your rentals buy water from a utility and you bill tenants through your own submeters, see "Utility Disclosures to Tenants". Where your city or county has adopted Kentucky's Uniform Residential Landlord and Tenant Act ("Where Kentucky's Landlord-Tenant Act Applies"), you must supply running water and comply with building and housing codes materially affecting health and safety (KRS 383.595(1)(a), (e)). Where it has not, the lease governs. Testing the well before each new tenancy, and keeping the results, is a sensible precaution.

title: What Kentucky Law Forbids a Tenant to Do
bodyText:
Kentucky has no single statute listing what a residential tenant may not do, but several rules reach it. In every Kentucky locality, a tenant who intentionally or wantonly damages residential rental property commits criminal mischief (KRS 512.010(5), (7)). It is a Class D felony if the loss is $500 or more (KRS 512.020(1)(a)3., (2)) and a Class A misdemeanor if it is less (KRS 512.030(1)(b), (2)). Lower penalties apply if the tenant repairs the damage, pays full restitution or does community service before trial (KRS 512.020(2)(b)-(c); KRS 512.030(2)(b)). A criminal case is for the police and prosecutor; your own claim for the damage is separate.

A tenant for life or years who commits waste without special written permission loses the thing wasted and pays treble damages (KRS 381.350). An eviction case does not bar a separate suit for waste (KRS 383.280), and the court may restrain waste while the case is pending (KRS 383.275). A tenant with a term of less than two years who assigns or transfers it without your written consent forfeits it (KRS 383.180(2); "No Subletting or Assignment" clause).

Where your city or county has adopted Kentucky's Uniform Residential Landlord and Tenant Act ("Where Kentucky's Landlord-Tenant Act Applies"), the tenant also must not deliberately or negligently damage or remove any part of the premises, or knowingly let anyone else do so. The tenant must not disturb the neighbors' peaceful enjoyment either (KRS 383.605(6)-(7); "Tenant's Duties Under the Act"). The tenant may not unreasonably refuse your entry for the purposes the Act lists (KRS 383.615(1); "Landlord's Right of Entry" clause). Unless you agree otherwise, the unit may be used only as a dwelling (KRS 383.620; "Unlawful Use Does Not Void a Kentucky Lease").

For a material breach, your written notice can end the lease on a date at least 14 days after the tenant receives it, unless the tenant cures within 15 days (KRS 383.660(1)). For a willful breach you may recover actual damages and reasonable attorney's fees (KRS 383.660(3)). Where the Act has not been adopted, the lease and the statewide rules above govern. The library's optional "Prohibited Acts by Tenant" clause puts the damage, peaceful-enjoyment and entry duties in the lease in both tiers.

title: Promises to Repair or Improve
bodyText: No Kentucky statute requires a promise to clean, repair or improve a rental to be in writing, to carry a completion date, or to be made before the lease is signed. The Kentucky Revised Statutes, the Kentucky Constitution, the 2025 and 2026 Acts and the state regulations on building and fire safety, public health, utilities, environment and human rights and those of the Attorney General and the Real Estate Commission contain no such rule. The general statute of frauds does require a signed writing to sue on a lease for longer than one year or an agreement not to be performed within one year (KRS 371.010(6)-(7); "Written Leases and Long Terms"); whether it reaches a spoken repair promise is case law. A promise you do make still binds you. Where your city or county has adopted Kentucky's Uniform Residential Landlord and Tenant Act ("Where Kentucky's Landlord-Tenant Act Applies"), the lease includes all agreements, written or oral, about use and occupancy, so a spoken repair promise can be part of it (KRS 383.545(11)). A material breach of the lease lets the tenant give written notice ending it on a date at least 30 days after you receive the notice, unless you remedy the breach within 14 days, and any breach supports damages or an injunction (KRS 383.625(1)-(2)). The tenant must not unreasonably refuse you entry to make agreed repairs (KRS 383.615(1)). Where the Act has not been adopted, a repair promise is an ordinary contract term, and how a court enforces it is case law. In every locality, Kentucky's consumer protection law makes false, misleading or deceptive acts in trade or commerce unlawful, and trade or commerce includes real property (KRS 367.110(2), 367.170(1)). Its private damages action covers goods or services leased for household purposes, and the statutes do not say whether a home lease counts (KRS 367.220(1); "Consumer Protection Act and Leases"). A licensed real estate broker or property manager who makes false promises likely to influence or induce can be sanctioned by the Real Estate Commission (KRS 324.160(4)(c)). Good practice: write any promised work and its target date into the lease or a signed addendum, and record the move-in condition ("Condition of the Property at Move-In" clause).

title: No Proposition 65-Style Chemical Warning
bodyText: Kentucky has no law like California's Proposition 65. No Kentucky statute or regulation requires you to warn tenants about exposure to chemicals known to cause cancer, birth defects or reproductive harm, or to post such a warning at a rental property. The Kentucky Revised Statutes, the Kentucky Constitution, the 2025 and 2026 Acts and the state regulations on building and fire safety, public health, utilities, environment and human rights and those of the Attorney General and the Real Estate Commission contain no such rule. The chemical warnings Kentucky does require are tied to particular businesses or work: alcohol-and-pregnancy posters for alcohol retailers and physicians (KRS 243.895, 311.378), tanning facility statements (KRS 217.924), and warning signs at asbestos abatement work areas (401 KAR 58:040). The hazard-specific rules that do reach rentals are the federal lead-based paint disclosure and methamphetamine contamination ("Contamination Disclosures"); see also "Asbestos in Rental Buildings". Do not copy a California Proposition 65 warning into a Kentucky lease; it would describe a law that does not apply here.

title: No Property Tax Rent Statement
bodyText: No Kentucky statute or regulation requires you to tell a tenant what part of the rent pays property taxes, whether yearly, on request or when the rent changes. None requires you to certify rent paid for a tenant's tax credit, and Kentucky statutes contain no renter's property tax credit. The Kentucky Revised Statutes, the Kentucky Constitution, the 2025 and 2026 Acts and the state regulations on building and fire safety, public health, utilities, environment and human rights and those of the Attorney General and the Real Estate Commission contain no such rule. This holds in every locality, whether or not the Uniform Residential Landlord and Tenant Act has been adopted. If your lease passes tax increases to the tenant, show the bill and the calculation ("Passing On Property Tax Increases"). For taxes charged on rent itself, see "Taxes on Rent".

title: Unlawful Use Does Not Void a Kentucky Lease
bodyText:
No Kentucky statute voids or ends a residential lease because the tenant uses the home for an unlawful purpose, or for a purpose other than the one it was rented for, in either tier. Where your city or county has adopted Kentucky's Uniform Residential Landlord and Tenant Act ("Where Kentucky's Landlord-Tenant Act Applies"), the tenant must occupy the unit only as a dwelling unless you agree otherwise (KRS 383.620). Another use is a breach you enforce with the Act's written notice to cure or end the lease (KRS 383.660(1); "Default by Tenant" clause). Where the Act has not been adopted, no statute limits the use; the lease's own use clause governs. The shared "Residential Use Only" clause, tagged for Kentucky, states the limit.

"Home-Based Business (Landlord's Permission)" clause lets you allow a home business ("Home Businesses in a Rental"). Some unlawful uses affect the property itself rather than the lease. A court can close a house of prostitution for a year, but not against an owner who, with the owner's agent, tried in good faith to prevent the use (KRS 233.020, 233.090, 233.100(1); "Nuisance Laws"). An alcohol nuisance can bar use of the premises for six months (KRS 242.350(2)). Real property used to commit or facilitate a drug offense, other than certain misdemeanors, can be forfeited. An owner's interest is forfeited only for acts or omissions done with the owner's knowledge or consent (KRS 218A.410(1)(k); "No Fast-Track Eviction for Crime").

So act promptly when you learn of illegal use ("Prohibited Acts by Tenant" clause, "Criminal Activity" clause). The Kentucky Revised Statutes, the Kentucky Constitution, the 2025 and 2026 Acts and the state regulations on building and fire safety, public health, utilities, environment and human rights and those of the Attorney General and the Real Estate Commission contain no lease-voiding statute.

title: No Recycling Notice Requirement
bodyText: No Kentucky statute or regulation requires you to tell tenants where or how to recycle, or to provide recycling service at a rental, in either tier. The Kentucky Revised Statutes, the Kentucky Constitution, the 2025 and 2026 Acts and the state regulations on building and fire safety, public health, utilities, environment and human rights and those of the Attorney General and the Real Estate Commission contain none. Collection is a county duty instead. Each county must run a universal collection program for municipal solid waste, by door-to-door collection, staffed convenience centers or another approved option (KRS 224.43-315(1)). Anyone providing collection service, including collection for recycling, must register each year with the county (KRS 224.43-315(2)). So recycling rules for your property come from the county or city program and its hauler. For trash, one state rule reaches apartment owners. A local board of health must require the owner of a building with two or more apartment units, where a refuse area is designated, to provide waste receptacles the board approves (KRS 212.210(4); "Local Health Department Rules for Rentals"). Where your city or county has adopted Kentucky's Uniform Residential Landlord and Tenant Act ("Where Kentucky's Landlord-Tenant Act Applies"), the tenant must dispose of ashes, garbage, rubbish and other waste from the unit in a clean and safe manner (KRS 383.605(3)). A sorting or recycling rule binds the tenant there only on the Act's conditions for rules ("Adopting or Changing House Rules"). Where the Act has not been adopted, the lease and your house rules govern. If you want tenants to sort recycling, say so in the lease or the rules ("Tenant Maintenance & Cleanliness" clause).

title: No Right to Pay and Stop an Eviction
bodyText: Kentucky gives a tenant no statutory right to pay the rent owed and stop an eviction once the lease has ended, a forcible detainer case has been filed, or a judgment has been entered. The Kentucky Revised Statutes, the Kentucky Constitution, the 2025 and 2026 Acts and the state regulations on building and fire safety, public health, utilities, environment and human rights and those of the Attorney General and the Real Estate Commission contain no such right. Where your city or county has adopted Kentucky's Uniform Residential Landlord and Tenant Act ("Where Kentucky's Landlord-Tenant Act Applies"), the tenant's chance to pay comes before termination. After your written nonpayment notice the tenant has seven days to pay, and only if the rent is still unpaid may you terminate (KRS 383.660(2); "Notice for Unpaid Rent"). If you then accept rent knowing of the default, you waive the right to terminate for that breach, unless you and the tenant agree otherwise after the breach (KRS 383.675; "Rent Cannot Be Collected Free of the Repair Duty"). In a nonpayment case, if the tenant's counterclaim leaves no rent due, judgment is entered for the tenant (KRS 383.645(1)). Where the Act has not been adopted, no statute gives a period to pay; the lease controls, and "Default by Tenant" clause gives the seven days in every locality. After judgment, in every locality, the court orders the tenant to vacate within seven days, and either side may appeal within seven days (AOC-217, Rev. 4-23). A tenant who appeals must deposit the rent owed since the case began and each month's rent as it comes due, and the case is then stayed (KRS 383.255). The deposit pauses the case; it does not end it. If no appeal is filed by the seventh day, the court issues the warrant on request (KRS 383.245). You may agree to let the tenant pay and stay, and the court's settlement form has a pay-or-vacate option (AOC-218, Rev. 3-12). See "The Eviction (Forcible Detainer) Process" and "No Statutory Relief From Lease Forfeiture".

title: No Religious or Cultural Display Right
bodyText: No Kentucky statute gives a tenant a right to display religious or cultural items, such as an item on the door or doorframe, despite the lease. The Kentucky Revised Statutes, the Kentucky Constitution, the 2025 and 2026 Acts and the state regulations on building and fire safety, public health, utilities, environment and human rights and those of the Attorney General and the Real Estate Commission contain none. The one statewide display right that overrides a lease is for the United States flag: whatever the lease says, a tenant may display a U.S. flag no larger than two feet by three feet from the residence (KRS 2.042; "Displaying the U.S. Flag"). Kentucky's fair housing law bars discrimination because of religion in the terms, conditions or privileges of a rental (KRS 344.360(2); "Kentucky Fair Housing Classes"). So apply any display rule the same way to religious and other items. Otherwise display and attachment rules are for your lease ("No Alterations" clause).

title: No Bar on Demanding Rent and No Required Rent Demand
bodyText: Kentucky has no statute that bars you from demanding or collecting rent because a unit has code violations or has been cited, and none that requires a separate demand for rent before an eviction. The Kentucky Revised Statutes, the Kentucky Constitution, the 2025 and 2026 Acts and the state regulations on building and fire safety, public health, utilities, environment and human rights and those of the Attorney General and the Real Estate Commission contain no such rule. Where your city or county has adopted Kentucky's Uniform Residential Landlord and Tenant Act ("Where Kentucky's Landlord-Tenant Act Applies"), rent is payable without demand or notice at the agreed time and place (KRS 383.565(2)). To terminate for unpaid rent you must still give written notice of the nonpayment and that the lease will end if the rent is not paid within seven days (KRS 383.660(2); "Notice for Unpaid Rent"). The Act also sets when rent stops or is reduced. Rent abates until you deliver possession (KRS 383.630(1)). A tenant who moves to substitute housing because you willfully fail to supply an essential service is excused from rent for that period (KRS 383.640(1)(c); "Tenant Remedies for Repairs and Services"). After a casualty that ends the lease, rent is accounted for as of the casualty date (KRS 383.650(2)). In a nonpayment case the tenant may counterclaim, the court may order rent paid into court, and if no rent remains due the tenant wins possession (KRS 383.645(1); "Counterclaims and Rent Paid Into Court"). Where the Act has not been adopted, no statute says when rent is due or requires a demand, so state the due date in the lease and that rent is due without demand ("Rent Payment" clause). In every locality, a tenant owes no rent for the rest of the term of a building destroyed by fire or other casualty without the tenant's fault or neglect, unless the lease says otherwise (KRS 383.170); where the Act is adopted, its casualty rule also applies, and a lease cannot take away the tenant's rights under it (KRS 383.650, 383.570(1)(a)). In every locality the forcible detainer complaint states that you gave written notice to vacate (AOC-216, Rev. 4-23). For units posted as unfit, see "Unfit or Condemned Units".

title: Paying Rent in Installments
bodyText:
You may have the tenant pay the rent in installments if the lease says so. Where your city or county has adopted Kentucky's Uniform Residential Landlord and Tenant Act ("Where Kentucky's Landlord-Tenant Act Applies"), rent is payable at the time and place you and the tenant agree. Unless otherwise agreed, periodic rent is payable at the beginning of a term of one month or less, and otherwise in equal monthly installments at the beginning of each month, and rent is apportionable from day to day (KRS 383.565(2)).

If the lease has no definite term, the tenancy is week-to-week for a roomer who pays weekly rent, and month-to-month in all other cases (KRS 383.565(3)). So weekly installments to a roomer with no fixed term may make the tenancy week-to-week, which either side can end on seven days' written notice (KRS 383.695(1)). An installment that is unpaid when due is unpaid rent, so the seven-day nonpayment notice applies to it (KRS 383.545(10), 383.660(2); "Notice for Unpaid Rent"). Where the Act has not been adopted, no statute says when rent is due or deals with installments, and the lease controls.

The Kentucky Revised Statutes, the Kentucky Constitution, the 2025 and 2026 Acts and the state regulations on building and fire safety, public health, utilities, environment and human rights and those of the Attorney General and the Real Estate Commission contain no rule on rent installments or partial payments of rent.

No statute says whether a scheduled installment is a partial payment of rent. The library's optional "Rent Paid in Installments" clause sets the schedule, says scheduled installments are not partial payments, and ties any late charge to "Late Fee" clause. See also "Rent Payment" clause, and "Deposit Installments and Alternatives" for deposits.

title: Rent Cannot Be Collected Free of the Repair Duty
bodyText: Where your city or county has adopted Kentucky's Uniform Residential Landlord and Tenant Act ("Where Kentucky's Landlord-Tenant Act Applies"), no lease, assignment, conveyance, trust deed or security instrument may let anyone collect the rent free of your maintenance duties: code compliance, repairs and fitness, common areas, facilities and appliances, and water and heat (KRS 383.575; KRS 383.595(1)). So a lease term, a sale of the rents or an assignment of rents to a lender cannot split the right to the rent from the repair duty; see "Landlord's Repair Duties" and "Habitability Duties Cannot Be Waived".
