A person authorized to sign leases for you who does not give the tenant the written names and addresses the Act requires becomes your agent for performing your duties, and must spend the rent it collects on them (KRS 383.585(3)). The Act has a second rule about taking rent. If you accept rent knowing of a default, or accept performance that varies from the lease, you waive your right to terminate for that breach, unless you and the tenant agree otherwise after the breach has occurred (KRS 383.675). A lease sentence signed in advance saying acceptance is not a waiver is not an agreement made after the breach; see "Accepting Rent After a Default". Where the Act has not been adopted, no statute ties the right to the rent to a repair duty or says when accepting rent waives a breach. The Kentucky Revised Statutes, the Kentucky Constitution, the 2025 and 2026 Acts and the state regulations on building and fire safety, public health, utilities, environment and human rights and those of the Attorney General and the Real Estate Commission contain no such rule. There the lease, local housing codes and case law govern. If you accept late or partial rent after a default and still mean to terminate, get the tenant's written agreement after the breach that acceptance is not a waiver.

title: No Right to End the Lease Because Repairs Cost Too Much
bodyText: No Kentucky statute lets you end a lease because a needed repair would cost too much compared with the rent or the value of the property. The Kentucky Revised Statutes, the Kentucky Constitution, the 2025 and 2026 Acts and the state regulations on building and fire safety, public health, utilities, environment and human rights and those of the Attorney General and the Real Estate Commission contain no such rule. Where your city or county has adopted Kentucky's Uniform Residential Landlord and Tenant Act ("Where Kentucky's Landlord-Tenant Act Applies"), your repair duty has no cost ceiling, and a lease cannot let you collect rent free of it (KRS 383.595(1), 383.575; "Habitability Duties Cannot Be Waived"). Cost matters in only two narrow ways there. If fire, casualty, the elements, an act of God or another cause damages the unit so that enjoyment of it is substantially impaired, you or the tenant may end the lease on 14 days' notice (KRS 383.650; "Fire or Casualty Damage" clause). And if meeting the building or housing code needs alteration, remodeling or demolition that would effectively deprive the tenant of use of the unit, you may sue for possession even after a recent code complaint (KRS 383.705(3)(c)). That suit does not release you from the tenant's claim for damages (KRS 383.705(4)). Where the Act has not been adopted, no statute gives you this right either. In every locality, a tenant owes no rent for the rest of the term for a building destroyed by fire or other casualty without the tenant's fault or neglect, unless the lease says otherwise (KRS 383.170); where the Act applies, a lease cannot take away the tenant's casualty rights (KRS 383.650, 383.570(1)(a)). Otherwise your ways out are the ordinary ones: the lease ends on its end date, a periodic tenancy ends on proper notice, or you and the tenant agree in writing to end it early. The library offers no repair-cost termination clause: where the Act applies such a clause would let you escape repairs you owe, which the Act does not allow. Where the Act has not been adopted no statute bars one, so if you want such a clause there, add your own after taking legal advice, since its enforceability is a question of case law.

title: No Small-Landlord Exemption From Repair Remedies
bodyText: Some states let a small landlord opt out of a tenant's rent-escrow or repair remedy by putting a set notice in the lease. Kentucky has no such exemption and no such notice, in either tier. Where your city or county has adopted Kentucky's Uniform Residential Landlord and Tenant Act ("Where Kentucky's Landlord-Tenant Act Applies"), the tenant's repair and essential-services remedies apply however many units you own (KRS 383.625, 383.635, 383.640; "Tenant Remedies for Repairs and Services", "Small Landlords"). Rent goes into court only when the court orders it in your nonpayment or rent action, after the tenant counterclaims (KRS 383.645(1); "What a Tenant Can Do When You Breach"). No statute lets you escape these remedies by a notice or by the number of units you own. Where the Act has not been adopted, no statute gives a tenant a rent-escrow or repair-and-deduct remedy, so there is nothing to be exempt from; the lease and the older statutes (KRS 383.010 to 383.302) govern ("Habitability Protections Kentucky Does Not Have"). The Kentucky Revised Statutes, the Kentucky Constitution, the 2025 and 2026 Acts and the state regulations on building and fire safety, public health, utilities, environment and human rights and those of the Attorney General and the Real Estate Commission contain no such exemption or notice. Don't put an escrow-exemption notice in a Kentucky lease; it describes a rule Kentucky does not have.

title: No State Rights Guide, but Give the Fair Housing Brochure
bodyText: No Kentucky statute or regulation requires you to give tenants a state-published guide to landlord and tenant rights and responsibilities, or to get a signed acknowledgment of one, in either tier. The Kentucky Revised Statutes, the Kentucky Constitution, the 2025 and 2026 Acts and the state regulations on building and fire safety, public health, utilities, environment and human rights and those of the Attorney General and the Real Estate Commission contain no such guide. The Uniform Residential Landlord and Tenant Act, where your city or county has adopted it ("Where Kentucky's Landlord-Tenant Act Applies"), sets no guide either, and no state tenant-rights summary goes with the lease ("Tenant Rights Statement"). One state fair housing handout does apply at rental. A person or entity engaged in real estate or real estate-related transactions must give owners and customers a copy of the Kentucky Commission on Human Rights' Fair Housing Brochure at the time of sale, purchase, rental, insuring or financing of real property (104 KAR 1:010, Section 4). It must also post the Commission's Fair Housing Poster where it regularly performs services, in an easily accessible, well-lighted place (104 KAR 1:010, Section 3). The regulation does not define who is engaged in such transactions. Kentucky's Civil Rights Act treats anyone who earns income, in whole or in part, from renting real estate as a real estate operator (KRS 344.010(8); "Kentucky Fair Housing Classes"). So the safe course is to give each new tenant the current brochure and post the poster at your rental office. The editions in force are dated August 2025 and are available from the Commission (104 KAR 1:010, Section 5). No local landlord-tenant ordinance may conflict with state law (KRS 383.198; "Local Landlord-Tenant Ordinances").

title: No Code Variance Notice
bodyText: No Kentucky statute or regulation requires you to tell tenants about a variance, waiver or exception from a health, housing or building code, or to attach one to the lease, in either tier. The Kentucky Revised Statutes, the Kentucky Constitution, the 2025 and 2026 Acts and the state regulations on building and fire safety, public health, utilities, environment and human rights and those of the Attorney General and the Real Estate Commission contain no such rule. Kentucky has no state sanitary or housing code for rental homes to vary ("Local Health Department Rules for Rentals"). The variances state law does provide are for building work, not for tenancies. In a neighborhood redevelopment zone, an owner whose rehabilitation plan for a residential building is disapproved may ask the Department of Housing, Buildings and Construction for a building code variance (KRS 99A.030(2)(a)). The department keeps a central file of those decisions and makes them available on request (KRS 99A.030(2)(c)). Septic system and zoning variances are granted by local boards and also need no tenant notice. Where your city or county has adopted Kentucky's Uniform Residential Landlord and Tenant Act ("Where Kentucky's Landlord-Tenant Act Applies"), a variance does not lower your duty to keep the unit fit and habitable (KRS 383.595(1)(b)). If a variance affects the unit, telling the tenant in writing is good practice, though no rule requires it. A local board of health may adopt regulations only if they do not conflict with the state health cabinet's (KRS 212.230(1)(c)), and no local landlord-tenant ordinance may conflict with state law (KRS 383.198).

title: Seasonal and Vacation Rentals
bodyText: Kentucky has no seasonal tenancy category: no rule that a summer, winter or vacation rental of a home ends by itself, skips the usual notices, or falls outside the landlord-tenant laws, in either tier. The Kentucky Revised Statutes, the Kentucky Constitution, the 2025 and 2026 Acts and the state regulations on building and fire safety, public health, utilities, environment and human rights and those of the Attorney General and the Real Estate Commission contain no such rule. What Kentucky has is a scope test. Where your city or county has adopted Kentucky's Uniform Residential Landlord and Tenant Act ("Where Kentucky's Landlord-Tenant Act Applies"), the Act does not govern transient occupancy in a hotel, motel or lodgings subject to the transient room tax (KRS 383.535(4)). The statewide room tax does not apply to accommodations supplied for a continuous period of 30 days or more (KRS 142.400(4); "Taxes on Rent"). The state hotel code does not treat apartments, single or multi-family homes or vacation rental cabins as hotels (902 KAR 7:010, Section 2). So a season-long rental of a house or apartment is best treated as an ordinary tenancy, with the full landlord duties. The Act also excludes a dwelling on land used to raise livestock, poultry, tobacco or other crops (KRS 383.535(7)), and an employee's occupancy that is conditional on work in and about the premises, on a farm or elsewhere (KRS 383.535(5); "Housing Provided to Employees"). Under the Act, you must supply reasonable heat between October 1 and May 1 unless an exception applies (KRS 383.595(1)(e)). State exact start and end dates. A fixed term ends on its last day without notice. Where the Act applies, a tenant who stays on without your consent may be sued for possession, with up to three months' rent or treble damages and attorney's fees for a willful holdover in bad faith (KRS 383.695(4)). Where it has not, a tenant holding over after a term of less than a year may be removed without demand or notice if you start proceedings within 30 days (KRS 383.160(2)); see "Holdover" clause. A lease signed long before the season starts may be an agreement not to be performed within one year, which must be in writing (KRS 371.010(7); "Written Leases and Long Terms").

title: Deposit Rights a Lease Cannot Waive
bodyText: Kentucky's deposit statute, KRS 383.580, has no non-waiver sentence of its own. Where your city or county has adopted Kentucky's Uniform Residential Landlord and Tenant Act ("Where Kentucky's Landlord-Tenant Act Applies"), the Act's general bar does the work. A lease may not have the tenant waive or forgo rights or remedies under the Act, and such a term is unenforceable (KRS 383.570(1)(a), (2)). The deposit rules are part of the Act: the separate account and its disclosure, the signed move-in and move-out damage lists, and the refund rules (KRS 383.580(1)-(7)). So a lease term giving up any of them is unenforceable there ("Security Deposit" clause; "Losing the Right to Keep a Deposit"). A court may also refuse to enforce a later settlement giving up a right under the Act if it was unconscionable when made (KRS 383.555(1)(b)). Where the Act has not been adopted, no landlord-tenant statute governs deposits, so there is no statutory deposit right for a lease to waive; your lease's own deposit terms govern ("Where to Keep the Security Deposit"). The Kentucky Revised Statutes, the Kentucky Constitution, the 2025 and 2026 Acts and the state regulations on building and fire safety, public health, utilities, environment and human rights and those of the Attorney General and the Real Estate Commission contain no other deposit statute. One regulation reaches every locality if a licensed real estate broker manages the property. The lease must then state the bank and account number of the broker's escrow or management account and contain a deposit-return provision in accord with KRS 383.580 (201 KAR 11:121, Section 10(2)(h)-(i)). That rule binds the broker; it does not say whether a tenant may waive it.

title: Deposit Standards and Broker-Managed Deposits
bodyText: No Kentucky statute requires you to post or disclose the standards you use to set deposit amounts, however many units you have, and none sets a formula or cap ("No Security Deposit Cap"). Whatever standards you use, Kentucky's fair housing law bars discriminating in the terms or conditions of a rental because of a protected class (KRS 344.360(2); "Kentucky Fair Housing Classes"). Applying one written standard to every applicant, and keeping the record, is good practice, not a statutory duty. Where your city or county has adopted Kentucky's Uniform Residential Landlord and Tenant Act ("Where Kentucky's Landlord-Tenant Act Applies"), prospective tenants must be told where the deposit account is and its account number (KRS 383.580(1); "Security Deposit" clause). If a licensed real estate broker manages your property, a Real Estate Commission regulation applies in every Kentucky locality, whether or not the Act has been adopted. The broker's written management agreement must state the amount of, or the method of determining, the minimum security deposit for each unit (201 KAR 11:121, Section 10(2)(g)). That standard goes in the agreement with the owner; the regulation does not require it in the lease. The agreement and the lease must both state the bank and account number of the broker's escrow or management account (201 KAR 11:121, Section 10(2)(h)). Both must also contain a deposit-return provision in accord with KRS 383.580 (201 KAR 11:121, Section 10(2)(i)), and deposit adjustments follow KRS 383.580 (201 KAR 11:121, Section 10(8)). A broker who also owns the property must comply with KRS 383.580 on receiving, depositing and adjusting deposits (201 KAR 11:121, Section 10(11)(b)). The library's deposit clauses ("Security Deposit" clause, "Return of Security Deposit" clause) follow KRS 383.580, so a broker can use them in every locality. Neither states the rule for a refund the tenant does not claim within 60 days (KRS 383.580(7); "Refunding the Security Deposit"), so a broker may want the lease to add it. The Kentucky Revised Statutes, the Kentucky Constitution, the 2025 and 2026 Acts and the state regulations on building and fire safety, public health, utilities, environment and human rights and those of the Attorney General and the Real Estate Commission contain no other rule on deposit standards.

title: No Work Card for Senior Housing Staff
bodyText: Kentucky has no work card, permit, registration or background-check rule for maintenance, office or other staff of rental housing, including housing for residents 55 or older, in either tier. The exception is licensing: a person who manages, leases or rents property for others for a fee must hold a real estate license, and license applicants undergo a national criminal history check (KRS 324.010, 324.020(2), 324.045(5)). A regular employee of the owner, or of the principal broker of a property management company, needs no license (KRS 324.030(5)(a)). Kentucky's fair housing law lets housing for older persons, as the federal Fair Housing Act defines it, limit residents by age without breaching the familial status rules (KRS 344.365(3); "Kentucky Fair Housing Classes"). That exemption says nothing about staff. Staff screening rules apply only to licensed care settings. A long-term care facility, a health care services agency staffing a nursing facility, or an assisted living community may not knowingly hire a person convicted of certain felonies for direct-care work (KRS 216.789(1)). It must also request each applicant's conviction information (KRS 216.789(3)). An apartment building that only restricts residents by age is none of these. Whether to screen staff who hold keys to units is your choice. The lease needs no term on it. The Kentucky Revised Statutes, the Kentucky Constitution, the 2025 and 2026 Acts and the state regulations on building and fire safety, public health, utilities, environment and human rights and those of the Attorney General and the Real Estate Commission contain no staff work-card or screening rule for age-restricted rental housing.

title: No Single-Family Lease Disclosure or Type-Size Rule
bodyText: No Kentucky statute or regulation requires a special notice or disclosure in the lease of a single-family home. None sets a type size, a relative font size or first-page placement for a residential lease disclosure, in either tier. The Kentucky Revised Statutes, the Kentucky Constitution, the 2025 and 2026 Acts and the state regulations on building and fire safety, public health, utilities, environment and human rights and those of the Attorney General and the Real Estate Commission contain no such rule. Kentucky also has no rule presuming that a tenant is not lawfully in possession unless the lease is notarized or signed by a licensed agent. Its quick removal procedure for unlawful occupants cannot be used against anyone who is or was a tenant, or who ever had a written or oral agreement with the owner to occupy (KRS 383.290(2)(a), (9); "Squatters and Unauthorized Occupants"). So a tenant under an unnotarized or oral lease must be removed through a forcible detainer case. Where your city or county has adopted Kentucky's Uniform Residential Landlord and Tenant Act ("Where Kentucky's Landlord-Tenant Act Applies"), a rental agreement includes oral as well as written agreements (KRS 383.545(11)). There, a single-family residence is a structure used as one dwelling unit, including a unit that shares walls with another if it has direct access to a street or thoroughfare and shares no heating, hot water or other essential facility or service (KRS 383.545(14)). Its tenant may agree in writing to take over the water, hot water and heat duties and specified repairs, in good faith (KRS 383.595(3); "Tenant Maintenance Agreement (Separate Document)" clause). Where it has not, no statute treats a single-family lease differently; the lease and the older statutes (KRS 383.010 to 383.302) govern. In Jefferson County, for new leases begun after June 27, 2025, an owner-occupancy rule limits leasing on some lots in traditional single-family zones (KRS 383.199(2); "Jefferson County: Leasing in Single-Family Zones"). It requires no lease text. The seller's disclosure form for single-family homes applies to sales, not leases (KRS 324.360(1)). A single-family dwelling needs a certificate of occupancy only where a local ordinance requires one ("No Certificate of Occupancy Disclosure").

title: No Shoreline Access Disclosure
bodyText: No Kentucky statute or regulation requires a lease to disclose shoreline, waterfront or public water access, in either tier. None requires you to tell a tenant what rights they have to use a lake, river or beach. The Kentucky Revised Statutes, the Kentucky Constitution, the 2025 and 2026 Acts and the state regulations on building and fire safety, public health, utilities, environment and human rights and those of the Attorney General and the Real Estate Commission contain none. Kentucky has no ocean coast; its lakes and rivers are governed by property law (your deed and any easements) and by the owners of the water. If the property has a dock, boat ramp or shared waterfront, describe in the lease only the access you actually control and the rules for it, and promise nothing over land or water you do not own. Where your city or county has adopted Kentucky's Uniform Residential Landlord and Tenant Act ("Where Kentucky's Landlord-Tenant Act Applies"), rules for common facilities bind the tenant only on the Act's conditions ("Adopting or Changing House Rules"); where it has not, the lease governs.

title: Shorter Notice for Showings
bodyText:
Where your city or county has adopted Kentucky's Uniform Residential Landlord and Tenant Act ("Where Kentucky's Landlord-Tenant Act Applies"), you must give the tenant at least two days' notice of your intent to enter, including to show the unit to prospective tenants or buyers, and may enter only at reasonable times (KRS 383.615(3)). The only exceptions are an emergency and a case where notice is impracticable. The tenant must not unreasonably refuse consent to a showing (KRS 383.615(1)). The section has no exception for an agreement to shorter notice, and a lease term by which the tenant waives a right under the Act is unenforceable (KRS 383.570(1)(a), (2)).

So a lease or addendum shortening the notice for showings does not work there, whether or not it is signed separately. The Act does not say whether a same-day invitation from the tenant for one particular visit excuses the notice; the cautious course is two days' notice for every showing. Repeated demands for entry that unreasonably harass the tenant let the tenant get an injunction or end the lease, with damages and attorney fees (KRS 383.700(2)). Where the Act has not been adopted, no statute sets an entry notice or a rule on waiving one, so there is no statutory notice to waive; the lease is your only source of an entry right and sets the notice ("Landlord's Right of Entry" clause).

The Kentucky Revised Statutes, the Kentucky Constitution, the 2025 and 2026 Acts and the state regulations on building and fire safety, public health, utilities, environment and human rights and those of the Attorney General and the Real Estate Commission contain no other entry-notice or waiver rule.

For those properties the library offers an optional clause allowing shorter notice for showings near the end of the tenancy ("Showings Near the End of the Lease (Only Where the URLTA Is Not in Effect)" clause); never use it where the Act applies.

title: No Smart Lock or Electronic Entry Law
bodyText: No Kentucky statute or regulation governs smart locks, keyless or app-based entry, or access codes in residential rentals, in either tier. None requires a physical key as a backup, limits the entry data such a system collects, or lets a domestic violence survivor make a device manager cut off another person's access. The Kentucky Revised Statutes, the Kentucky Constitution, the 2025 and 2026 Acts and the state regulations on building and fire safety, public health, utilities, environment and human rights and those of the Attorney General and the Real Estate Commission contain none. Kentucky's consumer data protection law (KRS 367.3611 to 367.3629, in effect from January 1, 2026) does not mention locks or entry systems. It applies only to a business that controls or processes personal data of at least 100,000 consumers in a year, or 25,000 if over half its gross revenue comes from selling personal data (KRS 367.3613(1)). Most landlords fall far below that; the lock maker or app provider may not. The general lock rules still apply ("Locks and Security Devices"). A tenant protected by a protective order may, after telling you and at the tenant's own expense, rekey the lock if it is in good working condition or replace it with a mechanism of equal or better quality, and must give you a key on request (KRS 383.300(4)(a); leases created or renewed on or after June 29, 2017; "Lock Changes by Protected Tenants"). Where your city or county has adopted Kentucky's Uniform Residential Landlord and Tenant Act ("Where Kentucky's Landlord-Tenant Act Applies"), entering with a code follows the same access rules as entering with a key ("Landlord's Right of Entry" clause). Where it has not, the lease governs entry. If you use a smart lock, say in the lease how codes are issued, changed and ended, and what data the system keeps.

title: No Smoke-Drift Rule, and No Smoke-Drift Waiver
bodyText: No Kentucky statute or regulation addresses smoke drifting between units, requires smoke-free rental housing, bans smoking in the common areas of an apartment building, or deals with a lease waiver of smoke-drift claims. The Kentucky Revised Statutes, the Kentucky Constitution, the 2025 and 2026 Acts and the state regulations on building and fire safety, public health, utilities, environment and human rights and those of the Attorney General and the Real Estate Commission contain no such rule. Kentucky has no statewide smoke-free workplace law that reaches a private apartment building; the state smoking-policy statute covers government buildings and workplaces and the Capitol (KRS 61.165, 61.167). A city or county ordinance may regulate smoking; check yours. Your tool is the lease: the shared Smoking Policy clause bars smoking anywhere on the property, and "Medical Cannabis in Rentals" explains the medical cannabis rules. Where your city or county has adopted Kentucky's Uniform Residential Landlord and Tenant Act ("Where Kentucky's Landlord-Tenant Act Applies"), a smoke-drift waiver does not work. A clause by which the tenant gives up claims against you over smoke from other units, or releases or limits your liability arising under law, is unenforceable (KRS 383.570(1)(a), (d), (2); "Liability Waivers"). Where the Act has not been adopted, no statute bars such a waiver, but whether a court would enforce one is case law. The library therefore offers no smoke-drift waiver; if you want one outside localities with the Act, take legal advice before adding your own.

title: No Benefit-Delay Defense
bodyText: Kentucky gives a tenant no special defense, continuance or reinstatement right when rent is late because a Social Security, public assistance or housing voucher payment was delayed. The Kentucky Revised Statutes, the Kentucky Constitution, the 2025 and 2026 Acts and the state regulations on building and fire safety, public health, utilities, environment and human rights and those of the Attorney General and the Real Estate Commission contain no such rule. The ordinary nonpayment rules apply. Where your city or county has adopted Kentucky's Uniform Residential Landlord and Tenant Act ("Where Kentucky's Landlord-Tenant Act Applies"), you may terminate only after written notice giving seven days to pay (KRS 383.660(2); "Notice for Unpaid Rent"). Where it has not, the lease and the forcible detainer statutes govern ("The Eviction (Forcible Detainer) Process"). Nothing stops you agreeing to wait for a delayed payment. The court's settlement form lets a tenant agree to pay a balance in installments, keep rent current or vacate (AOC-218). Where the Act applies, accepting rent knowing of a default waives termination for that default unless you agree otherwise after the breach ("Accepting Rent After a Default"). After a money judgment, what you can collect is limited. Public assistance cannot be assigned, is exempt from levy or execution, and the exemption cannot be waived (KRS 205.220(3)). Household furnishings, clothing and similar items up to $3,000 are exempt from execution and garnishment (KRS 427.010(1)). Federal law protects Social Security benefits from collection. If the tenant has a Housing Choice Voucher, the federal program rules and tenancy addendum also apply ("Federal Rules for a Housing Choice Voucher Lease").

title: No Special District Statement Required
bodyText: Kentucky has many special districts, which state law calls special purpose governmental entities. Examples are fire, water, sanitation, library and community improvement districts (KRS 65A.010(9) (effective until July 1, 2027)). No Kentucky statute requires a lease to say that the property is in a special district, or to have the tenant acknowledge district charges, rules or plans. This holds in either tier. The Kentucky Revised Statutes, the Kentucky Constitution, the 2025 and 2026 Acts and the state regulations on building and fire safety, public health, utilities, environment and human rights and those of the Attorney General and the Real Estate Commission contain no such statement or acknowledgment. The Uniform Residential Landlord and Tenant Act, where your city or county has adopted it ("Where Kentucky's Landlord-Tenant Act Applies"), says nothing about special districts. Where it has not, the older statutes (KRS 383.010 to 383.302) say nothing either. You may describe a district in the lease as information, but don't word it so that the tenant appears to take on a charge the law places on you. If you want the tenant to repay a local fee, the lease must say so; the library's optional "Local Government Fees" clause covers local registration and licensing fees and excludes fines and emergency response fees. Statewide, a special district may not bill you an emergency response fee for a response arising out of a residential tenant's or guest's actions, unless it resulted from your failure to keep the building to code (KRS 65.111(2)(a); "Passing Government Fines to Tenants").

title: Sprinkler Disclosures
bodyText: No Kentucky statute or regulation requires a private residential landlord to tell a tenant whether the building has sprinklers, in either tier. Kentucky's two sprinkler disclosure rules reach other housing. A college or university running on-campus housing must give a signed two-part disclosure, separate from the rental documents, in at least 14-point type, unless every facility has a working system (KRS 164.9492). A long-term care facility without sprinklers in every resident room must explain this before admission and get a signed acknowledgment (KRS 216.546). Neither reaches a private landlord. No Kentucky program offers grants, loans or tax credits to private owners for sprinkler retrofits. Insurers must, however, include a premium credit for buildings with automatic sprinklers in their filed rates (KRS 304.20-380). You may still tell tenants about a building's fire protection, and accurate information helps them; never describe a system the building does not have. For what the codes require of a sprinklered building, see "Fire Sprinklers in Rental Buildings" and "Kentucky's Fire Code". The Kentucky Revised Statutes, the Kentucky Constitution, the 2025 and 2026 Acts and the state regulations on building and fire safety, public health, utilities, environment and human rights and those of the Attorney General and the Real Estate Commission contain no sprinkler disclosure rule for private landlords.

title: Kentucky's Money Limits at a Glance
bodyText: Kentucky caps very few landlord charges. No statute caps, in any locality, the security or pet deposit ("No Security Deposit Cap"), late fees ("No Late Fee Cap"), application or screening fees ("Application Fees"), returned-payment fees ("Bounced Checks and Failed Payments"), pet rent ("Pet Deposits and Pet Rent") or rent increases. These limits do exist. In every locality, a tenant allowed an assistance animal may not be charged a pet fee, pet deposit or added rent for it (KRS 383.085(4)). Unpaid rent bears 6% interest a year from its due date (KRS 383.010(1)). A written contract rate on a principal of $15,000 or less may not exceed the lesser of 19% or 4% over the Federal Reserve discount rate on 90-day commercial paper (KRS 360.010(1)(a); "Interest on Unpaid Rent"). For the criminal bad-check rule, a check is made good with the face amount plus any posted handling fee of no more than $50 (KRS 514.040(4)(b)). Where your city or county has adopted Kentucky's Uniform Residential Landlord and Tenant Act ("Where Kentucky's Landlord-Tenant Act Applies"), a lease may not make the tenant pay your attorney's fees (KRS 383.570(1)(c); "Attorney Fees in Landlord-Tenant Cases"). Where it has not, a written agreement to pay reasonable attorney fees on default is enforceable only to the extent the fees are actually paid or agreed to be paid, and not for a salaried employee (KRS 411.195; "Attorney Fees (Only Where the URLTA Is Not in Effect)" clause). Four figures limit what tenants can recover from you. Where the Act applies, if you willfully and not in good faith fail to deliver possession, the tenant may recover up to three months' periodic rent or three times actual damages, whichever is greater, and attorney fees (KRS 383.630(2)). Where the Act applies, a tenant may repair a health-and-safety defect and deduct up to $100 or half the monthly rent, whichever is greater (KRS 383.635(1)). There, a tenant unlawfully removed, excluded or cut off from essential services may recover up to three months' periodic rent and a reasonable attorney's fee (KRS 383.655). In every locality, knowingly enforcing a lease term that penalizes calls for police or emergency help exposes you to punitive damages of up to two months' rent (KRS 383.302(2); leases created or renewed on or after June 29, 2017). The storage late-fee rule (KRS 359.215) covers self-service storage only, not homes. The Kentucky Revised Statutes, the Kentucky Constitution, the 2025 and 2026 Acts and the state regulations on building and fire safety, public health, utilities, environment and human rights and those of the Attorney General and the Real Estate Commission contain no other cap on residential landlord charges.

title: No Radiator Cover Requirement
bodyText: No Kentucky statute or regulation requires you to cover or guard steam radiators or heating pipes in a rental, or to give the tenant a radiator-cover notice or lease rider. The Kentucky Revised Statutes, the Kentucky Constitution, the 2025 and 2026 Acts and the state regulations on building and fire safety, public health, utilities, environment and human rights and those of the Attorney General and the Real Estate Commission contain no such rule. The only radiator rules found are for licensed care facilities, such as nursing, personal care and boarding homes, which are not residential leases. The Kentucky Building Code and Residential Code adopt the 2015 International Building Code and the 2015 International Residential Code by reference (815 KAR 7:120, 815 KAR 7:125). A guard rule in them is not ruled out; they govern construction, so check with your local building official (editions: "Which Code Editions Apply"). Where your city or county has adopted Kentucky's Uniform Residential Landlord and Tenant Act ("Where Kentucky's Landlord-Tenant Act Applies"), you must comply with building and housing codes materially affecting health and safety (KRS 383.595(1)(a)). You must also keep the heating facilities you supply in good and safe working order (KRS 383.595(1)(d)); see "Landlord's Repair Duties" and "Heat and Hot Water". Where it has not, the lease and local housing codes govern. In every locality, an owner must not let conditions exist on the premises that are dangerous to the health or safety of the occupants (KRS 65.8840(5)); local governments enforce that duty. A low-pressure steam heating boiler outside a private residence needs a state certificate of inspection every two years (KRS 236.060(3)(c), 236.110(1)(b)); see "Elevators, Boilers, Pools and Other Facilities". If a radiator in your building gets hot enough to burn, the cautious course is to cover or guard it.

title: Stoves and Refrigerators
bodyText:
No Kentucky statute or regulation requires you to supply a stove or refrigerator in a rental home, in either tier. Where your city or county has adopted Kentucky's Uniform Residential Landlord and Tenant Act ("Where Kentucky's Landlord-Tenant Act Applies"), you must keep in good and safe working order the appliances you supply or are required to supply (KRS 383.595(1)(d)). Your tenant must use them in a reasonable manner (KRS 383.605(5)). You may shift their repair to the tenant only by an agreement that meets KRS 383.595(3) or (4) ("Landlord's Repair Duties"). The Act also treats a tenant whose unit lacks its own stove or refrigerator as a roomer when those facilities are shared in a building where you live (KRS 383.545(12)). Where the Act has not been adopted, no statute governs; the lease decides whether you supply appliances and who repairs them.

In every locality, list the appliances you supply in the lease ("Appliances & Equipment Included" clause) and say who repairs them. The building codes define a one-family dwelling as having permanent provisions for cooking, but they do not require a particular appliance (815 KAR 7:120, Section 1; 815 KAR 7:125, Section 1). The plumbing code requires a kitchen type sink in an apartment unit in a Group R-2 or R-3 building (815 KAR 20:191, Section 3).

When you replace a refrigerator or freezer, do not leave the old one with its door on where children can reach it. An owner, lessee or manager who knowingly lets one stay there commits a misdemeanor (KRS 438.240). The Kentucky Revised Statutes, the Kentucky Constitution, the 2025 and 2026 Acts and the state regulations on building and fire safety, public health, utilities, environment and human rights and those of the Attorney General and the Real Estate Commission contain no duty to supply a stove or refrigerator.

title: Renting to Students
bodyText: No Kentucky statute governs a private landlord's lease to students: no rule on student leases, academic-year terms, parent guarantors or roommate changes, in either tier. The Kentucky Revised Statutes, the Kentucky Constitution, the 2025 and 2026 Acts and the state regulations on building and fire safety, public health, utilities, environment and human rights and those of the Attorney General and the Real Estate Commission contain no such rule. A student renting from you is an ordinary tenant. Kentucky's student-housing statutes bind colleges and universities. An institution that operates on-campus housing must give a potential lessee a separate signed disclosure of whether it has an automatic fire suppression system (KRS 164.9492). A college with a residential campus must give full-time students in its housing meningitis vaccination information in the housing application or lease (KRS 164.2867). Where your city or county has adopted Kentucky's Uniform Residential Landlord and Tenant Act ("Where Kentucky's Landlord-Tenant Act Applies"), it does not govern residence at an institution incidental to educational or similar services (KRS 383.535(1)). Nor does it govern a member's occupancy of the part of a building run for a fraternal or social organization (KRS 383.535(3)). A privately owned building that simply rents to students is covered. Where the Act has not been adopted, the older statutes (KRS 383.010 to 383.302) govern a student lease like any other. In every locality, the fair housing ban on sex discrimination does not apply to single-sex dormitory rental properties, or to rooms or units whose tenants share a bath or kitchen (KRS 344.362(1), (4)). It also does not apply to an owner-occupied rental of no more than 10 persons or units let only to men or only to women (KRS 344.362(3)); see "Kentucky Fair Housing Classes". Renting rooms with meals to three or more unrelated adults can make a home a boarding home that must register, but providing room or board to students needs no registration (KRS 216B.300(4), 216B.315). For several students on one lease, the library's "Joint & Several Liability" clause makes each responsible for the whole rent.

title: Housing Program Inspections
bodyText: No Kentucky statute or regulation addresses a housing program's inspection, either a landlord refusing a voucher because of it or a subsidized tenant refusing one. The Kentucky Revised Statutes, the Kentucky Constitution, the 2025 and 2026 Acts and the state regulations on building and fire safety, public health, utilities, environment and human rights and those of the Attorney General and the Real Estate Commission contain no such rule. State law does not make you join a voucher program, and no local government may require you to accept a tenant whose rent includes federal housing assistance (KRS 65.874; "Housing Vouchers and Source of Income"). Where your city or county has adopted Kentucky's Uniform Residential Landlord and Tenant Act ("Where Kentucky's Landlord-Tenant Act Applies"), a tenant may not unreasonably withhold consent to your entry to inspect, on at least two days' notice at reasonable times except in an emergency (KRS 383.615(1), (3)). If the tenant refuses lawful access, you may get a court order compelling access or terminate the lease, and recover actual damages and reasonable attorney's fees (KRS 383.700(1)). A program inspection you arrange is likely an inspection under that rule, but the statute does not say so. Where the Act has not been adopted, the lease's entry clause governs ("Landlord's Right of Entry" clause, "Inspection Rights" clause). The library offers no subsidized-housing eviction clause for inspection refusal. Follow the HAP contract and program rules on inspections ("Federal Rules for a Housing Choice Voucher Lease").

title: No Subsidy Rule for Rent Reductions
bodyText: No Kentucky statute or regulation says how a rent reduction for a defective unit is divided between the tenant and a housing subsidy, in either tier. The Kentucky Revised Statutes, the Kentucky Constitution, the 2025 and 2026 Acts and the state regulations on building and fire safety, public health, utilities, environment and human rights and those of the Attorney General and the Real Estate Commission contain no such rule. Where your city or county has adopted Kentucky's Uniform Residential Landlord and Tenant Act ("Where Kentucky's Landlord-Tenant Act Applies"), the tenant's remedies can stop or reduce rent. Rent abates until you deliver possession (KRS 383.630(1)). A tenant who moves to substitute housing because you willfully fail to supply an essential service is excused from rent for that period (KRS 383.640(1)(c)). Neither rule says whose share of the rent is affected; see "Tenant Remedies for Repairs and Services". Where the Act has not been adopted, no statute gives a rent reduction for defects; the lease and case law govern. If a housing agency pays part of the rent, the HAP contract and program rules govern the agency's payments when a unit fails program standards. Follow them ("Federal Rules for a Housing Choice Voucher Lease").

title: Late Fees When a Subsidy Pays Part of the Rent
bodyText: No Kentucky statute or regulation limits a late fee when a housing subsidy pays part of the rent, in either tier. The Kentucky Revised Statutes, the Kentucky Constitution, the 2025 and 2026 Acts and the state regulations on building and fire safety, public health, utilities, environment and human rights and those of the Attorney General and the Real Estate Commission contain no such rule. No Kentucky statute caps late fees at all ("Late Fee" clause, "Late Fees in Kentucky"). If a housing agency pays part of the rent under a federal program, its contract and program rules govern how late payments by the agency and by the tenant are handled. The cautious course is to charge any late fee only on the tenant's own share, and only as the HAP contract and program rules allow ("Federal Rules for a Housing Choice Voucher Lease"). Kentucky lets you decline voucher tenants; see "Housing Vouchers and Source of Income".

title: Passing On Property Tax Increases
bodyText:
No Kentucky statute regulates a lease term that passes property tax or insurance increases to the tenant, in either tier. None requires such a term to state the tenant's exact share or to refund a later abatement. The Kentucky Revised Statutes, the Kentucky Constitution, the 2025 and 2026 Acts and the state regulations on building and fire safety, public health, utilities, environment and human rights and those of the Attorney General and the Real Estate Commission contain no such rule.

Where your city or county has adopted Kentucky's Uniform Residential Landlord and Tenant Act ("Where Kentucky's Landlord-Tenant Act Applies"), you and the tenant may include terms the Act and other law do not prohibit, including rent (KRS 383.565(1)). A share of taxes the lease requires is rent unless the context requires otherwise (KRS 383.545(10); "Fees Count as Rent"), so the seven-day nonpayment notice applies to it (KRS 383.660(2)). Where the Act has not been adopted, the lease controls. A formula agreed at signing is not a change during the term; for raising rent mid-term see "Mid-Term Rent Increases".

The library's optional "Tax and Insurance Increases" clause states the tenant's percentage, requires the bill and the calculation, excludes your late-payment penalties and refunds a share of any reduction. Those terms keep the amount objective, which is the cautious course since penalty and certainty doctrines are case law.

title: When a Tenant Files for Bankruptcy
bodyText: Kentucky has no rule of its own on what happens to a tenancy or an eviction when a tenant files for bankruptcy. The Kentucky Revised Statutes, the Kentucky Constitution, the 2025 and 2026 Acts and the state regulations on building and fire safety, public health, utilities, environment and human rights and those of the Attorney General and the Real Estate Commission contain no such rule. Where your city or county has adopted Kentucky's Uniform Residential Landlord and Tenant Act ("Where Kentucky's Landlord-Tenant Act Applies"), the Act says general principles of law, including bankruptcy, supplement it unless it displaces them (KRS 383.510). Everywhere, federal bankruptcy law governs of its own force. A bankruptcy petition generally stays a court action against the tenant, enforcement of an earlier judgment, and any act to get possession of property of the bankruptcy estate (FEDERAL: 11 U.S.C. § 362(a)(1)-(3)). Two federal exceptions matter for evictions. If you got a judgment for possession before the tenant filed, the stay generally does not stop the eviction (FEDERAL: 11 U.S.C. § 362(b)(22)). But that exception waits 30 days if the tenant certifies that state law would let them cure the whole money default after the judgment, and deposits the next 30 days' rent with the bankruptcy court clerk (FEDERAL: 11 U.S.C. § 362(l)(1)). What Kentucky law adds: no Kentucky statute lets a tenant cure and keep the tenancy after a judgment for possession ("No Right to Pay and Stop an Eviction"). Whether a certification holds is for the bankruptcy court. An eviction based on the tenant endangering the property, or illegal drug use on it, may also proceed if you file and serve a sworn certification, unless the tenant objects within 15 days (FEDERAL: 11 U.S.C. § 362(b)(23), (m)). A willful violation of the stay can make you liable for actual damages, costs and attorneys' fees, and sometimes punitive damages (FEDERAL: 11 U.S.C. § 362(k)(1)). Treat a filing as a stop sign. When a tenant tells you they have filed, don't serve a notice, file, go to judgment, or ask for a warrant for possession until you get advice. Lease terms making bankruptcy itself a default, pre-filing rent and the deposit are federal questions. The library offers no bankruptcy-default clause.

title: Sharing Tenant Information
bodyText: No Kentucky statute generally bars a private landlord from sharing a tenant's or applicant's information, or sets a consent rule for it, in either tier. A few specific rules apply in every locality. If a tenant tells you in writing that they are in the Secretary of State's Safe at Home address confidentiality program, you must not knowingly disclose their name or home, work or school address (KRS 14.304(9)). You may do so if you also live, work or go to school at that address, or if the tenant consents in writing for that purpose (KRS 14.304(10)). The program serves victims of domestic violence, human trafficking, stalking, sexual assault, rape and other sexual crimes (KRS 14.302(2)). From January 1, 2027 it also serves prosecutors and certain other public attorneys (KRS 14.302 (effective January 1, 2027)). Victim information more generally is covered in "Victim Information". Kentucky's consumer data privacy law gives consumers rights to see, correct and delete their personal data and to opt out of its sale (KRS 367.3615(2)). It binds only businesses that handle the personal data of at least 100,000 Kentucky consumers a year, or 25,000 with most revenue from selling data (KRS 367.3613(1)). A landlord or manager that large must also give a privacy notice (KRS 367.3617(3)), and any contract term waiving those rights is void (KRS 367.3617(2)). A real estate licensee owes confidentiality to its own client or prospective client. To a tenant it does not represent, it owes good faith and fair dealing (201 KAR 11:121, Section 1(1)(d)-(f)). The state confirms a medical cannabis cardholder's status to a landlord only at the cardholder's request (KRS 218B.135(2)). Fair housing law limits what you may ask applicants ("Discriminatory Questions and Ads"). Breach notice and record disposal duties are in "Keeping Tenant Records". A lease or privacy policy may set your own limits on sharing. The Kentucky Revised Statutes, the Kentucky Constitution, the 2025 and 2026 Acts and the state regulations on building and fire safety, public health, utilities, environment and human rights and those of the Attorney General and the Real Estate Commission contain no general bar on a landlord sharing tenant information.

title: Housing Provided to Employees
bodyText: Where your city or county has adopted Kentucky's Uniform Residential Landlord and Tenant Act ("Where Kentucky's Landlord-Tenant Act Applies"), the Act does not govern occupancy by your employee whose right to occupy depends on employment in and about the premises (KRS 383.535(5)). A resident manager, maintenance worker or caretaker living on site is the usual example. Outside the Act, no Kentucky statute requires a signed disclosure of an employee's occupancy and move-out terms, a rental agreement offer when the job ends, or a set time to vacate, in either tier. No such rule appears in the Kentucky Revised Statutes, the Kentucky Constitution, the 2025 and 2026 Acts, or the state regulations on building and fire safety, public health, utilities, the environment and human rights or those of the Attorney General and the Real Estate Commission. One older statute ends a tenancy held under a contract to labor for the landlord at once, without demand or notice, if the tenant fails to begin or keep working without good cause (KRS 383.130). It sits among Kentucky's older farm-tenancy sections, so take legal advice before relying on it. Where the Act has not been adopted, an employee who holds the unit as a tenant at will may be owed one month's written notice to remove (KRS 383.195); whether an on-site employee is a tenant is case law, so give that notice. If an employee will not leave, recover possession through a forcible detainer case ("The Eviction (Forcible Detainer) Process"); do not lock the employee out. Write the housing terms down: whether the unit is part of the pay, and when the employee must leave if the job ends. If the employee also signs an ordinary lease that does not depend on the job, the exclusion may not apply and the usual rules govern.

title: Insurance Claims Between You and the Tenant
bodyText: No Kentucky statute lets a landlord claim on, see or control a tenant's renter's insurance, in either tier. None bars a landlord's insurer from suing a tenant after an accidental fire. Whether you may require renter's insurance is covered in "Renter's Insurance Requirements". Where your city or county has adopted Kentucky's Uniform Residential Landlord and Tenant Act ("Where Kentucky's Landlord-Tenant Act Applies"), a lease may not make the tenant excuse or limit your liability arising under law, or indemnify you for it (KRS 383.570(1)(d)). So a term in which the tenant waives claims against you for losses the tenant's insurance covers is unenforceable there (KRS 383.570(2); "Liability Waivers"). The Act's list of barred terms does not reach your own waiver of your insurer's claims against the tenant. Your repair duties stay yours. A lease there may not let you take rent free of the duty to keep the home fit (KRS 383.575; KRS 383.595(1)). So do not make repairs wait on the tenant's insurance ("Moving Repair and Maintenance Work to the Tenant"). Where the Act has not been adopted, no statute governs these terms. Whether a court enforces a waiver there is case law, so take legal advice before using one. In every locality, a tenant whose building is destroyed by fire without the tenant's fault or neglect owes no rent for the rest of the term, unless the lease says otherwise (KRS 383.170; "Fire or Casualty Damage" clause). Whether your insurer can recover from a tenant whose negligence caused a loss is also case law ("Damage Caused by Tenant" clause). The library offers no mutual waiver clause for Kentucky. No rule on claims involving tenant insurance appears in the Kentucky Revised Statutes, the Kentucky Constitution, the 2025 and 2026 Acts, or the state regulations on building and fire safety, public health, utilities, the environment and human rights or those of the Attorney General and the Real Estate Commission.

title: Tenant Portals
bodyText:
No Kentucky statute regulates tenant portals or bars you from requiring rent to be paid online, in either tier. Kentucky's Uniform Electronic Transactions Act lets records, signatures and notices be electronic (KRS 369.107). It applies only between parties who have each agreed to deal electronically, judged from the context and their conduct (KRS 369.105(2)). A tenant who agreed may still refuse to conduct later transactions electronically, and that right cannot be waived by agreement (KRS 369.105(3)).

So a lease term making the portal the only way to sign or receive documents cannot stop a tenant from opting out later. A notice the law requires in writing counts electronically only if the tenant can keep and print it (KRS 369.108(1), (3)). Where a statute requires a particular delivery method, that method must still be used (KRS 369.108(2)(b); "Delivering Notices"; "Notices That Must Be in Writing"). An electronic record is received when it enters a system the recipient designated or uses and can be retrieved there (KRS 369.115(2)).

Where your city or county has adopted Kentucky's Uniform Residential Landlord and Tenant Act ("Where Kentucky's Landlord-Tenant Act Applies"), a tenant receives a notice when it comes to the tenant's attention, is delivered in hand, or is sent by registered or certified mail (KRS 383.560(3)). So serve default and termination notices one of those ways, not only through the portal. Where the Act has not been adopted, the lease and the older statutes govern notice.

The library's optional "Online Tenant Portal" clause sets up a portal for payments, repair requests and notices. It keeps the lease's other notice methods and gives a fee-free way to pay when the portal is down. For payment methods generally, see "Acceptable Forms of Payment" clause. No tenant-portal or electronic rent payment rule appears in the Kentucky Revised Statutes, the Kentucky Constitution, the 2025 and 2026 Acts, or the state regulations on building and fire safety, public health, utilities, the environment and human rights or those of the Attorney General and the Real Estate Commission.

title: Keeping Tenant Records
bodyText: No Kentucky statute requires a landlord to keep a rent ledger, give a tenant a copy of one, or keep lease records for a set time, apart from the rules below. Fair housing records apply in every locality. An owner of housing covered by Kentucky's fair housing law, and not exempt from it, must keep records for two years (104 KAR 1:060, Section 4). They cover the race or national origin and familial status of each applicant and leaseholder, and your recruiting techniques. The regulation's title speaks of multiple dwelling developments, but that section's words reach any covered owner. So the cautious course is to keep these records ("Kentucky Fair Housing Classes"). You must ask for race or national origin on a separate form, may not require an answer, and must tell the applicant why it is asked (104 KAR 1:060, Section 3). If you own, or one manager operates, 25 or more units in Kentucky, you must also file an annual Multiple Dwelling Report with the Kentucky Commission on Human Rights by August 15 (104 KAR 1:060, Sections 1(1), 2(1)). A real estate broker who manages property must keep leases, owner and unit ledgers, owner statements and management bank statements for five years (201 KAR 11:121, Section 9(2)). The broker must give a receipt for money received (201 KAR 11:121, Section 10(6)). Where your city or county has adopted Kentucky's Uniform Residential Landlord and Tenant Act ("Where Kentucky's Landlord-Tenant Act Applies"), keep the signed move-in and move-out damage listings. The Act bars keeping any part of the deposit where it was not kept in a separate account and the listings were not provided; it joins the two failures with 'and' (KRS 383.580(4)), so to be safe meet both duties (KRS 383.580(1)-(3); "Losing the Right to Keep a Deposit"). Where the Act has not been adopted, no statute requires those listings. In every locality, data security rules apply. If computerized records holding a tenant's name with a Social Security number, driver's license number, or financial account number and its access code are taken without authorization, and the taking causes or you reasonably believe it has caused or will cause identity theft or fraud, you must notify affected Kentucky residents without unreasonable delay (KRS 365.732(1)-(2)). If more than 1,000 people need notice, tell the nationwide credit bureaus too (KRS 365.732(7)). When a business discards customer records it need not keep, it must shred, erase or otherwise make the personal information unreadable (KRS 365.725). Whether a tenant counts as a customer under that law is not settled, so follow it anyway; an injured customer may sue for damages (KRS 365.730(1)). Kentucky's consumer data privacy law, with its data security duty, reaches only businesses that handle personal data of at least 100,000 Kentucky consumers a year, or 25,000 with most revenue from selling data (KRS 367.3613(1); KRS 367.3617(1)(c)). That is so in the version in force since January 1, 2026 and the one effective July 1, 2027. Keep records at least as long as a claim on them could be brought ("Time Limits to Sue for Rent or Damage"). Limits on sharing tenant information are in "Sharing Tenant Information". No general rent-ledger or tenant-records duty appears in the Kentucky Revised Statutes, the Kentucky Constitution, the 2025 and 2026 Acts, or the state regulations on building and fire safety, public health, utilities, the environment and human rights or those of the Attorney General and the Real Estate Commission.

title: No Rent-Cap or Just-Cause Exemption Notice
bodyText: Some states give landlords an exemption from a rent cap, a just-cause eviction rule or a tenant's right to buy the property, and make the landlord claim it with a set notice in the lease. Kentucky has none of these rules, so there is no exemption to claim and no exemption notice to give, in any locality. Only the General Assembly may pass laws controlling rents on private property, and it has passed no rent cap apart from a short emergency price-gouging rule that has no exemption notice (KRS 367.374(1); KRS 65.875; "Local Landlord-Tenant Ordinances", "No Tenant Protection Act Notice"). No statute requires just cause to end a tenancy or gives a tenant a right to buy the property when you sell it. The Kentucky Revised Statutes, the Kentucky Constitution, the 2025 and 2026 Acts and the state regulations on building and fire safety, public health, utilities, environment and human rights and those of the Attorney General and the Real Estate Commission contain no such rule and no exemption notice. Don't put an exemption recital in a Kentucky lease; it describes a rule Kentucky does not have. Where your city or county has adopted Kentucky's Uniform Residential Landlord and Tenant Act ("Where Kentucky's Landlord-Tenant Act Applies"), the arrangements it excludes, such as hotel stays, job-tied employee housing and occupancy under a contract to buy, are excluded by what they are, not by a notice (KRS 383.535). Where it has not, no statute sets any exemption notice; the lease and the older statutes (KRS 383.010 to 383.302) govern. What governs instead is the rent and term you agree in the lease.

title: No Tenant Protection Act Notice
bodyText: Kentucky requires no lease notice of a rent cap, a just-cause eviction rule or a tenant right to buy, because it has none of those things. The Kentucky Revised Statutes, the Kentucky Constitution, the 2025 and 2026 Acts and the state regulations on building and fire safety, public health, utilities, environment and human rights and those of the Attorney General and the Real Estate Commission contain no such rule. There is no statewide rent cap or rent stabilization. Only the General Assembly may enact laws controlling rents on private property, so no city or county may adopt rent control (KRS 65.875; "Local Landlord-Tenant Ordinances"). The one exception is short-lived: during a declared emergency, once the Governor implements the price-gouging law by order, you may not rent housing in the declared area for a price grossly above the price before the declaration and unrelated to any increase in your costs (KRS 367.374(1)). Kentucky has no just-cause requirement for ending a tenancy and no rule that a notice state a cause ("No Just-Cause Eviction Rule", "No Good-Cause Eviction Notice"). It gives tenants no opportunity to purchase or right of first refusal when you sell, and no condominium-conversion notice ("Condominium Conversion", "Selling the Property or Changing Managers"). Where your city or county has adopted Kentucky's Uniform Residential Landlord and Tenant Act ("Where Kentucky's Landlord-Tenant Act Applies"), you may not raise rent to retaliate for protected complaints or tenant organizing ("Retaliation").

title: No Expiry Date on Kentucky Landlord-Tenant Law
bodyText: Some states' core tenant-protection laws are set to expire on a fixed date unless the legislature renews them. No Kentucky landlord-tenant statute is on such a clock, in either tier. Kentucky also has no rent cap or just-cause eviction law that could expire ("No Rent-Cap or Just-Cause Exemption Notice"). The Kentucky Revised Statutes, the Kentucky Constitution, the 2025 and 2026 Acts and the state regulations on building and fire safety, public health, utilities, environment and human rights and those of the Attorney General and the Real Estate Commission contain no landlord-tenant section with a sunset, expiry or dated repeal. Where your city or county has adopted Kentucky's Uniform Residential Landlord and Tenant Act ("Where Kentucky's Landlord-Tenant Act Applies"), the Act (KRS 383.505 to 383.715) runs without an end date. Where it has not, the older statutes (KRS 383.010 to 383.302) and the lease govern, also without an end date. Some Kentucky rules turn on a start date instead. For example, the ban on lease terms penalizing calls for police or emergency help applies to leases created or renewed on or after June 29, 2017 (KRS 383.302(3); "Calls for Police or Emergency Help"). Watch each new legislative session for changes, since the General Assembly can amend these laws at any time.

title: Trespass Warnings and Non-Tenants
bodyText:
Kentucky's criminal trespass law can help you keep out a person who is not your tenant, but it is never a way to remove a tenant or former tenant from possession. A person enters or remains unlawfully when not privileged or licensed to be there (KRS 511.090(1)). Knowingly entering or remaining unlawfully in a dwelling is first-degree criminal trespass, a Class A misdemeanor (KRS 511.060). Doing so in a building, or on premises fenced or otherwise enclosed against trespass, is second degree (KRS 511.070(1)(a)). Any other unlawful entry on premises is third degree (KRS 511.080(1)). A repeat offense within three years is charged one class higher (KRS 511.070(3)(b), 511.080(2)(b), as amended effective July 15, 2026).

Each separately secured unit in a building counts as its own building (KRS 511.010(1)). Posting: purple paint marks of the size and spacing the statute sets count as notice against trespass for the second-degree offense (KRS 511.070(2)). A posted sign matters by statute only for unimproved, apparently unused land that is not fenced (KRS 511.090(4)). On property open to the public, such as a leasing office during business hours, a person is there lawfully unless they defy your order to leave, given to them personally (KRS 511.090(2)). A license to the public parts is no license to the private parts (KRS 511.090(3)). Neither trespass law nor the police-removal procedure is a way to put a tenant, a former tenant or anyone who once had an agreement to occupy out of possession; that procedure does not apply to them (KRS 383.290(9)).

Recover possession from them only through a forcible detainer case ("The Eviction (Forcible Detainer) Process"; "No Lockouts or Utility Shutoffs"). For a squatter who never had any agreement, you or your agent may ask a law enforcement officer to remove them, using the statutory petition. The officer may arrest for trespass (KRS 383.290(2), (4)(d), (9); "Squatters and Unauthorized Occupants").

No Kentucky statute says whether you may bar a tenant's invited guest from the unit or the common areas. No such rule appears in the Kentucky Revised Statutes, the Kentucky Constitution, the 2025 and 2026 Acts, or the state regulations on building and fire safety, public health, utilities, the environment and human rights or those of the Attorney General and the Real Estate Commission.

So don't promise that trespass law will keep a guest out. The optional barred-person clause ("No Admitting a Barred Person" clause) makes keeping a named person away the tenant's lease duty instead. Give any ban in writing, hand it to the person, and keep a copy.

title: No Truth-in-Renting Act
bodyText: Kentucky has no truth-in-renting act. No statute or regulation requires you to give tenants a state statement of their rights, or a notice in the lease that some terms may be void, in either tier. The Kentucky Revised Statutes, the Kentucky Constitution, the 2025 and 2026 Acts and the state regulations on building and fire safety, public health, utilities, environment and human rights and those of the Attorney General and the Real Estate Commission contain none. What Kentucky does have is a short list of lease terms the law voids, which you leave out rather than explain ("Lease Terms Kentucky Voids"). Where your city or county has adopted Kentucky's Uniform Residential Landlord and Tenant Act ("Where Kentucky's Landlord-Tenant Act Applies"), a rental agreement may not have the tenant waive rights under the Act, authorize a confession of judgment, agree to pay your attorney's fees, or excuse or limit your liability under law. Such a term is unenforceable (KRS 383.570(1)-(2)). Where it has not, no statute lists barred terms, but in every locality a pre-suit power of attorney to confess judgment is void (KRS 372.140(1)). Also in every locality, for leases created or renewed on or after June 29, 2017, you may not include a term letting you end the lease or penalize a tenant for calling the police or seeking emergency help (KRS 383.302(1), (3)). Knowingly enforcing such a term exposes you to actual damages, attorney's fees, costs and up to two months' rent in punitive damages (KRS 383.302(2)). No state tenant-rights summary goes with the lease ("Tenant Rights Statement"). The one state handout at rental is the fair housing brochure ("No State Rights Guide, but Give the Fair Housing Brochure"). No local landlord-tenant ordinance may conflict with state law (KRS 383.198). Where a city or county has adopted the Act, it may pass no other ordinance on the subjects the Act covers (KRS 383.500; "Local Landlord-Tenant Ordinances").

title: No Unbundled Parking Rule
bodyText: No Kentucky statute requires you to price or lease parking separately from rent, or gives a tenant a right to rent without parking, in either tier. None sets a statewide minimum amount of parking for rental buildings; any such rule would come from local zoning. So whether parking comes with the unit, costs extra or is not offered is for you and your lease ("Assigned Parking Space(s)" clause, "Parking" clause, "Parking & Vehicle Requirements" clause). Where your city or county has adopted Kentucky's Uniform Residential Landlord and Tenant Act ("Where Kentucky's Landlord-Tenant Act Applies"), a parking charge the lease requires counts as rent, because rent means all payments except the security deposit (KRS 383.545(10); "Fees Count as Rent"). Where the Act has not been adopted, the lease governs. If you charge for parking, the parking-lot statutes may matter. If you take possession of tenants' cars and keep their keys, you are liable as a bailee for hire, and a contract limiting that liability is void (KRS 189.710, 189.720; "Parking Rules and Towing Signs"). A lot that parks cars for hire and acts as their bailee must also post a contents sign (KRS 189.715). Renting a specific space by the month is exempt from the posted-hours and attendant rule (KRS 189.705). The Kentucky Revised Statutes, the Kentucky Constitution, the 2025 and 2026 Acts and the state regulations on building and fire safety, public health, utilities, environment and human rights and those of the Attorney General and the Real Estate Commission contain no unbundled-parking rule.

title: Leases From a Life Tenant or Other Limited Owner
bodyText: Kentucky has no civil-law usufruct. Its counterpart is the life estate, and one Kentucky statute speaks to a lease by a life tenant. If a tenant for life lets land for the year and dies after March 1, the lessee may hold the land until the following December 31, paying a reasonable rent from the death (KRS 383.190). No statute says what happens to any other lease when the life tenant dies, or how rent is divided with the remainder owner. No other rule appears in the Kentucky Revised Statutes, the Kentucky Constitution, the 2025 and 2026 Acts, or the state regulations on building and fire safety, public health, utilities, the environment and human rights or those of the Attorney General and the Real Estate Commission. A deed that tries to pass more than the grantor owns passes what the grantor can lawfully convey, and a life tenant who does so does not forfeit the life estate (KRS 381.150). Whether that rule governs a lease is case law. So the cautious reading is that a lease from a life tenant is secure only while the life estate lasts. A tenant for life or years who commits waste without special written permission loses the thing wasted and pays treble damages (KRS 381.350), and the remainder owner may sue (KRS 381.360). Other limited owners have their own lease powers. A guardian may lease a ward's real property only until the ward reaches majority, and for no longer than seven years without court approval (KRS 387.125(7)). A trustee may lease trust property for a period within or extending beyond the duration of the trust (KRS 386B.8-160(9)). If you hold only a life estate, tell the tenant in the lease that your interest ends at your death. If the term may outlast you, have the remainder owners sign the lease or a separate consent. If you rent from someone who may hold only a life estate, check the recorded deed. These rules apply in both tiers; neither the Uniform Residential Landlord and Tenant Act, where your city or county has adopted it ("Where Kentucky's Landlord-Tenant Act Applies"), nor the older statutes elsewhere add one. Lease length rules are in "Lease Length, Formalities and Spouses".

title: Utility Allowances and Overage Charges
bodyText:
No Kentucky statute caps a utility allowance, or what you may charge a tenant who uses more than the allowance, in either tier. No such cap for electricity, gas or sewer appears in the Kentucky Revised Statutes, the Kentucky Constitution, the 2025 and 2026 Acts, or the state regulations on building and fire safety, public health, utilities, the environment and human rights or those of the Attorney General and the Real Estate Commission. Water is different. Some properties bill tenants for water through their own submeters. Such a property escapes the public water system rules only if each tenant pays no more than a share of the actual water bill.

The share must follow the tenant's actual usage in proportion to the whole property's usage (401 KAR 8:020, Section 2). For electricity, each unit in a nontransient multi-unit residential building whose building permit was applied for after May 31, 1981 must have its own electric meter, with listed exceptions (807 KAR 5:046, Sections 2 and 3).

Where your city or county has adopted Kentucky's Uniform Residential Landlord and Tenant Act ("Where Kentucky's Landlord-Tenant Act Applies"), a utility overage the lease requires counts as rent unless the context requires otherwise (KRS 383.545(10); "Fees Count as Rent"). Where it has not, the lease decides whether the overage is rent. In every locality, never cut off a utility to collect an overage ("No Lockouts or Utility Shutoffs").

The library's optional "Utility Allowance with Tenant-Paid Overage" clause covers a landlord-paid utility billed to the property alone. A federal housing program's utility allowance is a different thing, set by the program; follow the HAP contract and program rules ("Federal Rules for a Housing Choice Voucher Lease"). See also "Submetering and Utility Charge-Backs" and "Splitting Shared Utilities".

title: Utility Deposits You Collect
bodyText: No Kentucky statute or regulation governs a utility deposit that a landlord collects from a tenant, or says when you must return it, in any locality, apart from the Real Estate Commission's rules for a licensed broker who manages the property. Kentucky's utility deposit rules bind the utility, not you. If a principal broker manages your property, money the broker receives, including such a deposit, must go into the broker's escrow or management account within three business days, be entered in the owner and unit ledgers, and be receipted (201 KAR 11:121, Section 10(4)-(6)). A regulated utility may require a deposit from its own customer, must give a receipt, pays interest and credits the deposit to the final bill (807 KAR 5:006, Section 8(1), (4), (6)). A utility may not require a deposit just because the customer is a tenant or renter (807 KAR 5:006, Section 8(1)(b)). If your tenant opens the account in the tenant's own name, the utility handles the deposit ("Utilities Paid by Tenant" clause). Where your city or county has adopted Kentucky's Uniform Residential Landlord and Tenant Act ("Where Kentucky's Landlord-Tenant Act Applies"), a security deposit is money securing you against damage beyond ordinary wear and tear (KRS 383.545(13)). Any other payment under the lease counts as rent there (KRS 383.545(10)), so a utility deposit you collect is probably not governed by the deposit statute. If you collect one, say in the lease what it secures, when it will be returned and to what address. In every locality, a deposit made to secure payment for services that the tenant never claims is presumed abandoned after three years (KRS 393.080(1); "Unclaimed Deposits"). The Kentucky Revised Statutes, the Kentucky Constitution, the 2025 and 2026 Acts and the state regulations on building and fire safety, public health, utilities, environment and human rights and those of the Attorney General and the Real Estate Commission contain no rule for a utility deposit held by a landlord.

title: Utility Disclosures to Tenants
bodyText: No Kentucky statute or regulation requires a utility disclosure attached to the lease, in either tier. None requires you to give a prospective tenant past utility bills or energy-use data for the unit. The bill-content rules bind regulated utilities, not landlords (807 KAR 5:006, Section 7). One duty does reach some landlords. If you bill tenants for water through your own submeters, the property escapes the public water system rules only on conditions, including the charge limit in "Utility Allowances and Overage Charges" (401 KAR 8:020, Section 2(1)-(2)). You must also pass on to your tenants any boil water or consumer advisory you receive, in the way the regulation sets for advisories (401 KAR 8:020, Sections 2(3) and 3(10)). And you must pass on the water system's public notices and consumer confidence reports in the next billing period (401 KAR 8:020, Section 2(4)). Where your city or county has adopted Kentucky's Uniform Residential Landlord and Tenant Act ("Where Kentucky's Landlord-Tenant Act Applies"), the lease may include any terms not barred by the Act or other law (KRS 383.565(1)); where it has not, the lease governs. In every locality, the clear course is to say in the lease which utilities you supply, which the tenant pays, and how any charge you pass on is worked out ("Utilities Paid by Tenant" clause, "Utilities Paid by Landlord" clause, "Splitting Shared Utilities", "Submetering and Utility Charge-Backs"). No required utility disclosure or bill-history rule for landlords appears in the Kentucky Revised Statutes, the Kentucky Constitution, the 2025 and 2026 Acts, or the state regulations on building and fire safety, public health, utilities, the environment and human rights or those of the Attorney General and the Real Estate Commission.

title: Notice to Landlords of a Tenant's Utility Shutoff
bodyText:
No Kentucky statute or Public Service Commission rule requires a utility to tell a landlord that a tenant's service is about to be cut off. None lets a tenant name the landlord, or anyone else, to receive copies of shutoff notices, and none sets a special notice for master-metered buildings. Under the Commission's rules the termination notice goes only to the customer, in writing and separate from a bill, mailed or delivered to the customer's last known address (807 KAR 5:006, Section 14(5)).

For nonpayment, an electric or gas utility gives the customer 10 days' written notice, and a water, sewer or telephone utility 5 days' notice (807 KAR 5:006, Section 15(1)(f)). So if the account is in your tenant's name, you will hear of a pending shutoff only with your tenant's consent and the utility's own practice. The library's optional "Authorization for Utility Notices to Landlord" clause has your tenant authorize you to be listed as a contact and sign any form a utility requires. It does not oblige any utility to notify you, and it does not make you liable for your tenant's utility bills.

Where your city or county has adopted Kentucky's Uniform Residential Landlord and Tenant Act ("Where Kentucky's Landlord-Tenant Act Applies"), the Act's list of barred lease terms does not reach a consent of this kind (KRS 383.570(1)). Where it has not, the lease governs. If the account is in your own name, the notices come to you ("When the Utility Account Is the Landlord's").

In every locality, never cut off service yourself ("No Right to Cut Off Submetered or Landlord-Billed Utilities").
