The Kentucky Revised Statutes, the Kentucky Constitution, the 2025 and 2026 Acts and the state regulations on building and fire safety, public health, utilities, environment and human rights and those of the Attorney General and the Real Estate Commission contain no rule giving a landlord or other third party notice of a tenant's pending disconnection.

title: No Right to Cut Off Submetered or Landlord-Billed Utilities
bodyText: No Kentucky statute or regulation gives a landlord who submeters or bills a utility a right to cut off the tenant's service for nonpayment. That is so in every locality. The Public Service Commission's refusal and termination rules, with their written notices and medical and winter protections, bind a regulated utility toward its own customer, not you (807 KAR 5:006, Sections 14 to 16). Electric submetering by a landlord should be rare: each dwelling unit in a nontransient multi-unit residential building whose building permit application was made after May 31, 1981 must have its own electric meter, with listed exceptions (807 KAR 5:046, Sections 2 and 3). Whether a landlord who resells electricity, gas or water by meter is itself a regulated utility turns on whether it serves the public for compensation (KRS 278.010(3)); that is a Commission question, so take advice before reselling. A landlord running a master-metered gas system for an apartment complex falls under the Commission's safety jurisdiction (KRS 278.495(2)(b)). Water billed through your own submeters is limited to each tenant's share of the actual water bill, but that rule says nothing about shutoffs (401 KAR 8:020, Section 2; "Utility Allowances and Overage Charges"). Where your city or county has adopted Kentucky's Uniform Residential Landlord and Tenant Act ("Where Kentucky's Landlord-Tenant Act Applies"), you may not take possession by willfully interrupting, or causing the interruption of, heat, electric, running water, hot water, gas or another essential service (KRS 383.690). A tenant whose services you willfully interrupt may recover possession or end the lease, and recover up to three months' periodic rent and a reasonable attorney's fee (KRS 383.655). If you willfully fail to supply an essential service the lease or the Act makes yours, the tenant may give written notice and buy the service and deduct its cost, recover damages, or move to substitute housing (KRS 383.640). Where the Act has not been adopted, no statute governs; the lease and the common law do. In every locality, treat an unpaid submetered or billed charge as a debt under the lease and collect it through notice and the courts, never by cutting off service ("No Lockouts or Utility Shutoffs"). No Kentucky statute deals with short planned shutoffs for repairs, and the Act's remedy for a willful interruption states no repair exception. The library therefore offers no clause permitting planned interruptions; if you want one, talk to a lawyer first, and keep any repair shutoff short, announced and promptly restored. See also "When the Utility Account Is the Landlord's", "Utility Disconnection Rules" and "Submetering and Utility Charge-Backs". No shutoff right or procedure for a landlord appears in the Kentucky Revised Statutes, the Kentucky Constitution, the 2025 and 2026 Acts, or the state regulations on building and fire safety, public health, utilities, the environment and human rights or those of the Attorney General and the Real Estate Commission.

title: Moving Utility Accounts into the Tenant's Name
bodyText:
No Kentucky statute or regulation sets a deadline for your tenant to move utility accounts into the tenant's name, in either tier. None lets you cut off a service left in your name because the tenant did not transfer it, and none lets a court order or a military deployment move an account. The Public Service Commission's rules govern the account itself. A customer who wants service ended or moved to another address must give the utility three working days' notice (807 KAR 5:006, Section 13(1)(a)). The customer is not charged for service after that period if the customer gives access to the meter (807 KAR 5:006, Section 13(1)(b)). A utility may not require a deposit just because the customer is a tenant or renter (807 KAR 5:006, Section 8(1)(b)).

A utility need not start new service for a person who still owes it for past service, except under the winter hardship rule (807 KAR 5:006, Section 15(1)(d)). So keep accounts you hold in your own name until the tenant's account starts, and close them only with notice to the utility. Where your city or county has adopted Kentucky's Uniform Residential Landlord and Tenant Act ("Where Kentucky's Landlord-Tenant Act Applies"), you may not take possession by interrupting, or causing the interruption of, an essential service (KRS 383.690).

If you willfully do so, the tenant may recover up to three months' periodic rent and a reasonable attorney's fee (KRS 383.655). Where it has not, no statute governs, but the safe course is the same: never cut off a service to force a transfer. The library's optional "Transfer of Utility Accounts" clause has the tenant transfer each tenant-paid account by a date you set and repay the provider's actual charge for any period the account stays in your name. See "Utilities Paid by Tenant" clause, "When the Utility Account Is the Landlord's" and "No Right to Cut Off Submetered or Landlord-Billed Utilities".

No transfer deadline or landlord cutoff rule appears in the Kentucky Revised Statutes, the Kentucky Constitution, the 2025 and 2026 Acts, or the state regulations on building and fire safety, public health, utilities, the environment and human rights or those of the Attorney General and the Real Estate Commission.

title: No Veteran Landlord Incentive
bodyText: Kentucky has no state program that pays landlords to rent to veterans, such as signing bonuses, damage funds or lease guarantees. The Kentucky Revised Statutes, the Kentucky Constitution, the 2025 and 2026 Acts and the state regulations on building and fire safety, public health, utilities, environment and human rights and those of the Attorney General and the Real Estate Commission contain no such program. Two state programs touch veterans' housing without paying landlords. The Kentucky Housing Corporation may make a grant to reduce the rent of a servicemember with Kentucky as home of record who is deployed on active duty outside the United States. The same applies to a National Guard or Reserve member on federal active duty. The family income must be at or below 200% of the state or area median (KRS 198A.040(28)). The Kentucky Homeless Veterans Program builds a statewide network of services leading to permanent housing (KRS 40.340(1)). This holds in every locality. For servicemembers' lease rights, see "Servicemembers".

title: No Window Guard Requirement
bodyText: No Kentucky statute or regulation requires you to install window guards or window opening control devices, to offer them to tenants with children, or to give a window-guard notice in the lease. The state regulations on building and fire safety, public health, utilities, environment and human rights and those of the Attorney General and the Real Estate Commission do not regulate security or burglar bars on windows by name either. The Kentucky Revised Statutes, the Kentucky Constitution, the 2025 and 2026 Acts and the state regulations on building and fire safety, public health, utilities, environment and human rights and those of the Attorney General and the Real Estate Commission contain no such rule. The building codes adopt the 2015 International Building Code and the 2015 International Residential Code by reference for construction (815 KAR 7:120, 815 KAR 7:125). Those model codes may set window and emergency escape opening rules; ask your local building official before adding or changing windows (editions: "Which Code Editions Apply"). In buildings other than one- and two-family dwellings, the state fire code treats objects placed or installed so as to interfere with exits or exit routes as a fire hazard that must be fixed (815 KAR 10:060, Section 3(4)). So bars that cannot be opened from inside may be ordered removed; see "Kentucky's Fire Code". Where your city or county has adopted Kentucky's Uniform Residential Landlord and Tenant Act ("Where Kentucky's Landlord-Tenant Act Applies"), you must comply with building and housing codes materially affecting health and safety and keep the premises fit and habitable (KRS 383.595(1)(a), (b)); see "Landlord's Repair Duties". Where it has not, the lease and local housing codes govern. In every locality, an owner must not let conditions exist that are dangerous to the occupants (KRS 65.8840(5)). Check your city or county ordinances. If you fit guards or bars, the cautious course is a type that a person inside can release quickly in a fire.

title: Notices That Must Be in Writing
bodyText:
Kentucky requires writing for particular notices, statute by statute. Where a statute says a notice must be written, put it in writing even if the lease allows less. Where your city or county has adopted Kentucky's Uniform Residential Landlord and Tenant Act ("Where Kentucky's Landlord-Tenant Act Applies"), these notices must be written. (1) Your 7-day notice for unpaid rent and your 14-day notice for other material breaches (KRS 383.660(1)-(2); "Cure Periods"). (2) Your 14-day notice asking the tenant to fix a health-and-safety breach before you fix it and bill the cost (KRS 383.665). (3) A notice by either side ending a week-to-week tenancy (7 days), a month-to-month tenancy (30 days before the rental date) or a tenancy that began when a written lease ended (10 days) (KRS 383.695(1)-(3)). (4) The tenant's notices about your breach, failure to deliver possession, repairs and essential services (KRS 383.625(1), 383.630(1)(a), 383.635(1), 383.640(1); "Tenant Remedies for Repairs and Services"). (5) Your disclosure of the manager and of the owner or agent for notices, at or before the start of the tenancy (KRS 383.585(1); "Manager and Owner Disclosure" clause). (6) The tenant's consent to a new rule that substantially changes the bargain (KRS 383.610(2)).

A lease there may not make the tenant waive rights or remedies under the Act (KRS 383.570(1)(a)), so a clause allowing oral notice instead is likely unenforceable. Where the Act has not been adopted, you end a tenancy at will or by sufferance with one month's written notice (KRS 383.195). In every locality, an assignment without your written consent by a tenant at will or by sufferance, or with a term under two years, is a forfeiture, and where the Act has not been adopted you may recover possession after 10 days' written notice to quit (KRS 383.180(2)); where it has, you may recover possession only as the Act permits, by its written notice for a breach (KRS 383.690, 383.660(1)).

Beyond these, no statute there requires a landlord-tenant notice to be in writing; the lease and the older statutes (KRS 383.010 to 383.302) govern. No other statute requiring written notice between a residential landlord and tenant appears in the Kentucky Revised Statutes, the Kentucky Constitution, the 2025 and 2026 Acts, or the state regulations on building and fire safety, public health, utilities, the environment and human rights or those of the Attorney General and the Real Estate Commission. Everywhere in Kentucky, a protected tenant may end the lease by written notice at least 30 days ahead, with a copy of the protective order and, if the order came before the lease, a safety concern arising after signing. This applies to leases created or renewed on or after June 29, 2017 (KRS 383.300(1)(a), (5); "Early Termination by Protected Tenants").

An owner renting out property posted as meth-contaminated must disclose that in writing to a potential tenant (KRS 224.1-410(10); "Methamphetamine Contamination Disclosure" clause). Deliver each written notice as "When a Notice Counts as Received" and "Delivering Notices" describe, and keep a copy.

title: Checks Marked 'Paid in Full'
bodyText: Kentucky follows the Uniform Commercial Code rule on checks marked 'paid in full' (KRS 355.3-311). If a tenant, or anyone else you have a claim against, gives you a check or other payment instrument for less than you claim, with a conspicuous statement, on the check or in a writing with it, that it is offered in full satisfaction of the claim, then cashing it settles your whole claim, the unpaid balance included. This applies only when the payment was offered in good faith and the amount was not yet fixed or was subject to a genuine (bona fide) dispute, so writing 'paid in full' on a short check for rent nobody disputes does not by itself settle the rent owed. Writing 'under protest' or 'without prejudice' when you endorse the check does not save the balance: the rule on reserving your rights does not apply to an accord and satisfaction (KRS 355.1-308(2)). There are two ways out. If you are an organization (for example an LLC) and, within a reasonable time before the check, sent the tenant a conspicuous statement that communications about disputed debts, including checks offered in full satisfaction, must go to a named person, office or place, the claim is not settled if the check or the writing with it was not received there. And whether or not you are an organization, the claim is not settled if you offer to repay the amount of the check within 90 days after it is paid; an organization that sent the statement just described cannot use this second way out. Neither way out works if you, or your agent responsible for the disputed debt, knew within a reasonable time before the check was collected that it was offered in full satisfaction. The cautious course: don't cash a check for less than you claim that is marked as payment in full of a disputed amount; return it, and if one is cashed by mistake, offer the money back within 90 days.

title: Duty of Good Faith
bodyText: Kentucky's Uniform Residential Landlord and Tenant Act imposes a duty of good faith: every duty under the act, and every act that must be done before using a right or remedy under it, carries an obligation of good faith in its performance or enforcement (KRS 383.550). The act applies only where the city, county or urban-county government has adopted it (KRS 383.500); elsewhere in Kentucky, the landlord-tenant statutes impose no general duty of good faith, and whether courts imply a covenant of good faith and fair dealing in a lease is case law, so act as if the duty applies. In practice: give notices, enter, handle the deposit, enforce lease terms and end a tenancy honestly and for the purpose the law or the lease gives you the right, not as a pretext.
